Nearly impossible? How Fairphone built the ethical, repairable Fairphone Gen 6+

Ars Technica Long form September 04, 2026

Fairphone’s CTO explains how and why the Dutch company builds a different kind of smartphone.

Smartphone longevity didn’t used to matter. In the past, before you could wear out or break a phone, there was always some shiny new thing to buy. Today, we expect our smartphones to go the distance, but they’ve also become less repairable and, in many cases, more fragile. Fairphone, a Dutch smartphone maker that has just entered the US market, thinks about phones differently.

The new $650 Fairphone Gen 6+ is designed both for longevity and easy repairability. There are trade-offs to this approach if you’re used to the standard glass and aluminum sandwiches filled with glue, gaskets, and teeny-tiny screws. But the drawbacks could be worth it for the right buyer. Fairphone CTO Chandler Hatton told Ars that Fairphone’s goal is to provide a compelling mobile experience while also enabling the user to “fully own” their device. At the end of the day, this is what a lot of people say they want in a smartphone.

These days, Google, Samsung, and Apple support phones with software updates for the better part of a decade, but will the hardware last that long? And what happens when it needs a repair? You may be out of luck or out a lot of money, but Fairphone prioritizes the self-repair experience.

“We’re doing something that was long thought to be nearly impossible,” said Hatton. “Which is delivering high-performing modular smartphones that can last for a very long time.”

Fairphone designs devices to be sustainable, focusing on avoiding conflict minerals, using recycled materials, and paying workers a living wage. Fairphone says it doesn’t want to sell you a bunch of phones, just one that you can keep using even if something breaks.

“Our goal is that every single person that purchases a Fairphone uses it for at least five years, and we track that as a KPI [Key Performance Indicator],” said Hatton.

The standard way to design a modern smartphone is to cram as much as you can into an aluminum and glass sandwich, with the expectation that it will be assembled once in a factory and never opened by the buyer. Devices rely on glue and awkwardly placed screws to accomplish this, making the internals a little like metal spaghetti.

The Gen 6+ is designed so that anyone can replace parts, reducing e-waste and potentially saving consumers a lot of money. If you’ve had, say, a Samsung Galaxy phone for a couple of years and need to replace the screen or USB port, the cost might be higher than just buying a new phone.

“There is an incentive in terms of planned obsolescence to replace your device,” said Hatton. “On the one hand, it’s a good way to keep selling devices, but that’s simply not the proposition that we have.”

That means designing the phone differently—it’s not just a matter of skipping the glue. Inside, the Fairphone Gen 6+ is clean and orderly. It starts with a pair of T5 Torx screws exposed on the back of the phone. After removing those, the back cover slides off. With the same driver, you can extract the battery, camera modules, USB-C port, display, and more. In all, the phone supports user replacement of 12 different parts with just that one (included) screwdriver. One drawback is that the modular approach makes the phone a millimeter or two thicker than most glued-together phones.

The battery stares you in the face once the back panel is opened. You’ll have to remove a few more screws to get it out, but quick swapping isn’t the goal here—this is about longevity.

“We know that after about three years, it will be wise to replace your battery with a new one,” said Hatton. “Batteries aren’t meant to last forever, but your phone on the whole can last a lot longer than a battery.”

While the Fairphone is designed to be disassembled, what about the long haul? The Fairphone 6+ is mostly plastic rather than metal like a Pixel or iPhone. The phone still manages to feel solid, though, thanks to its internal metal frame, and the company has worked to ensure the device doesn’t become progressively less sturdy as you tinker with it.

“When we’re in our product development cycle, we introduce tests that are specifically dedicated to disassembly and reassembly,” said Hatton. “So we’re looking in part at the robustness.”

Robots work the assembly line, but humans are less predictable. Hatton pointed to tests that examine, for example, what happens when someone over-tightens screws while servicing their device. Does it warp the casing? Damage any nearby components?

Hatton said it takes her 15 minutes to fully disassemble a Fairphone Gen 6+, but she did have a hand in designing it. That said, it shouldn’t take a novice much longer. After a couple of minutes perusing Fairphone’s documentation, I was able to take the phone apart and remove all of the user-serviceable components in about 20 minutes. Everything went back together without issue and still works perfectly, with no new gaps or wobble.

The process is pretty intuitive, with most of the parts held in with flat board-to-board cable connectors. Just pop them off with a spudger or your fingernail, and the component lifts right out. There are a good number of screws to remove to get all the way down to the metal frame and screen, but again, they all use the same T5 Torx bit.

Glass backs are common on smartphones because they’re good for radio performance, and they add significant rigidity to the design. But they’re also easy to crack and difficult to remove (they’re almost always glued in place). Naturally, the only glass on the Fairphone 6+ is covering the 6.31-inch 1116 x 2484 OLED display, which is fully replaceable. This is probably the most challenging component to swap, but even this isn’t too bad. The screen is held in place by a handful of screws and has a generously long ribbon cable attachment, making a swap much less frustrating than your typical smartphone.

The OLED is about what you would expect for this price range—the resolution is more than sufficient, and the colors are great. The brightness is good enough to be legible outdoors, but at a mere 1,300 nits peak brightness, it’s harder to see than the displays you get on phones like the Pixel or Galaxy S26 that are a few hundred more expensive. Good luck replacing those displays on your own if you get a crack, though.

Smartphones have become more powerful over the years, but their designs have also been streamlined. Headphone jacks and microSD card slots are now rare, and even the SIM card slot is quickly fading away. OEMs often cite the space constraints when dropping these features.

“There’s a reason that most phone manufacturers prefer slightly larger footprints—because you can fit more stuff in there,” Hatton said. “So yes, it is legitimate if phone manufacturers are saying, ‘Hey, we dropped this feature to save space inside the device.’”

The Fairphone retains some of these elements, but not because there’s a surplus of space, Hatton said. The Fairphone 6+ still has a microSD slot and physical SIM card because people want them. These features don’t come free, though. In addition to the space constraints, adding more components adds to the price and complicates supply chains. That’s another reason some OEMs have removed features.

The Fairphone Gen 6+ plays to picky smartphone and DIY enthusiasts, but there’s still no headphone jack. Hatton notes that the team hears from a small but vocal cadre about headphone jacks every time it starts planning a new device, but it hasn’t made sense to include one in recent phones.

“In terms of how to actually get [a headphone jack] into the device, it is quite difficult,” Hatton said. “It’s a relatively large hardware component, but it’s not just the component itself. It’s also where it needs to be. You know, you’re not going to put the headphone jack in the middle of the back of the phone. You also need to make sure it attaches to the right things on the inside, and because we’re Fairphone, you need to make sure it’s repairable. So when we look at that total picture, we assess the needs of our customers to fulfill some other wishes at the expense of the headphone jack.”

Looking at spec sheets side-by-side, the Fairphone also lacks something that many of today’s phones have: IP6X water resistance. An upshot of making non-repairable phones that are chock-full of glue is that they’re relatively easy to seal against water intrusion. With an IP6X rating, a phone can be fully submerged in water for up to 30 minutes, at least in theory.

The Fairphone Gen 6+ is only rated as IP55, which will protect it from splashes. That could be enough, though. “Our phones are designed for what people need on a day-to-day basis,” said Hatton. “How often is it that people would like to take their hardware underwater? I think the answer there is less often than some manufacturers would have you think.”

While it might be comforting to think you could drop your phone in a pool, that’s still risky. OEMs don’t warranty the water-resistance of their phones, and if you’ve made any repairs, it’s possible the sealing of that difficult-to-open device was compromised. Hatton notes that it wouldn’t be impossible to make a repairable phone that’s also IP6X, but you’d have to design around that in numerous ways.

“There are a number of things that you need to weigh against a higher IP rating,” Hatton said. “You can achieve it in a very small form factor with higher costs, or you can achieve it with a larger form factor—you could increase the Z dimension and perhaps also the other dimensions, and that way you could create all sorts of gaskets and other things. But we assess the whole landscape and say, ‘Hey, the customer doesn’t want a phone that’s a brick.’ They also don’t want a phone that’s incredibly expensive. So within those boundaries, what IP rating meets their needs?”

It’s a trade-off, but it’s one that many people would probably make in the name of repairability if given the choice.

The Fairphone Gen 6+ is similar to the Gen 6 that launched in Europe last year, but there are a few notable changes. The new phone has a slightly upgraded Snapdragon chip, and it has more memory than the last Fairphone at a time when AI has driven up costs considerably.

“We decided to increase the RAM to 12 gigabytes,” said Hatton. “This is something that I think is a little bit unique, given the current circumstances in the consumer electronics industry. But the reason that we did is that it really underscores the value proposition of longevity that we’d like our customers to enjoy when they purchase the Gen 6+.”

Google, meanwhile, is catching some well-deserved flak for regressing from 16GB to 12GB of RAM in its latest Pixel phones, which start at $900. Samsung is also sticking with 12GB of RAM in its $2,000 foldables. And all those phones devote a lot of memory to AI services that not everyone cares about. The Fairphone has the Gemini app installed like all Google-certified Android devices, but the company has yet to create any on-device AI services of its own. That’s on Fairphone’s radar, but the team is taking a measured approach.

“We have not immediately jumped onto the bandwagon of creating AI features without really understanding what the use scenario is and what the customer really wants,” said Hatton. “We see that people are quite interested in understanding how their data is used and having control over their data and privacy. That means that as we continue to use more AI in all sorts of different settings, we’ll continue to work on AI features for our devices that focus on these aspects that are important.”

Fairphone has been offering devices with generous support windows for years. The Fairphone 3, which launched in 2019, just reached end-of-life a few weeks ago. The Gen 6+ will be supported through 2033 with software updates and replacement parts.

Hatton says that multiple factors go into determining the length of support. The availability of hardware in the supply chain is part of it, but it becomes impossible to update devices once vendors like Qualcomm stop supporting the underlying firmware. Seven or eight years is the functional limit for any smartphone due to vendor support, so it’s impressive to see Fairphone in the same range as the likes of Google and Samsung. It really can’t do more than it’s already doing here.

At $650, the Fairphone feels like a good deal in 2026. Maybe a year or two ago, the device wouldn’t have seemed as competitive, but with price increases and RAM regressions becoming standard, Fairphone comes out looking much stronger with the Gen 6+. It has a solid mid-range Snapdragon chip, ample storage (with a microSD card slot), and 12GB of RAM, which is still flagship territory.

There’s also something to be said for knowing that your phone is repairable if something goes wrong, and when the time comes to replace the battery, you can do it yourself in a few minutes. Fairphone is committed to keeping all these parts in stock for the duration of the phone’s support window, which runs through 2033.

The Fairphone may not be everyone’s style, but I like the utilitarian vibe. My design complaints are fairly limited and minor: the volume buttons are too low, and the power button (with fingerprint sensor) is too hard to find by feel.

The modular design allows for a little fun in the form of accessory back panels. You can swap them just by removing the two external screws. There’s a finger loop back (below), a card holder, and a lanyard that works with any of the backs. Hatton notes that the accessories also invite users to open up the phone to see how easy it is, something Fairphone recommends people get familiar with even if they don’t have any accessories to swap—it’s like knowing where the spare tire is in your trunk.

The Fairphone Gen 6+ runs a minimally customized build of Android 16, so it’s a bit behind the latest and greatest. Thankfully, Google doesn’t limit as many features to the latest builds of Android anymore. It has almost no bundled software outside of the standard Google apps, which is nice to see, but if you’re hoping for a phone that’s crawling with snazzy software features, this is not it.

One of Fairphone’s few software customizations is called Moments, which you can toggle with the brightly colored side switch. Moments can help limit distractions by hiding most of your apps behind a minimalist UI. It’s just a full-screen app overlay rather than a completely custom home experience, though. If you don’t fancy the digital well-being approach to mobile tech, you can remap that switch. Using it as a flashlight toggle is nifty, for example.

The camera may be the biggest compromise if you switch from a Google or Samsung phone. The hardware is typical for the mid-range, with a 50 MP Sony 700C joined by a 13 MP OmniVision OV13B10. That third lens on the back is actually a window for a time-of-flight sensor that helps with focus. With ample light, both rear sensors produce good images, and the primary even does fine in some more challenging conditions.

Capture speeds are long, though, making it hard to get clear images of moving subjects. Colors look a bit flat, too, and autofocus speed seems on the slow side. There’s a 32 MP selfie camera, which looks a touch dimmer than most devices in this price range.

With support increasing for making electronics more repairable, other companies may need to start moving in Fairphone’s direction. In Europe, regulators are preparing to require removable batteries, and more US states are enacting right-to-repair laws. The Fairphone CTO stresses that other OEMs have what they need to make phones more repairable.

“We’re producing our phones on the same production lines as our competitors, and often with many of the same components,” said Hatton. “It’s actually quite a small industry when you’re in it, and there is very little room for one of our competitors to say it’s impossible when on the next production line over it is happening.”

The Fairphone Gen 6+ is available directly from Fairphone, as well as on Amazon. It’s unlocked and works on both AT&T and T-Mobile.

TCL is right to question Samsung’s use of the term “Mini LED”

Ars Technica Long form October 02, 2026

Can it be Mini LED without a FALD backlight?

What makes a display a Mini LED display?

It’s a question that sounds like it should have a simple answer. But it’s now at the center of a lawsuit between two of the biggest names in TVs, with TCL accusing its longtime competitor Samsung of falsely advertising budget LCD-LED TVs as Mini LED sets.

TCL may have a point. Samsung’s M-series TVs, which range from $300 for a 43-inch model to $2,300 for a 100-inch model, do raise some legitimate questions about what should qualify as Mini LED. More broadly, though, the dispute highlights a problem for shoppers: Without agreed-upon standards for what “Mini LED” actually means, manufacturers have plenty of room to define the technology for themselves.

In a lawsuit (PDF) filed in the US District Court for the Central District of California in late August, TCL accused Samsung of resorting to “fraud” to compete with TCL’s QM-series of Mini LED TVs. Samsung’s M70H, M80H, and M90H are “merely recycled… pre-existing, low-end, standard LED televisions, [which are Samsung’s entry-level] Crystal UHD line… re-labelled… as ‘Mini LED,’” TCL’s suit says.

“Samsung’s M Models contain none of the technological advancements associated with Mini LED technology, including [full array local dimming],” the complaint reads.

Samsung didn’t respond to questions I sent about specific claims in TCL’s lawsuit. Instead, a spokesperson shared a statement noting that it intends to vigorously defend against the lawsuit.

TCL argues that M-series TVs don’t have backlights capable of true full array local dimming, or FALD, the most advanced type of backlighting technology available in LCD-LED displays.

A FALD backlight uses dozens to thousands of small LEDs, or Mini LEDs, grouped into different zones, each with individually controllable brightness levels. This helps boost contrast, which is critical for image quality and essential for delivering quality HDR on an LCD-LED display.

According to a specification line titled “Micro Dimming” on the M-series TVs’ product pages, the devices use “Supreme Mini LED Dimming.” The spec sheets (PDF) available for download from those pages include a tiny footnote that clarifies: “Supreme Mini LED Dimming is Software-based (not full-array hardware-based) technology.”

Samsung also uses the term “Supreme Mini LED Dimming” on product pages for its Neo QLED TVs, which TCL accepts as true Mini LED TVs. The Neo QLED spec sheets don’t include the footnote, though.

Software-based dimming without individually addressable LED zones differs from the FALD technology described above. With software-based dimming, a TV typically analyzes each frame of a video, breaking it into different zones and determining each zone’s ideal brightness level. Using that information, the display modifies the frame’s brightness to boost perceived contrast. Critically, though, the display’s brightness level remains uniform across the panel, unlike in a display using a FALD backlight.

Software-based dimming was more common on TVs from the 2010s, such as TCL’s P6-series and LG’s UH8500-series. But even then, software-based dimming paled in comparison to FALD, as Reviewed noted in 2016.

Software-based dimming “will never be as effective as a well-designed, hardware-based local dimming solution, especially in scenes that are more susceptible to blooming artifacts,” Guillaume Chansin, associate director of displays and XR at Counterpoint Research, told me.

“However, the software plays an important role to get the most out of the hardware, with some brands able to achieve comparable image quality with fewer LEDs or dimming zones,” he said.

Because displays that support software-based dimming work differently from those that use a backlight with individually addressable LED zones, they’re not what people typically think of when describing “FALD.”

Eric Virey, principal displays analyst at Yole Intelligence, considers FALD a hardware feature first and foremost. It requires a “2D array of LEDs uniformly distributed across the entire area of the display,” along with a good algorithm to help reduce blooming, he said, adding, “To me, a ‘software-based’ Mini LED dimming just doesn’t make any sense if you don’t have that full, 2D-array of LEDs or Mini LEDs in the backlight.”

An LED display with FALD should have better contrast than an equally specced display without it. But experts I spoke with took things further, suggesting that a display shouldn’t be considered Mini LED if it doesn’t support FALD.

“I think that is broadly agreed across the industry that FALD is a key and mandatory feature in Mini LED backlights,” Virey told me via email.

Bob O’Brien, Counterpoint’s research director, also equates Mini LED with FALD.

“Mini LED was originally introduced as an improved FALD technology, with more dimming zones. So among those in the industry, it has always been assumed that a Mini LED TV has FALD capability,” he told me.

Even Samsung’s own website describing Mini LED suggests that local dimming is essential. “Mini LED is an advanced backlighting display technology that uses tiny LEDs, smaller than standard ones, for more precise backlight control through local dimming zones—a technique where backlight zones are controlled independently,” it says.

In its complaint against Samsung, TCL says it disassembled an M70H and M80H, both Samsung sets, and confirmed they can’t perform local dimming because they lack the necessary LED control chip and circuitry and use the same processor as Samsung’s entry-level Crystal TVs.

Although FALD support is key to TCL’s argument, a more obvious question might be whether M-series TVs use actual Mini LEDs. Again, though, there’s no industry-wide rule for what makes an LED “mini.”

I’ve seen Mini LEDs referred to in various size ranges over the years, including 50-300 µm (0.05-0.3 mm), 100-200 µm (0.1-0.2 mm), 100-300 µm, and “typically below 200 µm.”

TCL’s lawsuit claims that Mini LEDs “are generally .1 mm to .3 mm” and that the LEDs in Samsung’s M-series TVs are 0.5 mm. I’ve been unable to find a reputable source that refers to an LED as large as 0.5 mm as a Mini LED. I have even seen LEDs measuring more than 0.2 mm or 3 mm be considered a traditional LED in some cases.

TCL further alleges that M-series TVs have a few dozen LEDs, while some Mini LED displays have thousands. Those LEDs aren’t arranged in an array on a panel; instead, they’re “arranged on two aluminum strips,” the filing says.

A teardown video from YouTube channel AP Tech also shows an M-series TV’s backlight consisting of two rows of LEDs.

The industry hasn’t established standards for how many LED zones or Mini LEDs a display needs to qualify as Mini LED. That can leave shoppers confused about what they’re actually buying. It also creates a gray area where manufacturers can set their own standards.

“There are no organizations with authority to make and enforce such standards. TV brands have historically exploited the lack of clear standards to be more creative in their marketing,” O’Brien said.

“I think that [TCL’s] claims are legitimate and raise some important question[s] for the entire industry, which lacks a clear definition of what a Mini LED display is,” Virey told me.

The problem can be seen elsewhere in the display panel industry with technologies like QLED.

The industry could try to create standards, but Virey thinks it would lead to “an endless race.”

“Each time there are new technologies, new marketing terms are invented and can easily be abused,” he said.

While enthusiasts may delight in digging into the complex underpinnings of backlight technology, most people just care about performance. So how are Samsung’s M-series TVs?

There aren’t many reviews. RTINGS found that the M80H had “low” contrast (6,440:1, according to the review site’s testing) that makes “dark scenes look washed out in a dark room.” Regarding HDR performance, RTINGs said, “Content mastered at 600 or 1,000 nits, which is most HDR content, cuts off rapidly at the TV’s peak brightness. This lets the TV get as bright as it can, but there’s less gradation in bright parts of the scene, so highlights can seem to blend together.”

By comparison, Samsung’s $1,200 Mini LED Neo QLED QN80H, which uses individually addressable dimming zones, reached a contrast of 80,000:1 after calibration, according to RTINGs. That translated into visible improvements during actual use. RTINGs reported that the QN80H “looks good in a dark room thanks to its high contrast ratio and great black uniformity, making it a good choice for a home theater room.”

The AP Tech video below shows how an M-series TV and one with FALD handle dimming differently.

TCL’s budget QM6K ($550 MSRP as of this writing), meanwhile, reached a contrast ratio of 118:059:1 after RTINGs’ calibration. But even this set falters in areas where you might expect Mini LED to shine. Its HDR performance, for example, is reportedly lacking.

“Visually, the TV doesn’t impress, although its black levels are quite good due to its impressive contrast and good black uniformity. Unfortunately, there’s more haloing around bright highlights than you’d like, but it’s alright. Its HDR brightness is mediocre at best, so the TV doesn’t provide an impactful HDR experience overall,” RTING’s review says.

TCL has an obvious stake in challenging Samsung’s marketing. The companies are longtime rivals, and casting doubt on Samsung’s claims could help TCL sell more TVs. But the underlying question is still worth asking: What should consumers expect when a TV is marketed as Mini LED?

I’d argue that a TV with slightly smaller LEDs than average but without local dimming shouldn’t be considered Mini LED with local dimming. The important distinction isn’t simply the size of the LEDs; it’s how they’re used to deliver improved contrast and HDR performance.

But even that definition has limits, as small LEDs and local dimming zones aren’t enough to guarantee good performance. TCL’s own budget line of Mini LED TVs can disappoint in areas where the technology should have an advantage, such as HDR support. And compared with Samsung’s more expensive Mini LED TVs, the M-series has worse HDR performance and black levels and is harder to use in a dark room, according to RTINGs’ testing.

That leaves shoppers in an awkward position. Terms like “Mini LED” or “QLED” are now used liberally, but they don’t always tell you how a TV will perform. Manufacturers often fail to disclose basic details, like the size of the LEDs, the number of dimming zones, or accurate contrast and brightness measurements.

For shoppers, then, it’s important to remember that comparative pricing and independent testing are ultimately much more useful than a label on a box.

Pope diagnosed with lung cancer but had successful surgery, Vatican says

BBC News Tue, 13 Oct 2026 20:46:06 GMT

Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer but had successful surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung, the Vatican has said in a medical bulletin.

The 71-year-old underwent a 90 minute surgery on Tuesday at Rome's Gemelli Hospital and was subsequently diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.

"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room on the 10th floor," the Vatican said in a statement.

The lump was first detected during what the Vatican has described as "routine checks".

Earlier, large crowds gathered outside the hospital to greet the Pope, with some waiting for several hours.

They cheered greetings and well wishes as he passed, while he waved and smiled back through the lowered back window of his car.

He was then met by staff on the hospital steps. "I'm sorry," one of them commiserated, to which the Pope gave a smile and a shrug. "We're here for you," he was assured.

In its statement, the Vatican said the whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical".

A Vatican source told Agence France-Presse news agency further tests were being carried out to see if there was any sign the cancer had spread.

It was Leo XIV himself who on Sunday announced news of his operation to the world, speaking from the balcony in St Peter's Square after delivering the traditional Angelus blessing.

He said the nodule, or growth, on his lung was "contained" and had been found "at a very early stage", but that doctors had advised him to have it removed.

Gemelli's thoracic surgery team operated on the Pope, whose schedule has already been cleared until 20 October to give him time to recover.

Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was pulmonary adenocarcinoma, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said.

The Vatican has stressed that the pontiff, who is generally thought to be fit, had no symptoms of infection or illness.

Cardinal Kikuchi Tarcisio Isao of Tokyo wrote on social media that he'd had an audience with Pope Leo on Monday, and said the pontiff felt "nothing wrong" physically.

He said the Pope had decided to check in for surgery as soon as possible because he was due to travel to Latin America in early November, and was keen to stick to that plan.

The trip is particularly significant because it includes a visit to Peru, where the pontiff was a missionary and then a Bishop for many years.

Despite all the reassurances, the news has shaken Catholics all over the world.

"Am I worried? Yes, because I certainly wasn't expecting anything like this," Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Parolin told journalists on Tuesday.

He agreed that the news was like a "bolt from the blue", but said the cardinals had been struck by the Pope's "serenity" and were confident in his recovery.

Outside Gemelli Hospital, which has treated several popes and is home to a large statue of John Paul II, a few Catholics lingered after the pontiff was admitted.

Carla had come specially, wanting to be close.

"He seems calm, so we are calm too - even though illness is always unpleasant," she told the BBC. "We will wait here and pray."

"I was in St Peter's Square when he made the announcement, and I felt really awful," said Elsa, who was also present. "I was really taken aback," she said, explaining that when Pope Leo was elected she had thought he was a younger, healthier pontiff.

"It turns out he's vulnerable too," she added.

Missiles intercepted near Riyadh after Saudi coalition hits Yemen fuel depot

BBC News Tue, 13 Oct 2026 20:02:15 GMT

Missiles and drones have been intercepted over Riyadh after the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen struck a fuel depot near the Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa, its spokesperson says.

Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki said several projectiles targeting the Saudi capital and other cities were intercepted after the coalition carried out a strike on the Yemen Petroleum Company's al-Sabaha facility on Tuesday night.

The Houthis warned they would target the airport and Aramco refinery in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, and Aramco's headquarters in the eastern city of Dammam.

Al-Maliki later said missiles targeting cities including Dammam had been intercepted, while shrapnel had fallen in a residential area in Dhahran.

It came as the Saudi cabinet, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, said the Iran-backed group would "bear the consequences" of its recent deadly attacks on the kingdom.

Thirteen people were killed when a missile hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday, while another person was killed in a similar attack there the following day.

On Tuesday, the coalition said its forces had destroyed three drones north of Riyadh.

The Houthis have said they are targeting airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones in response to deadly Saudi strikes on territory that they control in western Yemen, including Sanaa.

The Saudi-led coalition has been providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces mounting an offensive on Yemen's Red Sea coast and several other front lines.

A correspondent for AFP news agency reported that queues formed at petrol stations in Sanaa on Tuesday afternoon following the coalition's warning of an impending operation against the al-Sabaha oil facility, with many residents worried about shortages.

The Yemen Petroleum Company, which is run by the Houthis, issued a statement that sought to reassure them, saying the facility "does not contain any stock of petroleum products".

The company also said it had "taken all necessary precautionary measures to address any emergency, ensuring the stability of the supply situation and the continued meeting of citizens' needs in a normal manner".

After al-Maliki confirmed the strike, first reported by Houthi media, explosions were heard over Riyadh and other Saudi cities, with al-Maliki reporting four missiles and two drones had been intercepted near the capital.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.

US President Donald Trump said on Truth Social on Tuesday the Houthis were "behaving very badly... and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices".

Speaking to reporters, he did not answer a question on whether he'd made a decision to help the Saudis retaliate against them, but said he "might" ask Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan to intervene.

Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes.

Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed in Yemen since August. The UN's human rights office says they include at least 54 civilians, half of them children.

More than 216,000 people have also been displaced across the country, and suspected cholera cases have tripled in three weeks, rising from 217 to 647, according to the UN.

Ex-gang boss sentenced to 40 years for orchestrating Tupac Shakur's murder

BBC News Tue, 13 Oct 2026 19:51:14 GMT

Former gang boss Duane "Keffe D" Davis has been sentenced to at least 40 years in prison for orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur.

A jury found Davis, 63, guilty in September of one count of murder with a deadly weapon for the rap superstar's death in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996. He has said he will appeal the verdict.

Prosecutors argued that although Davis did not fire the gun himself, he was the ringleader of the group that committed the murder. He admitted in his memoir that he had provided the gun used in the crime.

Davis' conviction was the first in a cold case that has intrigued hip-hop fans for nearly 30 years.

Prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo argued during Tuesday's sentencing hearing that Davis spent years "publicly grandstanding" and bragging about his role on Shakur's death, which he said, "had wide-ranging effects upon the world".

Shakur's sister, Sekyiwa Shakur, told the court: "The loss of Tupac, for a long time, crippled my family."

"He had so much promise, intentions for a better world," said adding that her brother had hoped to help his local community.

Sekyiwa Shakur asked the judge to give Davis the maximum sentence, telling Davis he will sit in prison and "contemplate what you've done to the world, not just to me".

Shakur's brother, Maurice Shakur, also addressed the court, asking the judge for "the longest possible sentence".

Davis was asked by Judge Carli Kierny if he had anything to say, to which he replied: "I'm good. I'm gonna appeal this case for sure."

Before handing down the sentence, Kierny told him: "You don't get to take a man from his family.

"You don't get to take his very life, his whole future from him, and just walk away from it. Especially when that man is Tupac Shakur. The world never forgot about him and his death."

The key evidence in the case were Davis' own words, in which he repeatedly and publicly acknowledged being inside the white Cadillac from where the deadly shots were fired.

In exchange for being shielded from criminal prosecution, he told authorities about his role in Shakur's death during a secret 2008 police interview relating to the death of fellow rapper Notorious B. I. G., real name Christopher Wallace, who was killed in a shooting just months after Shakur.

Davis elaborated further on his role in his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend, which led to publicity and media interviews.

But the book and interviews he offered elaborating on his role in Shakur's killing voided a protective agreement he had established with authorities that had blocked any criminal charges from being filed. A judge then allowed his police interview to be used in the murder trial against him.

Shakur was 25 years old and at the height of his career as one of rap's most influential voices at the time of his death. He has sold more than 75 million records worldwide.

For three decades, the investigation into his killing remained one of America's most famous cold cases, spurring countless conspiracies - until the conviction of Davis last month.

Throughout the trial, Davis' defence team tried to persuade jurors that his comments were fiction - bravado and exaggeration intended to sell books and make money.

Prosecutors argued that although Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang, did not himself fire the gun, he ordered the shooting and supplied the gun that his nephew Orlando Anderson used to open fire.

Anderson died in an unrelated shooting in 1998, having denied involvement in the killing of Shakur.

Man killed in tiger attack identified as William Chapman

BBC News Tue, 13 Oct 2026 19:35:21 GMT

The man who was killed by a tiger after entering its enclosure at a wildlife park has been identified as William Chapman, the BBC understands.

Chapman, who visited Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster on his own, entered the enclosure shortly after 13:30 BST on Saturday and was pronounced dead at the scene, according to South Yorkshire Police.

An eyewitness described seeing him wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in. Mobile phone footage, believed to be from Chapman, appears to show the inside of the enclosure as he approaches the tiger across a patch of grass.

A force spokesperson said his family was aware and was being supported by specialist officers.

The park was evacuated after the incident and remains closed as investigations continue.

Chapman, who was in his mid-20s, was a former pupil of the Jackie Palmer Stage School in High Wycombe.

As a child, he appeared in the ITV production May Contain Nuts alongside Shirley Henderson - who is best known for playing Moaning Myrtle in the Harry Potter films - and Darren Boyd.

He also portrayed Edward Jenner in the BBC series True Stories.

In a social media statement, a spokesperson for the stage school said: "We are deeply saddened to hear of the passing of our former student William Chapman.

"Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with William's family and friends during this incredibly difficult time.

"We loved watching William grow, both as a person and as a performer, during his time with us.

"It was a privilege to be part of his journey, and he will be remembered with great fondness by everyone who had the pleasure of knowing him."

They added that Chapman would be "truly missed" and he would "always hold a special place in our hearts".

City of Doncaster Council earlier confirmed it had launched a health and safety investigation into Chapman's death, which a spokesperson said was "in line with our statutory duties".

Staff at Yorkshire Wildlife Park said their "thoughts and heartfelt sympathies" were with Chapman's family and confirmed the rare Amur tiger, called Altai, remained in the enclosure and would not be euthanised.

Chapman was reported to have entered the enclosure after climbing down from a walkway.

Those who saw the attack said some witnesses had tried unsuccessfully to distract the tiger.

A video posted on a social media account believed to be Chapman's appears to show the moments before the attack.

In the footage, shot on a mobile phone, the inside of the enclosure can be seen as he approaches the tiger - perched on a wooden platform - across a patch of grass.

The account has since been removed.

A spokesperson for the Born Free Foundation, which campaigns to phase out zoos, called for an "urgent review" into "how the man managed to enter the enclosure and what happened next".

Dr Campbell Murn, a previous member of the government's zoo expert committee and lecturer at the University of Reading, said while it was a tragic incident, determined people could get inside zoo enclosures.

"I view it in the same way a determined thief will get into somebody's house or somebody's car and despite the best security systems and enclosures sometimes these things happen," he said.

Ella Ford, 24, from Moreton, Wirral, had visited the park with her boyfriend and filmed the tiger moments before the attack.

She described seeing Chapman by the tiger enclosure "pacing around with his headphones in".

A few minutes later, she saw he had "climbed up onto the barriers".

A woman was close by talking to him, she said, before "he jumped in and crawled in front of the tiger, where the tiger was perched and just lay there".

Ford said she then witnessed the tiger grab hold of him, and he was "shouting for help".

She estimated about 15 to 20 people were on the enclosure's raised visitor walkway before staff quickly evacuated the area and, shortly afterwards, the park.

She described members of the public as being "confused, like what on earth's going on?"

"I just know some man was obviously trying to bang on the fence to try and deter the tiger away, but it obviously wasn't doing anything," she said.

Karmelle Pelham, 39, from Worksop, had been enjoying a family day out when park staff told them the site was being evacuated.

She said she had heard what sounded like "gunshots" and an air ambulance had circled above.

Pelham added: "There was a big, black tarpaulin over the tiger enclosure."

She praised park staff for their handling of the incident, saying it had been "very, very well organised".

Trump ousts Kimberly Guilfoyle as US ambassador to Greece after corruption allegations

BBC News Tue, 13 Oct 2026 19:23:28 GMT

President Donald Trump's administration has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign from her position as US ambassador to Greece, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has announced.

Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host, had been facing mounting scrutiny after reports she allegedly asked a Trump donor to pay her hefty credit card bill in exchange for access to his administration and behaving inappropriately while in Athens.

Trump said she had done a good job, but she will "not be there" in Greece any longer. "I didn't like what I read," he said.

Guilfoyle vowed to defend herself against the "false" claims and said the ambassadorship had been the "honour of a lifetime".

Zacharia announced during her first - and unusually short - media briefing that Guilfoyle "had been asked to resign" without providing more details.

"She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well," she said.

Guilfoyle, the 57-year-old ex-wife of California Governor Gavin Newsom, was first nominated as envoy to Athens in December 2024, a month before Trump returned to the White House as president.

In a lengthy post on X, Guilfoyle thanked President Trump, said she would always be a loyal supporter and denied any wrongdoing.

"I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity," she wrote, adding that she will "not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service".

Her position had become increasingly tenuous as allegations of improper behaviour mounted over the past week.

A series of text messages seen by the BBC - and first reported by The Wall Street Journal - appear to show Guilfoyle asking for the money from Eric Deters, a long-time Trump ally.

"It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express," she wrote in one Signal message.

In another message - dated just days before her US Senate confirmation hearing last July - Guilfoyle wrote: "Honey please I need you to get this done for me today."

Guilfoyle's lawyers disputed the authenticity of the messages and said she was asking for money owed to her for speeches and consulting work conducted on his behalf before she became ambassador.

Audio recordings obtained by the Wall Street Journal reportedly include Guilfoyle bragging about her connections to prominent Greek business tycoons who she said bankrolled luxury travel and flights on private jets.

According to the newspaper, she also boasted to an official in Athens that the US could topple the Greek government.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was pictured alongside Guilfoyle during a trip to Athens last week, also had reportedly become unhappy with the allegations.

Following the news that Guilfoyle was being asked to leave, Deters told the BBC that "it's a great day for American diplomacy".

Deters, who said he did not ultimately pay Guilfoyle, also said it was a "complete lie" that he owed her money for speaking and consulting fees and said he is planning to take legal action against her.

Guilfoyle was a longtime political ally of Trump's and was for years in a relationship with his son Donald Jr, to whom she got engaged in 2018.

That relationship ended in 2024, around the time she was appointed to the position in Greece.

Trump noted on Tuesday that "she, I guess, dated my son a long time ago" but was not like a family member. The US president said he did not speak with Guilfoyle before she was asked to resign. "She went to Greece, she was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading," Trump said.

The president also said he thought Zacharia was "very good" in her first White House press briefing.

Zacharia, a longtime conservative commentator and Trump supporter, only answered a handful of questions during the 14-minute briefing.

For the first eight minutes, she read a list of what the administration sees as policy achievements. Then Zacharia answered questions about Guilfoyle, Ukraine, her family and administration policies towards non-traditional media outlets.

She said she viewed her job as working to "amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump's incredible agenda".

Cornell bans all fraternity parties over gang sex assault allegations

BBC News Tue, 13 Oct 2026 18:25:28 GMT

Cornell University is banning all parties at fraternity houses as the school faces backlash over its handling of an alleged sexual assault on campus two years ago.

Last month, a woman known as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit alleging she was plied with drugs and raped by several men in 2024 at a party at a Cornell fraternity house.

In a statement on Tuesday, Cornell's president, Michael Kotlikoff, announced a series of measures responding to the alleged assault, including the end to fraternity parties for the rest of the school year.

"I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community," he said.

"It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action," he added.

Fraternities have existed at university campuses across the US for decades and function as all-male social clubs where the students live, study and socialise. Over the years, the groups have become notorious for binge-drinking, partying and dangerous hazing rituals.

In a statement, a lawyer representing Doe said she filed a civil lawsuit "to achieve her aim of improving Cornell and its response to abuse claims".

"While the steps announced today are helpful to achieve this goal, they are too late to protect Ms. Doe," said lawyer Thomas Giuffra.

Cornell's president said anyone who violated the new fraternity party policy at the New York university would be suspended.

The school also said it planned to improve support for survivors of sexual assault, including more staff to help people report sexual misconduct and navigate other support systems as well.

Through Title IX, the federal law that governs how universities handle sexual assault claims, schools are required to provide measures of support to help survivors stay in school after assaults. Doe's lawyer has said she dropped out after the alleged assault.

The president said the school will allow New York State Police's trauma-informed officers to investigate allegations of sexual assault on its campus.

These officers will interview survivors who want to pursue criminal charges and prepare "comprehensive investigative summaries for the appropriate law enforcement agency", Kotlikoff said.

Cornell has faced criticism over the information shared with the local district attorney's office about Jane Doe's allegations.

Out of hundreds of documents that US media outlets have obtained from Cornell's investigation into the assault, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said that in 2024, his office received only a six-page statement signed by the victim as well as Snapchat messages in which the men at the fraternity party advertised a free sexual encounter with Doe.

State officials have also criticised Van Houten's decision not to bring charges or interview victims and witnesses himself. New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, to investigate the case.

Kotlikoff said Cornell would be bringing in national sexual violence prevention experts to examine "the factors leading to campus sexual violence and strategies to promote responsible sexual citizenship".

He said the steps were the first toward "systematic change" on campus.

The Argentinian government has begun legal action seeking to stop the exploration of oil and gas fields north of the Falkland Islands in an escalating row with the UK.

Buenos Aires said in a statement the request lodged with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea aimed to block activity authorised "illegally" by the UK.

The claim comes a fortnight after Argentinian President Javier Milei demanded the scrapping of the Sea Lion oilfield project, a joint venture between Israeli and British companies.

UK Foreign Office minister Uma Kumaran criticised the "escalating campaign" from Argentina against companies operating in the Falklands, while announcing new protections for them.

The developments heighten tensions between the UK and Argentina over the sovereignty of the self-governing British territory, known in Argentina as Las Malvinas, more than 40 years after a British military task force ejected Argentinian forces which had invaded the territory.

Earlier last month Milei also threatened to impose economic sanctions on firms exploiting oil close to the Falkland Islands.

Uma Kumaran accused the Argentinian government of "economic coercion" against the people of the Falkland Islands.

"We will do whatever it takes to support them," she told the House of Commons on Tuesday.

The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.

The Falkland Islands government extended exploration licences last month and the field is expected to start pumping in 2028, potentially generating huge revenues for the roughly 3,500 inhabitants of the islands.

Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – have insisted they have valid licences issued by Britain.

The Argentinian government claims the marine environment of disputed maritime areas is protected by international law.

Its application "seeks to preserve Argentina's sovereign rights over its continental shelf and prevent activities authorised unilaterally and illegally by the United Kingdom".

In a post on X, Argentinian Foreign Affairs Minister Pablo Quirno said the government was requesting the tribunal make a number of orders against the UK, including halting new exploration permits.

But the UK government insists Sea Lion is lawful, located on the Falkland Islands shelf and regulated by the islands' government.

While the Falkland Islands government grants exploration licences, they must be signed off by the UK Foreign Secretary.

Kumaran said the tribunal application "does not invalidate licenses issued by the Falkland Islands government, alter the islands' regulatory authority, or require lawful hydrocarbon development activities to cease".

The tribunal that will consider the dispute is an independent judicial body based in Hamburg which is responsible for the fair application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea.

FCDO officials have made clear the UK will engage with the tribunal but resist Argentina's claim firmly.

They said the aim was not to escalate the dispute but respond firmly to Argentina's latest move, and defend what the UK sees as legitimate economic activity.

They also hope to provide reassurance to businesses fearful of Argentine retribution. That is why they are introducing measures under the Protection of Trading Interests Act that would protect firms from any extra-territorial impact of Argentine laws following Milei's sanctions threats.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said: "Argentina's attempts to intimidate businesses and individuals engaged in legitimate commercial activity are unacceptable. Companies should be free to make lawful commercial decisions without the threat of political coercion."

The latest move comes after Milei roundly criticised the UN in his speech at the General Assembly late last month for failing to act over the sovereignty of the Falkland Islands.

He said the UN had become "a useless organisation" which only serves "arrogant parasites dressed up as well-intentioned bureaucrats".

On Tuesday Kumaran described Milei's remarks at New York as "inflammatory".

Despite its defeat in 1982, Argentina has always maintained its right to the Falkland Islands. But over the years successive governments have pressed their claim with varying degrees of aggression and diplomacy.

UK officials believes the current Argentine leadership is deliberately picking a fight ahead of elections next year.

Horrified witnesses recount fatal rollercoaster incident at Six Flags

BBC News Tue, 13 Oct 2026 17:10:50 GMT

Warning: This article contains some graphic details

One person has died and others were injured after an incident on a rollercoaster at an amusement park in the US state of Georgia.

The Cobb County Police Department is investigating Monday's death at Six Flags Over Georgia, about 15 miles (24km) from Atlanta.

The ride involved has not been specified but aerial footage from news helicopters showed the Goliath rollercoaster stopped midway, with riders being helped off by workers.

Horrified witnesses have told local media they saw a man ejected from the ride and police say preliminary information indicates this was the case.

Six Flags said it was temporarily closing nine rides across the US and Canada as a precaution.

It said it was "deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today. Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones".

The Cobb County Police Department said the incident happened just before 16:00 local time (20:00 GMT) on Monday.

It said officers working at the park found the man, identified as Atlanta resident Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, 42, beneath the ride. He was unresponsive and not breathing.

"Preliminary information gathered through witness and employee interview indicates Kariem was ejected from the ride and struck other patrons before falling beneath the attraction," police said in a statement.

The Office of Commissioner of Insurance and Safety Fire, which enforces amusement park safety rules and standards in Georgia, said it was also reviewing the incident "to ensure full compliance with all applicable policies and procedures".

Local CNN affiliate WXIA quoted a witness saying Kariem had come loose from his seat and had then struck the rollercoaster and some of his fellow riders before falling onto the roof of a nearby haunted house attraction.

The incident was captured in souvenir photos that were automatically taken of the rollercoaster while it was in motion, the witness added.

A husband and wife, who were on the ride, also told WXIA that Kariem fell from the ride and was struck by it. They said workers at the park had checked their safety harnesses before the ride set off.

"We were having a great time and to just screaming 'Oh my God, what is happening?'," the woman said.

Another witness, CiCi Nelson, told CNN she was in line to ride Goliath when the rollercoaster returned and she saw an empty seat with a loose safety bar and a girl covered in blood.

Nelson described a scene of hysteria, adding that one man was "freaking out, saying someone fell off".

Brittany Landry, who believes she saw Kariem ejected from the rollercoaster, told Fox News she was in tears.

"I broke because we were just on there," she said said.

A park spokesperson said in a statement that its team and local authorities had responded immediately and that they were cooperating on an investigation into the incident.

Mableton Mayor Michael Owens said the city's public safety director was also coordinating with local police and park security on the situation.

The death at Six Flags Over Georgia is at least the seventh there, according to the Doan Law Firm, which tracks amusement park accidents and represents victims.

The Goliath ride opened in 2006, and it has an elevation of 200ft (60m), a 170ft plunge, a 540-degree spiral, and a speed of up to 70mph (112km/h), according to the park website. On its "thrill scale", Six Flags ranks Goliath at level four out of five.

Brian Avery, a University of Florida professor with an expertise in amusement ride and device operations, told the BBC that rollercoasters are not federally regulated, leaving it up to states to determine the necessary safety protocols and maintenance procedures.

"When these types of tragedies happen, you got to get to the bottom as to why, so we can move forward and address those issues so that they never happen again," Avery said.

He explained that one of the main factors considered when designing a rollercoaster is how to contain the rider. This specifically includes determining where to place their harness - something that changes depending on the ride type.

"We design these rides, the industry does, to flirt with danger," Avery said. "We're taking people up to the edge, but we're not actually putting them in danger. That is the goal."

Six Flags is the largest amusement park operator in North America, with 20 amusement parks, 14 water parks and nine resorts across Canada, the US and Mexico.

The death in Georgia comes just weeks after one of Six Flags' parks in southern California announced it would close the popular X2 roller coaster after more than 100 people alleged brain injuries from the ride.

Six Flags said that ride had passed a range of safety tests, but that it had decided to retire the attraction because it was "the right thing to do".

MI5 chief warns against overstating Russian interference in Brexit vote

MI5 chief Sir Ken McCallum has said there was Russian interference in the the Brexit referendum, but warned against overstating its impact on the result.

It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham provoked a backlash from some Brexit campaigners by saying it was "clear" there had been interference by Moscow in the 2016 vote.

Sir Ken said it was "a matter of public record" that there was interference in the referendum by online trolls and bots.

However, he suggested Russian trolls would be "delighted" to be front page news again, "despite the comparative unimpressiveness" of their efforts.

He added: "There is a really important difference between interference attempted and outcome swayed.

"I am a little bit anxious that we don't play into our adversaries' hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall."

Conservative deputy leader Alex Burghart branded Sir Ken's comments "an extraordinary slap down to the prime minister".

In an interview released on Monday, Burnham told The Rest is Politics podcast that upon arriving in Downing Street, he had asked if there had been Russian interference in the 2016 vote, adding: "I've had the clear answer that, yes, there was."

He did not provide details about the extent or nature of Russian activities during the interview, and when pressed on the subject in the House of Commons on Monday afternoon appeared to be less definitive.

The PM denied claims from Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch that he was implying the referendum result was illegitimate because of Russian interference.

He said it was a "matter of record" that Russia sought to interfere in the 2019 general election, adding: "We think it is inconceivable that this was the first time".

A No 10 spokesperson also clarified that while the prime minister believed it was highly likely Russia tried to influence the referendum result, he did not believe those efforts were successful.

The Conservatives accused Burnham of making an "embarrassing retreat" after "being caught out trying question the legitimacy of the referendum result".

Answering questions after his annual speech at MI5's London headquarters earlier, Sir Ken said: "It is openly on the record that Russia Today and Sputnik and other Russian media organisations came in pretty strongly around the referendum.

"And it is also a matter of open source record that there was a certain amount of interference attempted through trolls and bots and so forth."

He added that he agreed "strongly" with the PM that there was a hack and leak during the 2019 general election campaign.

However, he raised concerns about the impact of the debate on Russian interference.

"It is kind of up to us how far we allow our various adversaries to divide us," Sir Ken said.

"And I'm a little bit worried that if we all stay in this debate for another few days, that Russian trolls who didn't appear to do all that much at various points over the years, they'll be delighted because they are front page news again despite the comparative unimpressiveness of what they do at all points along the journey."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has accused Burnham of lying, saying there was "no Russian interference" in the referendum.

Meanwhile, former Prime Minister Boris Johnson said that in 2016, when he became foreign secretary, the security services had told him "there was no evidence of any successful interference in the 2016 referendum, by Russia or any other power".

He added: "Either the security services have changed their view - which would be very odd - or Burnham is lying about what he has been told."

In 2020, a parliamentary report did not reach a firm conclusion on whether Russia had tried to intervene in UK elections and referendums, but criticised the government for failing to fully assess and counter the threat from Russian "troll" accounts on social media.

A "multiple murder" investigation has begun after four people, including two children, died in an arson attack on their family home in County Waterford.

The parents have been named locally as Philip and Kim English.

Two more of their children are critically injured in hospital as a result of the blaze which was reported shortly after 05:00 local time on Tuesday.

Addressing the media outside Waterford Garda Station on Tuesday afternoon, Ch Supt Anthony Pettit said officers believe the house "was attacked by a person or persons unknown and that the fire was started deliberately".

"The house at Birch Avenue has been declared a crime scene and is currently subject to a technical examination by the Garda Technical Bureau," he added.

The officer said the four bodies have been removed from the scene and post-mortem examinations would be carried out at University Hospital Waterford.

The two injured children are being treated at a hospital in Dublin.

Firefighters, ambulance staff and gardaí all responded to the emergency at the family home in the Birchwood housing estate, about 3km (1.8 miles) outside Waterford city centre.

Waterford Fire Service said it was alerted to the fire at 05:13 local time and its crews arrived to a well-developed fire at a two-storey house.

It said a number of casualties were removed from the house before the blaze was extinguished and the scene was handed over to gardaí.

A senior investigating officer is leading the murder inquiry, which is being coordinated from an incident room at Waterford Garda Station.

Family liaison officers have also been appointed to the bereaved family.

Addressing reporters, Ch Supt Pettit appealed for witnesses to what he described as a "multiple murder and arson attack".

"In particular gardaí wish to speak to anyone who was in the vicinity of Birch Avenue, Birchwood, between 04.30am and 05.30am this morning," he said.

"Gardaí are also appealing to anyone who was driving in the vicinity of Birchwood, or the adjoining roads, between 4.30am and 5.30am this morning, who may have dashcam footage or images to make such footage available."

Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan has described the arson attack as a "brutal and heinous act" and insisted those responsible would "face the full rigour of the law".

"This shocking event has had a very significant impact not just on the people of Waterford but on the whole country," he said.

"There is no place in a civilised society for such a heinous act of violence."

O'Callaghan said the murder inquiry was being supported by the National Bureau for Criminal Investigation.

He expressed his condolences to the family and friends of the bereaved and to the two children in hospital.

The housing estate is just off the Killure Road on the outer edge of the city.

Sinn Féin's David Cullinane, who represents Waterford in the Dáil (Irish Parliament), said he knew the family and said his heart went out to their relatives.

"I'm just utterly heartbroken," Cullinane said.

"There is such devastation in the housing estate itself but also in the wider community in Waterford city."

His party colleague, Sinn Féin councillor John Hearne, also knows the family and described it as a "terrible tragedy".

Hearne told BBC News NI that residents living in the estate noticed the blaze at about 05:00 and they went out to wake up their neighbours to try to help.

But he said it "all happened so fast" and was "hugely distressing for everyone involved".

Independent councillor Donal Barry had also been working with the family very recently.

Speaking to the BBC's Evening Extra programme, he was audibly upset by their deaths.

"Only last Thursday I was speaking to Kim on the phone in relation to a matter I was dealing with," he said.

"As soon as I went up there this morning and I looked and saw the house, my heart sank. I knew who it was then."

Barry said the immediate family were "well thought of" in Waterford and the community has been "numbed" by the attack.

The councillor added that there was "devastation" in local schools where the couple's children were pupils.

He praised the efforts made by the local council which set up a support hub at Butler Community Centre in St John's Park in the aftermath of the attack.

"Waterford City and County Council won't be found wanting in any support which they can give the community," he said.

The Bishop of Waterford and Lismore, Alphonsus Cullinan, described it as an "unspeakable tragedy" which had shocked the entire city.

In a statement, he said: "Our hearts go out to the families who have suffered such unimaginable loss.

"We stand in solidarity with all those whose lives have been devastated", he added.

He said the Catholic Church would "reach out as best we can" to help those affected and the parish priest would minister to the bereaved family and support the local community.

"We also wish to express our sincere gratitude to the emergency services, gardaí, firefighters and medical personnel who responded to the scene and who have faced such distressing circumstances," the bishop added.

Local parish priest, Fr Gerry Chestnutt, said the family will be supported by the community.

"Some of the children went to our primary schools so they will have lots of friends and parents of friends, they will rally around, while this is a big parish, around this area is very tight knit," he told RTÉ.

The mayor of the Waterford Metropolitan District, Lola O'Sullivan, urged people not to speculate about the cause of the fire.

"It upsets me no end to see people commenting on social media about something that they don't have firm facts on," she said.

Regulator would quit over Man City interference

BBC News Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:00:18 GMT

This video can not be played

'We have to go on the evidence' - Kogan

The head of English football's independent regulator says he will resign if he encounters any political interference over the future of Manchester City.

As chairman of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR), David Kogan has the power to assess the suitability of club owners and executives.

If an independent commission's findings that the club broke Premier League financial rules are upheld, the watchdog could even force a sale.

Last month, the Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised for saying he would be "really concerned" if the scandal led to Manchester City's Abu Dhabi owners selling the club.

"They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is," he added.

When asked about Burnham's comments, Kogan told BBC Sport: "The Prime Minister is entirely entitled to make his own observations on anything.

"We are independent. That is in the name. I am the chairman of the Independent Football Regulator and independence absolutely runs through everything we're doing.

"And no politician has tried to influence and would try to influence anything we do on that."

When asked what he would do if he did come under political pressure over the case, Kogan replied: "I would resign."

An independent commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018. Owners Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy prime minister Sheikh Mansour - are said to have topped up the value of commercial deals as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to the scale of £830m.

City insist they are innocent and have appealed.

How much did Man City's rule breaking cost your team?

'Criticised for what?' - Maresca defends celebrations

Kogan, a former sports media rights executive, was appointed to the regulator role one year ago

The prime minister initially told the BBC of his concerns, before later denying his reaction had "downplayed the seriousness of the findings".

However, some Premier League clubs were so "astonished" by Burnham's stance that sources told BBC Sport they were "concerned" about political interference in the appeal process.

Burnham's previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester has led to questions about his relationship with City's Abu Dhabi ownership.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch demanded all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club are released. The government released these details on Monday.

Speaking at the launch of the IFR's State of the Game report, Kogan said, "As far as we, as the regulator, are concerned, we have a very clear course of action that is governed by statute and we are going to follow that course of action, and no comment by any politician or indeed any individual is going to affect what we do".

Kogan's hiring as IFR chair was the subject of an inquiry by the Commissioner for Public Appointments over his historic links to the Labour Party, having contributed money to the leadership campaigns of former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer and culture secretary Lisa Nandy.

Shadow Culture Minister Louie French has written to the government, citing "concerns about the IFR's ability to adjudicate this case fairly, free from political interference".

In response, Kogan said: "I can tell you absolutely categorically that any politician who's trying to meddle in this for political purposes is welcome to try and welcome to do it, but I am going to stand by the probity of the organisation that I lead. If anybody wishes to challenge those after we've acted, that's entirely up to them."

The independent panel will hold a sanctions hearing - which could take months to convene - to decide on City's punishment.

The club can appeal both the guilty verdicts and the sanction, leaving the league in a state of uncertainty.

City's punishment could range from a huge fine, being deducted points or being ejected from the Premier League.

Asked how crucial it is that it was resolved as soon as possible, Kogan said: "I think it's very important."

Kogan added that the case was "raising very serious issues if Manchester City on appeal is found to be guilty of the allegations within those findings".

"We are waiting like everybody else to see what the independent panel will do… and then we will bring in a view in terms of our own investigation and statutory powers if we need to do so.

"Our powers relate to individual owners, directors and senior executives. They refer to whether people are in a position to run a club in a way that is safe, coherent and done with probity, and we will be examining those things."

When asked if the IFR could withhold a club license from City when it starts awarding them from next month, Kogan said: "I'm not going to begin to comment on any actions we may take until we've had a chance to assess it."

And on whether the case had raise questions about the state-connected ownership of clubs, Kogan replied: "No, I don't think specifically it does. We have no powers to prevent state ownership of clubs. It's not within our remit. But I don't think you can apply a general observation about type of ownership to one particular example."

An independent commission held a 42-day hearing in 2024 that led to the verdict announced last month, with City also guilty of all charges except one relating to non-cooperation with the Premier League investigation.

The commission's report said that "a number of important club witnesses gave false evidence in key respects and that some knowingly gave untrue and dishonest evidence".
