Act is pledging to reinstate a tax rule that could benefit residential property investors to the tune of $300 million a year.

The party wants to allow investors to once again deduct losses from their rental properties from all their income, including their wages/salaries.

Investors could do this until a loss ring-fencing rule was introduced by the Labour-led Government in 2019 in a bid to make the tax system “fairer”.

Under this rule, which the coalition Government kept in place, an investor who suffered a $10,000 loss on their rental property over a year and received a $100,000 salary from their unrelated day job would have to pay tax on $100,000.

They could then carry their $10,000 rental loss forward to the following year.

Under Act’s proposal, the investor would be able to deduct the $10,000 loss from their salary and would only have to pay tax on $90,000.

Act leader David Seymour pitched the change, which would make property investment more attractive, as being good for renters.

He warned his policy would provoke “the usual cries of ‘tax cuts for landlords’”.

However, he said there was “no such thing as a tax on landlords that renters can safely ignore”.

“When Labour made rental housing more expensive to provide, tenants faced the consequences,” Seymour argued.

“Labour’s policy meant legitimate losses could not be offset when cashflow is tightest, forcing landlords to wait until a property became profitable – when cashflow relief is needed least. If cashflow is tight, it’s much harder to carry out essential repairs if the tax deduction is delayed for years.

“The only way to secure more affordable housing for renters is to build more homes and reduce the costs that get passed through to renters.”

Seymour said rents, which soared under Labour, flatlined under the coalition Government.

He also argued changing the rules back to how they were before 2019 would make the tax system more consistent.

“If you’re a sole trader or make other investments, such as commercial property, your losses can be offset against your personal income,” he said, arguing that allowing residential property investors to make these deductions would “level the playing field”.

When the Labour-led Government changed the rules in 2019, it argued it too was levelling the playing field.

However, the playing field it referred to was between property investors and owner-occupiers, who couldn’t deduct the expenses they incurred from owning their homes from their wages/salaries.

Inland Revenue and Treasury recognised this in the regulatory impact assessment they prepared for ministers in 2018.

They noted that without a change, investors could have part of the cost of servicing their mortgages subsidised by the reduced tax on their other income sources, helping them to outbid owner-occupiers for properties.

The agencies recognised the process of negative gearing – investors reducing their taxable income with rental losses – had become relatively widespread in the New Zealand rental market, with 40% of taxpayers with residential investment property reporting rental losses and an average annual tax benefit of $2000.

“We expect the practice of negative gearing of rental properties to continue if no further action is taken,” Inland Revenue and Treasury said.

While the agencies said the magnitude of losses claimed depended on the state of the housing market, they noted numerous other countries had some form of loss ring-fencing of residential property.

Coming back to Seymour, he clarified Act would abolish loss ring-fencing for existing homes and new builds. Losses already ring-fenced would remain subject to the existing rules.

Act expected the policy to cost the Crown $246m in its first year, rising to $303m in its fourth year.

It said these figures were based on Budget 2018 numbers, adjusted for the increase in the size of the economy.

National says it will abolish the blanket ban on minimum car parking requirements as the party announces its policies focused on Auckland.

National transport spokesman Chris Bishop and Auckland spokesman Simon Watts today released the party’s “Backing Auckland to succeed” policy document, which was filled mostly with already announced policies addressing housing, cost of living and crime.

However, it also included a commitment to abolish the ban on minimum car parking requirements and to allow councils to use those requirements in suburban areas outside those identified for intensification, like in city centres or near rapid transit stops.

“New homes should come with the parking residents need in the right places,” National’s policy document read.

“National will unclog our streets and make them safer and more manageable, enabling our suburbs to be more liveable.”

Luna has overtaken Charlie as Christchurch’s favourite dog name.

This year, 421 Lunas were registered with Christchurch City Council, just overtaking 420 dogs named Charlie.

Poppy was next with 394, and Bella rounded out the top four with 390 pooches.

The top 10 was capped off with Ruby, 342; Daisy, 338; Max, 326; Molly, 300; Frankie, 288 and Archie, 284.

Food names were also surprisingly popular with Basil, 73; Cookie, 56; Taco, 24 and five dogs called Sausage.

Human names are also in – with 30 dogs called Kevin.

There were 24 Trevors, 15 Garys and 25 Colins.

Labradors dominated the list with 5026 dogs, ahead of the second-placed Staffordshire bull terrier on 2964.

Border collies, 2606; golden retrievers, 1843 and miniature schnauzers, 1548, round out the top five.

Poodles were more popular collectively than people might expect.

Miniature poodles, toy poodles and standard poodles totalled 1605 dogs, placing them among the most popular breed groups overall.

Corgis are having a moment. Combined, 74 Welsh pembroke corgis and 52 Welsh cardigan corgis total 126 dogs, narrowly edged out by 127 Yorkshire terriers.

There are rare breeds with one registered dog, including the bolognese, eurasier, pumi, Sussex spaniel, Tenterfield terrier, great Swiss mountain dog, and Korea jindo.

Email us

Christchurch City Council animal services manager Lionel Bridger said it was always interesting seeing what people call their best friend.

“The top few names tend to stay the same, but it’s great seeing the more creative names people give their dogs,” Bridger said.

“I think some people struggle to pick a name because we have a few dogs called Boy, Big Boy or Good Girl.”

Lionel said whether it’s a Labrador called Luna, a border collie called Scout or a tiny dog with a larger-than-life name, the diversity of names and breeds shows there really is a dog for everyone in Christchurch.

“Dogs are an important part of many Christchurch households, and this data offers a light-hearted snapshot of the pets that bring so much companionship, fun and character to our communities.”

Scientist blasts decision to close Palmerston North’s FoodHQ as ‘problematic’ in the long-term

New Zealand Herald October 13, 2026

Emerging proteins like fungi were one of the growth opportunities FoodHQ explored. Photo / Unsplash

By Monique Steele of RNZ

A science advocate is describing the decision to close the North Island’s FoodHQ research hub as “problematic” in the long term, as it could stifle New Zealand’s future food innovation and technological developments.

FoodHQ was set up in 2013 as New Zealand’s “food super campus” to develop, launch and investigate food science and innovation opportunities at its Palmerston North base near Massey University.

Projects included reports into emerging proteins such as hemp and fungi, developing a food market for GLP-1 patients, dairy’s next opportunity and the aquaculture sector’s future.

Its private-public board decided it would close the entity, which was reduced to just several scientists, including its chief executive since 2023, Victoria Hatton, with no property assets remaining.

At the board table were main shareholder Plant and Food Research, now the Bioeconomy Science Institute (BSI), Palmerston North City Council and Fonterra.

Adjunct freshwater and environmental science professor Dr Troy Baisden, who was also co-president of the Association of Scientists, said the closure came during significant reform in the science sector.

“It looks like the FoodHQ issues that are causing it to close its doors are really par for the course with the simplifications in the science system,” said Baisden.

“Unfortunately, these feel a lot like we’re playing musical chairs with things that matter.

“I think in the long term, it’s definitely a problematic move.”

Baisden said FoodHQ had said earlier this year that New Zealand needed to think harder about growing innovation capacity and developing the workforce, which were issues left unaddressed by the cut.

“One of the concerns is that we weren’t putting enough focus onto the intersection of where tech meets our existing strengths, including food, including primary sector,” he said.

“When the shareholders say they’re closing it, it means that BSI now believes it can go it alone in terms of the things that FoodHQ was doing.

“Is that really the case? We’re seeing an ageing sector; we need innovation that continues to turn the things that we can grow in New Zealand into high value products overseas; and we continue to need to develop a workforce that can do that.”

Baisden said FoodHQ was run under a public-private model, but it was effectively independent to support small companies, start-ups or innovators with research and development.

He said the public foundation for the belief that business-led research and development would drive the future was being lost.

“Sadly, what that tends to mean is that we won’t be developing the new innovative things in the future because that’s where productivity increases, and the big and surprising innovations of the future come from.”

Half of FoodHQ’s revenue – which came to $840,000 in the last year – came from its shareholding members, with the rest from programme funding.

Hatton also ran and led the E Tipu Future Food and Fibre Summit events, showcasing local and international talent, including nanobiotechnologists, food futurists and experts in areas such as sustainability, food production and agritechnology.

Chairman Mark Piper said shareholders decided FoodHQ would no longer operate as a standalone organisation, which was not the best way to progress the work.

He said funding was part of it, but not the sole reason behind the “tough” decision to close it, and the formation of the BSI had also changed the environment.

“The board and the owners over the last few months made the decision that now it’s probably the right time to exit Food HQ.

“The collaboration is happening better than it ever was in 2013, and the opportunity for us to keep that going in the respective organisations is kind of where the decision came from.”

Piper said it was a mutual agreement when the backers said they would not continue to fund it.

“[We] had unanimous support from the owners and funders that they [wouldn’t continue to fund FoodHQ] because of what they were doing in their own organisations, that they thought the money was best spent in their own organisations.

“And we as a board also agreed that it was a good time to disband.”

Piper was chief executive of the newly formed BSI since its establishment in July 2025, before former head of global dairy genetics company CRV Angus Haslett took over in July.

Piper believed much of the work would continue.

He said regardless of FoodHQ, there was a broader question around the appetite for New Zealand’s public and private sectors to invest in more long-term, higher-risk research and development.

“Blue sky research, in a broader sense, is that stuff that’s a little bit risky, the stuff that maybe people can’t quite see whether it’ll succeed, and it’s probably ahead of where industry or consumers are.

“It’s harder to justify because it doesn’t have an immediate return on investment.

“I think there’s a there’s a challenge globally at the moment on that.”

Piper said it would know later this month if the annual food summit events would continue.

Earlier this month, the Ministry for Business Innovation and Employment said investment in primary industries and bioeconomy will be $194m each year by 2029/2030 – down by a third from 2026/27 forecasts.

BSI said it had no further comment.

Hatton was approached for comment.

An Auckland woman claims she bit into a chocolate almond containing a rotten human tooth. Photo / Irene Atia

An Auckland woman fears for her health after claiming she bit into a chocolate almond containing what she suspects was a rotten human tooth.

At least two investigations are underway days after North Shore resident Irene Atia made the startling discovery in a small sealed nut package she had bought from a supermarket earlier this month.

New Zealand Food Safety (NZFS) confirmed it was following up on the complaint, and Woolworths told the Herald it was treating it as a “matter of urgency”.

Atia said she came across the disturbing find in a pack of Atkins Endulge Chocolate Almonds, which she bought online from Woolworths Browns Bay a few days earlier.

Pictures of the suspected tooth show a small yellowed tooth-shaped object with dark staining and red flecks.

A spokesperson for Atkins’ parent company, The Simply Good Foods Company, said they received a report about the find on October 9.

“We immediately initiated a comprehensive investigation with the manufacturer, which includes both ingredient and processing records.”

Contact the New Zealand Herald newsroom

It was Atia’s first time buying the product, which contained packets of chocolate almonds.

“I was sitting there and just enjoying each one, and then one of the almonds didn’t feel right; it felt a bit hard,” Atia said.

“I spat it out.”

She claimed she discovered the suspected tooth in the chocolate, where the almond was supposed to be.

“The first thing I checked [was] my teeth to check it wasn’t mine.”

Thankfully, all her teeth were intact.

She said the suspected tooth appeared “rotten” and had two red stains that seemed like “very dry blood”.

Atia said she knew the foreign item was a tooth because she could see the enamel.

She said the “horrible” bite worried her because the tooth may have carried disease or viruses, and she did not want to get sick.

After the discovery, Atia said she alerted Atkins, Woolworths and the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI).

New Zealand Food Safety (NZFS) acting deputy director-general Jen Radich told the Herald that NZFS received a complaint about possible foreign matter in a packet of chocolate almonds.

“We are following up. As we do in all cases, if there is a food safety issue, we will take the necessary actions to manage the issue,” Radich said.

A Woolworths NZ spokesperson said they were investigating and had contacted their supplier about the product.

“It is being treated as a matter of urgency.”

In the meantime, the spokesperson said they were refunding the customer and had contacted them last week.

“At Woolworths New Zealand, we take food safety very seriously, and we expect the highest standards of the products on our shelves.

“We are concerned to hear about our customer’s experience.”

The spokesperson for Simply Good Foods said it was committed to conducting a thorough review and would take appropriate action based on the findings.

“We take all consumer complaints seriously and remain committed to maintaining the highest standards of food safety, product quality, and consumer trust.”

The spokesperson said they contacted the consumer and were collaborating with the MPI as part of the ongoing investigation.

Warm, muggy weather is giving way to plunging temperatures, strong winds and heavy rain for much of New Zealand today, while snow could even be on the cards tomorrow.

Rain will fall across the South Island today as a front moves up the country, with an orange heavy rain warning in place for Buller until 9pm. Streams and rivers could rise rapidly and surface flooding and slips are possible, and drivers are being urged to take care and avoid low-lying areas, MetService says.

Elsewhere, severe weather watches affect southern and central New Zealand, with strong wind watches for Wellington and the Marlborough Sounds that could bring gusts of 100km/h tonight.

Auckland also faces a bleak start this morning, with periods of heavy rain easing to showers later today and more rain expected tomorrow.

Many areas that started the week in the low-mid 20Cs could see temperatures tumble today. Christchurch was basking in 24C on Tuesday and one Dunedin weather station recorded 26C, but today those cities can expect respective highs of just 15C and 12C.

It’s set to get even colder by the end of the work week. Snow is possible on higher roads in the South Island on Thursday, while by Friday high roads in the northern South Island and central North Island could also get snow.

The unsettled weather could also bring further rain and wind watches and warnings on Thursday and Friday, according to MetService.

However, a ridge of high pressure will arrive on the weekend, with more settled conditions expected for most of the country by Sunday.

Buller has been under an orange heavy rain warning since 1am, with 90-110 mm of rain expected by 9pm tonight and peak rates of 15-25 mm/h expected.

The Tararua Range and Taranaki Maunga is under a heavy rain watch from 9am today till 9am Thursday. In the South Island, the ranges of Westland and Grey Districts north of Mt Cook, as well as eastern parts of the Canterbury high country, are also under a heavy rain watch until 6pm today.

From 6pm tonight till 3pm Thursday, a heavy rain watch applies to North Otago, Dunedin and Clutha.

All those watches could be upgraded to warnings.

Strong wind watches apply to Wellington and the Marlborough Sounds from 8pm tonight till 3am on Thursday.

“Northerly winds may approach severe gale in exposed places,” the forecast says, with a moderate chance of upgrading to a warning.

People are advised to keep up to date with the latest forecasts, with a fresh update from MetService expected at 10am.

NZTA Waka Kotahi is warning South Island travellers to plan for snow disruptions, with potential for up to 5cm on higher parts of Porters Pass (SH73). On Friday, up to 4cm could fall on Arthur’s Pass (SH73) and on SH7 east of Lewis Pass, according to private forecasting provided to NZTA.

SH8 and SH80 in the Mt Cook Village and Tekapo areas could also receive lesser amounts of snow, NZTA said.

The agency said road users should drive carefully and plan ahead, including checking road conditions and bringing warm clothes, food and water in case of delays.

HamiltonJet appoints Sam Hamilton as fourth-generation chairman

New Zealand Herald October 13, 2026

Sam Hamilton is taking over the family business, HamiltonJet in Christchurch. Photo / Supplied

HamiltonJet has handed the chairmanship to Sam Hamilton, marking the fourth generation of the Hamilton family to lead the Christchurch-headquartered marine propulsion company founded by Sir Bill Hamilton in 1939.

The appointment, announced at Irishman Creek Station in the Mackenzie Basin where the company began, sees Sam take over from his father Mike Hamilton, extending an unbroken line of Hamilton family leadership that stretches back to founder Sir Bill Hamilton.

The transition marks a rare fourth-generation succession for a major New Zealand manufacturer, with the chairmanship passing directly from Bill Hamilton to Jon Hamilton, Mike Hamilton and now Sam Hamilton.

“My father had the role land on him with very little warning,” said Mike Hamilton.

“I wanted Sam to take it on while I am still here to support him. He has the board, the leadership team and the family behind him.”

Sam Hamilton has served on the board since 2019 and is the company’s technical director.

“HamiltonJet is a family business, and will remain that way,” he said.

“Bill built this company on resourcefulness, trustworthy engineering, resilience and looking after people.

“Those values have carried us for more than 80 years, and can be seen in the way people here design, make and back our products every day.”

Sam Hamilton was grateful his father was staying on while he learned the new role.

“I intend to keep building on what he, the generations before him, and everyone working here today have made,” he said.

HamiltonJet remains privately owned, mainly by the Hamilton family, and has remained in New Zealand ownership throughout its history despite interest from overseas.

Managing director Ben Reed said the transition reflected the long-term thinking that sets the company apart.

“Four generations of family leadership is rare anywhere in the world,” he said.

“Our customers, our distributors and our people value the stability that comes with it.

“Family ownership lets us plan in decades, not quarters, and that is exactly how we intend to keep operating.”

HamiltonJet designs and manufactures waterjets for commercial, defence, rescue and patrol vessels, supported by regional offices in Singapore, Seattle, London and Perth and a global distributor network.

The company’s mission is “to continually optimise performance, efficiency and safety through innovation” by delivering “the latest in efficient, robust, high-performance propulsion technology”.

Bowel cancer treatment: Whangārei solo mum pays more than $230K to stay alive

New Zealand Herald October 13, 2026

A solo mother of three who has paid more than $230,000 to fight cancer says people need to realise the cost of cancer treatment in New Zealand.

Jacqualine “Jay” Findlater, from Whangārei, was diagnosed with stage 4 colorectal cancer in August 2024, months after battling to get a diagnosis.

She was given six to nine months to live after the cancer spread to her stomach lining, lungs, spine and lymph nodes.

Now 40, she has beaten the odds but still pays $2000 a fortnight for treatment to be intravenously administered.

“Unfortunately, every single angle is not funded.”

Colorectal cancer, also called bowel cancer, is the second most common cause of cancer death in New Zealand, after lung cancer.

Northland had the third-highest rate of bowel cancer diagnoses out of 20 regions in 2023, according to the most recent data available.

Findlater said more needed to be done in New Zealand to fund earlier screening and advanced treatment.

She started on targeted therapy bevacizumab, known by the brand name Avastin.

While this is funded in New Zealand for selected cancers, it is not funded for colorectal cancer.

Findlater paid about $75,000 for this treatment by cashing in her KiwiSaver and through donations. She also underwent funded chemotherapy.

About a year ago, Findlater was given compassionate access to second-line targeted therapy cetuximab, which would have cost more than $200,000.

While cetuximab is funded for some colorectal cancers, it was not funded for her due to her type of genetic mutation and the side of her body the cancer is in.

Findlater had to pay $46,000 for companion treatment encorfenib. She also has to pay at least $2000 a fortnight for the unfunded treatments to be administered.

She has also had to start aggressive chemotherapy after a recent scan showed cancer progression.

Alongside the health and financial battles, Findlater went through a break-up, sold her home in Ōnerahi and moved into her father’s house in Parua Bay.

“I have lost everything; I have nothing,” she said through tears.

While she appreciated being a full-time mother, Findlater was concerned about her children, now aged 4, 10 and 17.

“I can’t really do what I want to do with my kids because I have no money. I can’t even go to town when I want - a tank of gas has to last almost a fortnight.”

Findlater was grateful for what she called her village: those who rallied around her.

This included her sister Bex Yovich, friends – including fundraising champion Gina Maddox – oncologist Edmond Ang, North Haven Hospice and former colleagues at Otaika Valley School, where she worked as a teacher aide.

Findlater said it was difficult to ask for funds but she was grateful for the support.

“I wouldn’t be able to get through anything without my village but to actually have to fight to find money all the time, I just can’t even bring into words what that does.”

Findlater said New Zealand needed to keep pace with overseas jurisdictions in funding therapies: “We’re 10 years behind the rest of the world”.

She considered moving to Australia, where Avastin is funded, but the move was too difficult in the middle of treatment.

Her 17-year-old son Cohen Ace also got into advocating for more health funding and last year used his position as a youth MP for Whangārei’s Shane Reti to raise the issue with Prime Minister Christopher Luxon.

“I’m not saying the Government’s not putting money into health but the system is being forced to fund cuts while ordinary New Zealanders like Mum have to experience the consequences of long wait times, under-resourced hospitals and over-crowded hospitals,” he said.

Findlater also wanted to see free bowel cancer screening in New Zealand start at a younger age, having been diagnosed at just 38.

She went to Parliament last year to help advocate for a lower screening age, alongside friend Jackie Robertson, who has since died.

New Zealand recently lowered its screening age to start at 56 but that was still a far cry from 45 in Australia.

Before the 2023 election, Luxon promised to match Australia’s age range but was unable to deliver. National recently promised to lower the age to 50 by 2029.

“It’s not good enough,” Findlater said. “People put bowel cancer as an ‘old people’s cancer’ and it’s just not.”

Colorectal cancer was the second most common cause of cancer deaths in 25 to 44-year-olds and 45 to 64-year-olds, according to the latest statistics, from 2023.

While Findlater wants to fight for the bigger picture she was focused on her own battle, including raising enough money to get treatment through to Christmas.

Her friends are helping with a new Givealittle page and a large raffle coming soon, including a table handmade by her father.

Denise Piper is a news reporter for the Northern Advocate, focusing on health and business. She has more than 20 years in journalism and is passionate about covering stories that make a difference.

James and Russo lead rout of Greece as ruthless England set up Ukraine playoff

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 20:41:36 GMT

Playoff semi-final second leg: England 5-0 Greece (agg 8-1)

Goalscorers: Russo 3 75, James 16 34, Stanway 30

A mercurial Lauren James scored two and provided an assist in a thrilling four-goal first 45 minutes against Greece, as England put themselves two games away from securing their place at the World Cup.

James’s double was matched by Alessia Russo, who scored either side of the break, and her Arsenal ­teammate Georgia Stanway was also on the scoresheet, with the Lionesses setting up a playoff final against Ukraine in November and December. It was a clinical and slick statement from England, albeit against a team they should bypass with ease.

Any Greek hopes of arriving in Leicester and launching a Trojan horse-style smash and grab, after a hugely impressive performance in their 3-1 defeat by an ­unconvincing Lionesses team in Crete, were quickly dashed.

Sarina Wiegman had said on the eve of the game that she wanted to see improvement in the final third. “It’s staying onside, having the final pass, the right pass at the right moment, the run at the right time and deciding what option you choose,” she said.

In the King Power Stadium, which had a club vibe to it before kick-off as dance remix after dance remix blared out, the Lionesses responded to their manager’s call, Russo producing the first goal from the first shot and first attack in the third minute.

James was the architect, the ­Chelsea player driving forward and picking out the No 9 who shrugged herself clear of Eleni Markou’s ­challenge before firing a low shot into the net.

It was Russo’s fourth goal in four games for club and country, with the Arsenal forward having gone five Women’s Super League matches without a goal prior to this run, and it was a sign of things to come from a team keen to shake off criticism of their lack of ruthlessness.

James was in majestic form, her injury worries behind her this season, and England fans were treated to a glimpse of what they missed at the Euros in Switzerland in 2025 where a less than half-fit James struggled and looked frustrated as her body failed to meet her demands on it.

She delivered England’s ­second and fourth in Leicester, her two first-half goals sandwiching ­Georgia ­Stanway’s header into the far ­corner from Lauren Hemp’s chipped cross. For her first, the 25-year-old ­cushioned Maya Le ­Tissier’s pass before sending a rising drive ­goalwards with her left foot and her ­second was far simpler, the unmarked forward turning in Hemp’s ball from close range.

It was an emphatic first 45 minutes from England, who converted four of their six shots on target and allowed Greece only 16% possession. The only disappointment was the ­debutant Lexi Potter’s goal being ruled out for a fairly innocuous challenge by ­Stanway on Markou that the referee, Rasa Grigone, deemed a foul.

Job well and truly done, James was withdrawn at half-time in favour of Beth Mead, Wiegman’s jewel safely nestled back in a velvet pouch after shining so brightly.

England picked up where they left off after the break. Stanway was denied by a VAR check on the ­narrowest of offside calls after she beautifully brought the ball down with her outstretched foot in mid-air before firing a half-volley into the net.

Wiegman leapt on the ­opportunity presented by the 7-1 aggregate ­scoreline to rotate further at the hour mark, with Niamh Charles, Jess Park and Freya Godfrey given a chance to demonstrate why they should be on the plane to Brazil should England overcome Ukraine.

Whether the changes took the sting out of the game or England just eased back on the intensity given the margin did not really ­matter, because the home team remained in ­complete control of the ball. Their more than 50-place superiority in the Fifa world rankings was far more ­evident in Leicester than it had been in Heraklion.

Russo was the beneficiary of ­England’s patience as the clock ticked down, collecting Keira Walsh’s angled pass before she raced clear, stepped around the goalkeeper, ­Styliani ­Katergiannaki, and rolled the ball into the empty net.

Chants of “we want six” rang round the buoyant ground as added time approached but that another did not arrive could not dampen the mood of the crowd and the show they had been treated to.

Ultimately, despite the ­performance put on, there is very ­little to be learned from a game against a team so far below ­England’s level. Any slip-up would only ever have been of England’s own ­making, as the poor ­defending for Greece’s goal in Crete ­demonstrated. ­However, perhaps that ­sluggishness could be ­attributed to a rustiness after a four-month break from ­international football.

Ukraine are up next, the homeless team preparing to face the European champions after a 4-1 aggregate defeat of Slovakia.

England met Ukraine in their World Cup qualifying group and, with a 9-1 aggregate win secured earlier in the year, it would take the most almighty of collapses for England to fail to book their place in Brazil now.

Frank and Percy review – bromance becomes romance for Ian McKellen and Roger Allam’s dog walkers

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 20:05:34 GMT

London film festival: McKellen and Allam reprise their roles for the film version of Ben Weatherill’s play in a star-filled bittersweet comedy about finding love later in life

There is a tender sweetness to this silver-years romance of new experiences and new ideas – and also some sugary sentimentality, an autumnal woodwind score telling us how to feel, and a bit of sitcom-cartoony characterisation in the all-star gallery of supporting turns. Sometimes that works and sometimes it doesn’t. But the movie’s easy-going good nature wins out – and there’s a terrific contribution from Joanna Lumley, playing Belinda, an elegant woman poignantly suffering from early onset dementia. Screenwriter Martin Sherman adapts the two-hander stage-play by Ben Weatherill in which Roger Allam and Ian McKellen originally starred. They return here for the expanded movie version and Sean Mathias once again directs.

Allam plays Frank, a retired history teacher whose wife died of cancer a few short years ago (Belinda is his sister-in-law) and who now likes to walk his dog Toffee on Hampstead Heath. McKellen is Percy, an academic sociologist and climate scientist who can be found there too, with his dog Bruno. Percy is rather acrimoniously separated from his now ex-partner, a waspish and querulously self-pitying figure gamely played by Stephen Fry.

In their differing ways, the men are lonely; Frank has nothing to do but mope around the garden centre, brooding over memories from his marriage, and volunteering at a charity shop where he has to stand, and Derek Jacobi, as a salaried employee, is allowed to sit. Percy goes in for age-gap dates from a niche website called Papa Search – some broad comedy cameos here for Ncuti Gatwa and Hugh Skinner – but he’s not satisfied. His friendship with Frank grows, his mischievous donnish sense of fun vibing unexpectedly with Frank’s stolid northern common sense. Then one day over a drink, Percy asks if it might be quite all right if he kissed Frank. Wonderingly, Frank agrees – and it is the start of something new; he says: “I felt like I did when I had a cataract removed.”

This leads Frank to ponder if he is bisexual – but perhaps it is more that he is simply sexual, and sexual in a way that he never expected to be at this time of life, or any time of life, and could only have been with this individual person. We get some bittersweet comedy as Frank and Percy realise that their social life consists of funerals, and Percy has a startling Yorick moment looking at the churchyard’s headstones. “Oh my God! I’ve had him!”

Naturally, the course of true love, or any sort of love, does not run smooth and at one stage Belinda, in a moment of lucidity, tells Frank: “How lucky you are to have a broken heart at 77!” True enough. It’s a love story as comforting as the cups of tea and slices of cake to which the characters are partial.

Frank and Percy screened at the London film festival.

Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis sentenced to 40 years to life over Tupac Shakur’s murder

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 19:43:45 GMT

‘You don’t get to take a man from his family … and just walk away from it,’ judge says as former gang leader sentenced

Tupac trial spotlights decades of US police failures in solving the case

Duane “Keffe D” Davis, the former California gang leader convicted of murder for orchestrating the 1996 fatal shooting of rapper Tupac Shakur, has been sentenced to 40 years to life in prison.

“For three years, I’ve heard you say some variation of the same thing … ‘Yeah, I was involved in this. But I’m different. I’ve moved on. I got out of Compton. I’m a grandfather now,’” Judge Carli Kierny said Tuesday as she delivered the sentence.

“You don’t get to take a man from his family. You don’t get to take his very life, his whole future from him and just walk away from it,” Kierny continued.

On 7 September 1996, Shakur was gunned down near the Las Vegas strip shortly after a Mike Tyson boxing match. He succumbed to his injuries days later.

For decades, his murder remained unsolved and one of hip-hop’s most enduring mysteries. Davis is the only person to be convicted in connection to Shakur’s murder.

“It was hard sitting, listening over and over and over again to someone describe – bit by bit, how they hunted Tupac Amaru Shakur down,” the rapper’s sister, Sekyiwa Shakur, said on Tuesday minutes before Davis was sentenced.

She described her brother as a father figure. “He was who God trusted to take care of me,” she told the court.

The grief from her brother’s murder led Sekyiwa Shakur to be hospitalized several times for depression, suicidal ideation and PTSD, she said.

She and the rapper’s stepbrother, Maurice Shakur, called for Davis to face the maximum penalty.

“Time to sit down and contemplate what you’ve done to the world, not just to me,” Sekyiwa Shakur said.

Davis stared intently, but appeared stoic as the relatives spoke. He vowed earlier during the hearing to appeal the case.

A confluence of several factors hindered the investigation. The code of silence within street culture made some witnesses averse to police cooperation. Las Vegas police were skeptical about leads from their Compton counterparts, given that the head of security for Shakur’s record label was a former Compton cop.

Orlando Anderson, a gangster and Davis’s nephew, was on law enforcement’s radar as the possible gunman. The night Shakur was killed, the young rap star got into an altercation with Anderson. Las Vegas police interviewed Anderson, but he was never arrested. Anderson later died in 1998.

But then, in 2023, Davis was arrested on a murder charge.

It was Davis’s own media tour, touting his status as one of the last surviving eyewitnesses, and a 2019 “tell-all” memoir that led to the breakthrough.

Davis had felt emboldened by a 2008 backdoor deal he brokered with police. He spoke candidly to investigators about Shakur’s shooting, who had actually been seeking information about the death of Christopher Wallace, known as Biggie Smalls or The Notorious BIG. Under a proffer agreement, Davis was not to face charges for any offenses he shared.

In his memoir, Compton Street Legend, Davis wrote that he and a group of other men targeted Shakur and his entourage, seeking retribution for the scuffle with his nephew.

The memoir and the interview became central to prosecutors’ case. They argued the details amounted to a confession and that his public remarks voided the proffer agreement.

During Davis’s murder trial, his defense team maintained that these details were embellished. They also argued, during the trial, that there was no physical evidence, such as a murder weapon, tying Davis to the Las Vegas slaying.

Ultimately, jurors sided with the state.

The Chicks review – exquisite harmonies and hard-won vindication in anniversary show

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 19:05:18 GMT

Beacon Theatre, New YorkTwo decades after country music blacklisted the band for their Iraq war protest, the trio celebrate their unapologetic album Taking the Long Way

Last month, with almost no fanfare, the US formally completed its withdrawal of troops from Iraq, after 23 years of violent quagmire. But it was the beginning of that conflict that loomed over New York’s Beacon Theatre on Monday night, where the Chicks played the second of three sold-out shows. In March 2003, eight days before the US invaded Iraq, the country supergroup’s lead singer, Natalie Maines, said on stage in London she was “ashamed” that then president George W Bush was from the trio’s home state of Texas, triggering a swift, self-righteous and scarily prescient backlash.

More than one person at the Beacon wondered aloud where fellow fans were back then, when a single comment, circulated on AM radio and cable news, led to CD-burning protests and death threats. (High school, was a common answer.) I myself was nine, with a child’s stark view of morality and consequence. Our country was at war, I knew, in an impossibly faraway place, and my favorite band bore the cost of criticizing it. One day, I could catch blue-sky hits including Travelin’ Soldier, Landslide and Cowboy Take Me Away on the radio on the way to school; the next, they were gone.

The incident, AKA “the blessing”, as Maines put it on Monday, was pointedly addressed on Monday night, at one of a handful of shows commemorating the 20th anniversary of Taking the Long Way, the Chicks’ scorched-earth, chart-smashing retort to what many now recall as early “cancellation” (though it is perhaps more accurately, and ominously, seen as a form of proto-social media, post-truth coordinated harassment). Though it looms large for a particular demographic – largely white and female, many queer – I almost didn’t recognize the moment when the band played that 2003 clip on stage as a prelude to their bitter barn-burner Not Ready to Make Nice, because in it Maines is laughing, speaking off-handedly. People forget, it was never supposed to be that serious.

If only. The band revisited several clips from Shut Up and Sing, Barbara Kopple’s essential 2006 documentary on their fall and rise, throughout this statement of show; in one, a montage of cable news hosts and vox pop randos decry “Saddam’s angels” as “traitors” who disrespected the troops, spoke too loudly, broke country music’s rah-rah rules.

“Well, imagine that … we thought that was the worst it could get,” Maines told the rapturous crowd on Monday, still laughing. “Now I would give George W Bush a big kiss. Because now we’re ashamed that the president of the United States is from the United States.” Time has not been kind to the country, unfortunately foreseen on the group’s seminal fourth studio album as hypocritical, vindictive and perhaps irrevocably divided. But it has been kind to the artists formerly known as the Dixie Chicks (they dropped the “Dixie” in 2020), whose exquisite, industry-standard harmonies and liberatory bluegrass-pop has aged like fine wine.

The trio appeared enriched and polished by the two decades since Taking the Long Way’s release – which included a 14-year hiatus, a couple tours, one more album (2020’s Gaslighter) and one bitterly fractured nation. The album, played in full during the show’s first act, now appears unnervingly prescient, at turns an elegy and a kiss-off to home towns perhaps permanently estranged. Maines – along with sisters Martie Maguire and Emily Strayer on fiddle and banjo, respectively (and, fitting for their Rick Rubin-aided pivot toward pop and rock, a full backing band) – kept the 14-track run-through as potent and trained as her never-better vocals, lucid as ever. It was just the songs, interspersed with documentary clips illustrating both the public and the private storms – the backlash but also young mothering, touring around IVF (So Hard), finding words for, say, a grandmother’s struggle with Alzheimer’s (Silent House).

The group used brief interludes to shout out collaborators including the Red Hot Chili Peppers’ Chad Smith (who, I learned, played drums on Not Ready to Make Nice); Maines’s father, the renowned pedal steel guitar player Lloyd Maines; Semisonic’s Dan Wilson, who wanted to call the album Undivided and initially proposed an apology ballad (“We said, ‘fuck that,’” Maines recalled on stage). They also made nods to Mike Campbell, who lent his experience with Tom Petty to Lubbock or Leave It, the Chicks’s most straightforward rock tune, and the gospel steel guitarist Robert Randolph, whose closing track I Hope, with its outdated faith in disagreeing “lovingly”, is afforded some bite via background footage of civil rights protests then and now.

But perhaps nothing proves a point like a blistering second act that tears through the hits, reminding that even scratching the surface of the group’s electric discography will get a full-throated and complete singalong. From karaoke staple Goodbye Earl into emancipation anthem Wide Open Spaces, a welcome bluegrass down moment in White Trash Wedding into a sublimely record-faithful version of Cowboy Take Me Away, the nine-song finale is more of a mutual catharsis than a concert. By the time the band reaches its torrid finale in Sin Wagon – the Chicks being perhaps one of few mainstream shows where a fiddle solo is met with raucous applause – the case is long past made. The incident may have made the Chicks a cautionary tale, but there’s vindication in the long run.

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 18:41:46 GMT

The parents of the victims of paedophile nursery worker Vincent Chan have reacted with fury to the news that he was cleared to return to work after “significant concerns” were raised by the parent of a young girl.

As first revealed in the Guardian, Chan was reported to his employer, the nursery chain Bright Horizons, by a concerned parent in 2021.

After being investigated by Bright Horizons, with the knowledge of Camden council, Chan was cleared to return to work at the nursery on the Finchley Road in north-west London. A year later, in 2022, Chan filmed himself abusing three-year-old girls in his care.

“I feel a level of anger that I can barely put into words,” said one mother. Images of her daughter were found on Chan’s personal devices after his arrest.

She added: “In 2021, around the time serious concerns had been raised about Vincent Chan, he was made my daughter’s key worker. We trusted him with her most intimate care, believing she was safe.

“Knowing there was a chance to stop him before he had such extensive access to her is unbearable. I am heartbroken, but above all furious at Bright Horizons for failing to protect our children.”

The families have called for an immediate “independent examination” of how the 2021 complaint was handled.

In a statement issued by the law firm Leigh Day, which is representing 50 families affected by Chan’s abuse, they called for a “full and independent account of what happened, who knew what, when they knew it and why these decisions were made”.

The parents of Chan’s victims have been promised answers in the form of a repeatedly delayed safeguarding review, led by an independent reviewer appointed by Camden council. But many expressed fury that they only learned the review had been pushed back to 2027 in the Guardian article.

“Expressions of regret are meaningless,” said the parents in a statement. “Families deserve the truth about what happened, accountability for the decisions that were made, and action to make sure this cannot happen again. We cannot wait until 2027 for answers.”

“We have shared all relevant documents and information with the independent review team. We want families to get the answers they deserve, in full, through the outcome of the independent review.”

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 18:16:07 GMT

University bans parties at frat houses for rest of academic year to conduct ‘thorough review’ of campus Greek life

Cornell University has announced that it is suspending parties and other social gatherings at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year amid intensifying backlash over its handling of allegations that a female student was sexually assaulted at a fraternity house in 2024.

The university has also said that Cornell will involve New York state police in investigating sex crimes on campus.

Michael Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, announced the measures on Tuesday.

The suspension of all parties and social gatherings at houses governed by Cornell’s interfraternity council is meant to be in effect through the end of the academic year ending in the spring of 2027 – and it is subject to a “zero tolerance” policy that would lead to the immediate emergency suspension of any chapter found to be in violation, Kotlikoff said.

“These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue,” Kotlikoff wrote in a letter to the campus community.

Kotlikoff also committed to adding a case manager to Cornell’s office of civil rights to help those who report sexual misconduct at the Ivy League institution navigate the processes. Kotlikoff also pledged to work with the New York state police to allow their trauma-informed criminal investigators – who are independent of Cornell University – to investigate allegations.

Such allegations otherwise have been handled by Cornell’s campus police force.

A civil lawsuit filed in September by a woman identified by the pseudonym of Jane Doe alleges that several men assaulted her at Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity house after she went there in an intoxicated state looking for a friend.

Two of the accused men were subsequently expelled after an internal investigation by Cornell – while others were allowed to resume their studies after writing an essay, attending a workshop or serving a short suspension.

None were ever arrested or charged by local authorities, and disgust over the treatment of the alleged offenders grew when the woman’s lawsuit was made public.

Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, on 2 October announced that she was appointing Letitia James, the state’s attorney general, to take over Jane Doe’s case as a special prosecutor.

If warranted, James would present evidence to a grand jury that could lead to criminal charges, Hochul said.

Two of the men named in Jane Doe’s lawsuit have challenged James’s appointment. Hochul said James’s appointment is necessary because local police and prosecutors who were obligated to protect Jane Doe “failed” her.

Far-right and Iran add to mix of terror threats UK faces – not to mention AI

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 17:58:40 GMT

Annual update from MI5 chief highlighted a complex cocktail that could have real-life consequences for Britain

MI5’s annual threat update covers so much ground it is easy to feel anxious. The terror threat has become more diverse, with far-right anti-migrant threats on the rise; while Iran has now firmly emerged alongside Russia as a country seeking to undertake violent and deadly plots in the UK.

“There is no law of physics dictating that rising state threats will be accompanied by diminishing terrorist threats,” MI5’s director general, Ken McCallum, said, although one of his core messages was that people and the country at large needed to focus on being more resilient. “In this new world, we should expect to be tested.”

A key issue highlighted by McCallum was that years of anti-migrant, anti-Muslim hostility had now led to an increase in cases where people were “tipping into terrorist intent” – that is crossing the line from rhetoric to violence. It is a complex area, but one certainly fuelled by political hate narratives and online subcultures.

It is also fuelled by toxic rhetoric from abroad. Authoritarian regimes, McCallum said, were investing heavily “in trying to distort and divide our society” – although he was too polite to mention that there is plenty of evidence that voices from the US led by X owner Elon Musk are keen to sow division in the UK too, as they post about flashpoint events such as the June rioting in Belfast and Southampton.

A second trend is that seemingly far-off conflicts, such as the wars the UK did not start in Ukraine or Iran, have a habit of rippling back home.

It is less than eight months since the US and Israel attacked Iran, subsequently with a little help from Britain, but already Iran is trying to direct terror plots in the UK.

Both MI5 and the counter-terror police may have to do a little better to explain precisely what five men from London were doing in a village next to RAF Fairford in three white vans shortly after midnight on 27 September, given that nothing of significance was found in the vans and nobody has been charged.

But McCallum warned that Iran had “ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites” – a likely reference to Fairford. That came a day after the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was “almost certainly” behind the episode. It would be surprising if both were wrong.

That is not the only possible example. At the beginning of October, two Iranians from Liverpool and Salford were charged, accused of trying to make a chlorine powder bomb to target Jewish sites in Manchester. Prosecutors alleged they were directed by a third party, believed to be in Iran. The two have not yet pleaded to the charges; a trial at the Old Bailey is scheduled.

Yet, if these fast-emerging threats were not enough, the normally sober McCallum decided to reference AI.

He warned that AI could refine terror plots, supercharge hackers, produce individually targeted propaganda – and even help develop a novel bioweapon. This, he added, with emphasis, was a subject on which they were “particularly focused”, as if it was episode one of a TV thriller.

While concerns were recently raised about scientists who have used AI to design viruses, as Anthropic warned of five examples of scientists who had used Claude for researching novel pathogens, both instances provoked a scientific debate as to what is actually possible. And what McCallum did not mention was that AI is also an extraordinary and potentially intrusive tool for MI5 to seek out threats.

There is already enough for the intelligence agencies to think about, as the MI5 review makes clear: a country made more dangerous by blowback from strongmen starting what they think will be short wars; a rising tide of hatred that may start online but is morphing into violent intent in real life; a complex cocktail of external and internal threats that could have real-life consequences.

As McCallum himself recognised: “The protection of democracy – its institutions, its representatives, its principles – has never felt more vital.”

Wes Streeting’s unintelligible jargon shows how well he’s bedded in at the MoD

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 17:42:24 GMT

For the first time in his life, Wes is enjoying keeping secrets – though he did admit he isn’t ‘keen on fighting a war’

When Andy Burnham announced his first cabinet in July, few would have had Wes Streeting marked down as a likely defence secretary. Not even Wes. And no one is more bullish about Wes’s life chances than Wes. It just didn’t seem a natural fit. Defence secretaries tend to be more the unsmiling types who operate in the shadows. Politicians like John Healey, with the pallor of someone who has spent too long in underground bunkers with military chief of staffs. People who slide in and out of rooms without making a fuss.

Wes has always been someone who likes to be noticed. Enjoys the theatre of Westminster. The first to arrive at a party and the last to leave. A natural gossip. “Psst – you’ll never guess what Zelenskyy just said to Trump.”

But in the past few months, Wes has had something of a personality change. At the recent Labour party conference, he kept his appearances distinctly low key. No longer the life and soul of Liverpool, out till 2am before getting up to do the media round just four hours later. It can’t be long before we see him driving a tank somewhere near the Russian border. Wes is gonna be Wes.

He also has the distinct advantage of not being Penny Mordaunt, the former Tory minister who has done more to terrify a nation than any living defence secretary. A few weeks ago, Sky broadcast The War Game, a reality show for superannuated politicians in which Michael Gove was cast as the prime minister and Penny as defence secretary. The set up was that Russia had torpedoed a ship off Scotland, with the politicians and the military placed in a mock-up Cobra meeting and left to come up with responses as the situation developed.

This could have been the moment to restore faith in our democratic institutions. To admire the insight and clarity with which our leaders handle a crisis. To see how they repay the trust and power which we bestow on them. In which case, you should think again. What actually emerged is that politicians are no brighter than the rest of us. They just have egos which make them believe they are the right people in the right place at the right time. And that we are lucky to have them.

To put it bluntly, The War Game was a total shitshow. Just one bad decision after another. For the first two episodes, The Govester was like a rabbit in the headlights. Completely clueless as the UK came under increasing levels of attack. The best he could offer was to repeat back the last thing that was said to him and bark “ASAP!”

Penny, though, was a total menace to herself and the country from the word go. If this is really how defence secretaries behave, we should all be out digging bunkers in open land and stocking up on tinned food. Not that it would do much good. From the outset, Penny was hell-bent on escalating the conflict despite being told Britain’s military defences were totally threadbare and that the UK was only a middle-ranking global power. She couldn’t wait to use up the UK’s arsenal of weapons, and by the end two nuclear warheads were 20 minutes away from annihilating two major cities. Bye bye Britain. Still, at least she would go down as our last ever defence secretary.

So Streeting’s first appearance before the defence select committee was, first and foremost, a moment to give thanks he wasn’t Penny and that we are all – more or less – still here. And Wes looked as if he was now thoroughly bedded in at the MoD. He now talks mainly in letters – SDR, DIP and NAD – and jargon that is designed to be unintelligible to most mortals. Mostly, he wanted to get through the entire session by saying as little as possible and to send any stray reporters who had wandered into the committee room by mistake to sleep. He’d have liked to be more open, he said. But if he was, he’d have to kill us. For the first time in his life, Wes is enjoying keeping secrets. If not exactly his happiest place, then still a happy one.

Wes began by telling the committee that the UK and its Nato allies were facing their gravest threat since the cold war. Given that, you could understand why he wan’t particularly keen on telling us just how unprepared we were for some kind of an attack as our enemies might be listening. When Streeting had taken on the defence job he had spent most of the first week telling the media that he would – like his predecessor – resign if he thought the money being allocated was inadequate.

Three months on and he was rather dancing on the head of a pin. He couldn’t say how, when or even if the commitment to reach 3% of GDP by 2030 would be met. We just had to keep the faith that somehow it would all work out OK. John Healey said it would all end up OK, and if John Healey said so then we ought to believe him. After all, it wasn’t just a question of spending more money – it was also about spending the money he did have better.

It also turned out that some of our defence capacity was largely illusory. Both because it took six years for most military contracts to be delivered, by which time there was a fair chance the hardware would be obsolete, and because much of the increased spending had been backloaded until after the next election. Politicians never tire of passing on costs to future governments.

The MoD’s permanent secretary, Jeremy Pocklington, spent at least five minutes trying to persuade the committee that backloading wasn’t really backloading even if it looked like backloading. For that kind of mind-numbing bullshit, Jezza has been awarded the Companion of the Most Honourable Order of the Bath. Still, Wes did say at one point that he “wasn’t keen on fighting a war”, which I suppose is a start. Gives him the edge over Penny at the very least.

The Guardian view on Burnham’s Brexit reset: an overdue show of ambition

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 17:30:25 GMT

The prime minister is correct to judge the time is right to push for closer links with the EU. The political risk is far outweighed by the potential rewards

The German philosopher GWF Hegel famously evoked the owl of Minerva when discussing the historical wisdom that comes through hindsight. This autumn, she has flown tirelessly over the landscape of British politics. Party conference season was dominated by conflicting Labour and Conservative accounts of the 1970s and 80s. And a decade after the United Kingdom voted to leave the European Union, Andy Burnham this week abandoned all equivocation over the damage – economic but also strategic – that resulted from that decision.

Having declared that it is time to “face up to the reality that Brexit has done more harm than good”, Mr Burnham told the House of Commons on Monday that it would be a “dereliction of duty” not to explore all options for closer relations with Brussels. Though he confirmed that in this parliament he will honour the red lines in Sir Keir Starmer’s Labour manifesto, all bets will subsequently be off.

A long-delayed reset summit, Mr Burnham also announced, will take place next month with deals on food and drink and youth mobility to be negotiated. The former Labour leader Neil Kinnock asserted to an Italian newspaper on Tuesday that the prime minister’s “obvious” eventual objective was to rejoin.

That might well be contested in Downing Street. But as has become the norm in this overture phase of Mr Burnham’s premiership, his Commons statement was bracingly expansive and forthright. It also had the signal virtue of being correct in its diagnosis and prescription. Nevertheless, the reality of reopening the most divisive debate of recent British history will be drawn out, obstacle-strewn and fraught with political risk.

Labour’s hyper-caution over revisiting the EU relationship has increasingly been at odds with polls indicating a substantial majority of the public supports closer ties. But the devil will be in the detail. In the red wall, in particular, much will depend on the prime minister’s undoubted persuasive powers. The need to undo the economic self-harm of Brexit was not something that Mr Burnham chose to emphasise while campaigning for his seat in the leave-voting constituency of Makerfield.

For its part, the EU itself is in flux and may have new red lines of its own. Responding to a more menacing geopolitical environment, Brussels is contemplating deeper coordination in areas such as defence and economic policy. The direction of travel is already evident in the “Made in Europe” strategy, which threatens to leave British-based car manufacturers out in the cold.

As that risk illustrates, it is overwhelmingly in Britain’s interests to be acting in concert with the EU, rather than flailing in sorry isolation on the sidelines. Following the visceral mutual distrust of the Tory Brexit years, Sir Keir restored a basic if circumscribed civility to relations between the UK and the EU. Mr Burnham’s boldness can now open up new possibilities down the line for “a real reset”, to use the formulation of one EU diplomat.

It will not have escaped Mr Burnham’s notice that such a prospect would unite progressive Britain behind it, and could significantly boost Labour’s percentage vote share. His overriding early theme has been the need to rectify the political “wrong turns” of past decades. Beginning the long task of doing so on Brexit is brave, but it promises significant dividends for his premiership and, much more importantly, the country.

The Guardian view on probation: overcrowded prisons need an outlet

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 17:29:03 GMT

To win support for early releases, the government will have to show that community supervision works

The early release of thousands of prisoners was bound to be awkward for a new prime minister. Politically speaking, Andy Burnham’s decision to exclude those convicted of manslaughter and some other offences made sense. But with about 2,000 offenders being freed this month, the risk is that by cutting the numbers, he has added to overcrowding problems inside. With the prison and probation services under huge pressure, and a ballot on industrial action expected, there is an urgent need for moves from the government to strengthen both.

Shielded from view as prisons are, and despite the efforts of campaigners and writers such as Jimmy McGovern to draw attention to them, conditions have been allowed to deteriorate to a shocking extent. The latest annual report from the prisons watchdog drew a dismal picture of rampant drug use, organised crime and governors wasting time on form-filling. It warned that the Prison Service’s managers appear to favour crisis management over improvement.

Criticisms of the probation service of England and Wales contained in the latest report by the Institute for Government’s (IfG) appear measured, by comparison. Probation’s problems are less attention-grabbing, and senior leaders are not singled out for blame. But analysis of the impact of sentencing reforms, combined with ongoing staff shortages and tagging failures, are cause for very serious concern all the same. This is a vital public service that was already facing serious difficulties before its caseload was massively enlarged.

Problems date back to the failed part-privatisation of the service. The IfG highlights the toll of “near-constant organisational change”. One result has been de-skilling, with staff increasingly reliant on risk-management protocols rather than judgment. The number of recalls to prison due to breached conditions, rather than new offences, undermines rehabilitation and worsens overcrowding. But an overstretched workforce seems unable to break this cycle. There is simply not enough time to build relationships.

The failure to fit 45% of tags on time is obviously unacceptable; ministers need to get a grip and explain what is happening. The IfG also recommends further sentencing reforms aimed at making the system clearer. Rightly, it points out that the growing gap between jail sentences imposed in court and time actually served risks undermining trust and angering victims. Similarly, licence periods should end at the point where supervision ceases. Currently, there is a pretence that more people are serving community sentences than is actually the case. This places the probation service in a false position.

The pay dispute is the immediate challenge. As part of a settlement, ministers should pledge to rebuild capacity and fill vacancies. Looking further ahead, probation needs closer links to the local services that can help offenders to get back on their feet. The merger with the Prison Service has failed to deliver promised gains.

Managing risks to the public must remain a priority. But Enver Solomon, who leads Nacro, the criminal justice charity, is right to argue for a more “person-centred” style of probation work. No one who knows anything about prisons thinks that they are fulfilling their rehabilitation remit. A renewed focus on purposeful activity inside jails is needed. But as increased numbers of prisoners are diverted towards probation, the service needs resources to deliver what is asked of it.

Earlier the Saudis also struck what they believe to be a Houthi leadership hide-out in the Bani Mu’in area in the Razih border district, west of Saada governorate, northern Yemen.

The strike on the oil depot appeared to be the Saudi response to a Houthi attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people and left 300 injured. The airport is closed until Saturday at the earliest, a blow to an economy that is trying to show its security makes the country a safe place to invest.

A Houthi spokesperson responded to the attack on its oil storage by warning “all employees and citizens present near any facility affiliated with Aramco Petroleum in Riyadh to evacuate it and stay away from it, as it is a legitimate target for our forces”.

Later in the day, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a missile fired at Dharan, the location of the headquarters of Saudi Aramco. It said fragments from the interception fell on a residential area. Witnesses reported hearing loud booms. An evacuation order ​for the building ‌had been ‌issued, four sources told Reuters. There was no official comment ​or ​confirmation ​from ​Aramco.

The incident underlined how Saudi Arabia has complete air dominance over Yemen while the Houthis have to reply using drones and missiles which can be intercepted.

Baraa Shiban, a Yemen specialist at the defence thinktank Royal United Services Institute (Rusi), warned “Saudi Arabia is struggling to respond to the Houthi’s improved arms technology. Until relatively recently Houthi missiles and drones fell in desert areas or if they got through were intercepted. They have learned how to deploy drones that fly lower and are smaller, and are less easy to detect. They are cheap and it does not take many to get through to be effective”.

But the two sides’ dramatic threats to set ablaze the enemy energy infrastructure symbolised how the conflict is escalating rather than blowing itself out.

Donald Trump complained that the Houthis were “behaving very badly” and said he would “never forget” their attacks, which he suggested were an attempt to influence the US midterm elections next month. But he stopped short of announcing any new military action.

The latest phase of the conflict between the Saudis and the Houthis began last month after the rebels seized key areas along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical waterway for the transportation of Gulf oil and other goods at the southern end of the Red Sea off Yemen.

This week, the Houthis have come closer to throttling the southern city of Taiz, drawing close enough to the city edges to fire rockets into residential areas. City leaders have made repeated appeals to the Yemeni government for military equipment while public health professionals warned of a shortage of medicines for patients in intensive care.

Government-aligned forces sent reinforcements to the south-western district of Al-Mudarabba in Lahij governorate as well as the mountain district of Al-Waz’iyya.

But anti-Houthi forces inside Yemen are not themselves united: a group known as the Southern Transitional Council has been taking a more prominent role in the fight against the Houthis – even though its main objective is to secede from the country’s north.

On Tuesday, Aidarous al Zubaidi, the exiled STC leader, gave a rare address declaring “a popular mobilisation in defence of the south, and its national liberation project” – including by repelling the invading Houthi militia.

Al Zubaidi, now based in Abu Dhabi, made clear he still supported a plan to eventually hold a referendum on the independence of South Yemen.

Zubaidi’s organisation remains banned in Yemen and he has been charged with treason, but there are incremental behind-the-scenes talks under way testing whether the Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman is prepared to legitimise the STC and even permit Zubaidi to return. Reinstatement of the STC would be seen as a betrayal by the current Yemen president, Rashad al-Alimi, but his usefulness to Saudi Arabia is reduced if he does not have the same military forces at his disposal as Zubaidi.

Yes, obesity is a problem – but a greater one is the food industry and its greed

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:50:55 GMT

Ultra-processed foods are displacing traditional diets, warns Prof Kent Buse. Plus letters from Hugo Harper, Dr Pawan Randev and Patricia Hampton

Your editorial on cancers in under-50s (8 October) rightly names food among the culprits. But the confrontation it calls for should be aimed less at obesity than at what produces it. Obesity is the intermediary; the exposure is a food system engineered for profit.

The Lancet’s series on ultra-processed foods showed these products displacing traditional diets worldwide and driving chronic disease, and documented more than 200 interconnected lobby groups through which the industry organises its influence to block regulation.

I was diagnosed with bowel cancer at 51, narrowly escaping these statistics; the generations below me have eaten ultra-processed diets from birth.

Governments know what works: marketing restrictions, warning labels, fiscal measures, schools and hospitals free from ultra-processed food, and policymaking protected from industry interference.

Yvette Cooper should treat the companies that shaped our diets in the same way that her predecessors eventually treated tobacco: not as partners to consult, but as an industry to regulate. Prof Kent Buse Chair, policy and prevention committee, World Obesity Federation

The worrying rise in early-onset cancers underlines the urgency of government intervention on obesity. Our food system is broken when high-fat, -salt and -sugar options are consistently the most accessible and affordable.

Advances in cancer research and weight-loss drugs will play a key role in managing diet-related illness, but treatment alone cannot solve a public health crisis. We must fix the food environment driving obesity in the first place. That requires changing the incentives for large food businesses that make and market the food we eat.

The government’s proposed healthy food standard sets out the most ambitious action for reforming the food environment to date, but progress has stalled since its announcement. It has the potential to reduce national obesity rates by about one fifth in adults and a quarter in children. Nothing else on the table comes remotely close to that.

The first step is establishing mandatory health reporting so that companies can no longer mark their own homework. Then we need clear targets for major food businesses to improve the health of what they actually sell. Ultimately, we cannot protect future generations from preventable diet-related disease until healthier food is the easiest and most affordable option. We cannot let our strategy be “wait for people to get sick and then put them on the drugs”. Hugo HarperDirector, Nesta

Cancer has become the greatest cause of death among people with type 2 diabetes in England and the problem of metabolic risk and cancer is one of the great threats to health. However, this is not known by health professionals or the 4 million patients with this condition.

Cancer screening programmes work effectively with informed participation. GPs and their practices can use the annual diabetes check to highlight the cancer prevention. Screening programmes and primary care can work together to prevent cancer, if resources are targeted in the best way. The World Cancer Research Fund report has added urgency – let’s use it effectively. Dr Pawan RandevFormer Cancer Research UK GP

I read with interest Anna Bawden’s article (Cancer rates rising more quickly among younger people, international research finds, 6 October. It seems that “lifestyle choices” are largely responsible for this, but I wonder just how much of a choice is open to us nowadays. We can choose to drink less alcohol, not smoke, exercise more and eat more healthily, but our choice of healthy food is limited, as products become increasingly industrialised with the addition of chemical additives, and we have little or no control over environmental or agricultural pollutants. To all this we might add the stress of the increasing cost of living and difficulty in finding jobs.

I believe it is perhaps not so much a question of poor lifestyle choices, but a lack of lifestyle choices. Patricia HamptonMilan, Italy

The Conservatives’ ‘better tomorrow’ only includes rich people

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:50:50 GMT

Terry Peach responds to Kemi Badenoch’s conference speech, while Penelope Turton writes on her promise to cut inheritance tax

Kemi Badenoch’s conference speech rehearsed the argument that Andy Burnham’s economic policies were warped by his “nostalgia” for the 1970s, unlike her own forward-looking programme for “a better tomorrow” (Tories accused of prioritising rich voters as Badenoch lays out inheritance tax cut plan, 7 October).

She appears not to see that her preference for a lesser-regulated capitalist market economy, with lower public expenditure, taxes and national debt, coupled with “tough love” welfare policies, is itself harking back to arguments that have circulated for centuries.

Admittedly, her position is not as extreme as the one espoused at the beginning of the 19th century by the leading political economist David Ricardo, who argued that Great Britain would be happy and prosperous if the “evil” of the national debt was extinguished completely, and the country embraced a system in which trade is left “perfectly free” and taxation reduced to a bare minimum.

His own “tough love” proposal was to scrap the Poor Laws, as they encouraged overbreeding by the working class, thereby depressing market-determined wages. Terry PeachChester

Kemi Badenoch says “people who work hard and save should be rewarded for that effort” and regards inheritance tax (IHT) as unfair double taxation on people who have already paid tax on their earnings. In fact, most IHT revenue is driven by inherited and asset-derived wealth, which expands through unearned capital appreciation and is untaxed during a person’s lifetime.

Badenoch has elsewhere called IHT immoral. The real moral injury is borne by all those low-paid, hard-working people who face a choice between heating or eating, and for whom acquiring sufficient wealth in a lifetime to leave money to their children is an unimaginable dream. Penelope TurtonLondon

Yes, the music is lovely, but cathedrals are crumbling

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:50:39 GMT

They are some of our oldest and most historically significant buildings, yet they receive no secure state funding, writes Dr Coco Parkinson-Huggins

Jonathan Davies’ article (Abide with me: English choral music is a living part of our cultural heritage – we should cherish it, 7 October) speaks beautifully to the contribution of English choral music to our living cultural heritage, highlighting the importance of cathedral choirs in particular, in giving children access to “world-class musical training, extraordinary cultural experiences and educational opportunities that might otherwise be beyond their reach”.

What he misses however, is just how under threat these bastions of England’s religious, cultural and spiritual heritage actually are.

Despite recent research from the Theos thinktank suggesting 74% of adults in England have visited a cathedral over the last three years, 80% of cathedrals in England are now in structural deficit. Several have recently reached crisis point, including those in Peterborough and St Davids. One in four cathedrals in England is now charging for entry, and even after significantly diversifying their income portfolios (including through controversial silent discos), they continue to struggle.

More than 90% of visitors surveyed by Theos (including 94% of non-religious visitors) thought of cathedrals as a hub for community life, and the same number see them as a symbol of local identity and a way to connect with history and tradition. Despite their significant social and cultural contributions to communities, and being some of our oldest and most historically significant buildings (two are Unesco world heritage sites and many are almost 1,000 years old), cathedrals receive no secure state funding and limited contributions from central church authorities. Unlike museums and galleries offering free admission, cathedrals are also not subject to the same VAT exemptions on repairs or maintenance.

This has left many cathedrals crumbling, and their finances with them. Without cathedrals, English choral music would cease to exist. If more is not done to protect them, that reality could be closer than we think. Dr Coco Parkinson-HugginsResearcher, Theos
