‘You’re honoring a life well-lived’: embalmers describe their work (in great detail)

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:50:30 GMT

Embalming is one of the most common options for temporarily preserving bodies after death – but what exactly does it entail?

Most people don’t like to think about what happens to people’s bodies after they die. Victoria Bilstein is an exception.

“I’ve actually wanted to be an embalmer since I was 10 years old!” says the funeral director, embalmer and author based in the midwest. As a child, Bilstein had two leg surgeries that incorporated bones from two deceased donors. After that, she wondered about the people who had helped save her life and the families who had lost them.

She saw this work as an opportunity to help grieving families. “I wanted to be able to do postmortem reconstruction on donors so their families had the option for a viewing,” she says. “It felt like such an amazing way to honor my donors.” In her six years in the industry, she estimates she’s worked on at least a thousand embalmings.

Most people who are planning burials and viewings for loved ones choose to have them embalmed.

But fewer and fewer American families are choosing burials. According to the National Funeral Directors Association (NFDA), the burial rate in 2025 was 31.6%, while the cremation rate was 63.4%. By 2045, the NFDA expects the cremation rate to reach 82.3%.

Part of the reason is price. According to the life insurance company Unity Financial, the average cost of a simple cremation is between $1,000 and $3,000, while the average cost of a full funeral service with embalming, visitation, a casket and a ceremony is between $10,000 and $15,000.

Some clients fear that embalming is a “very cold and detached process”, says Bilstein. She does her best to disabuse them of this.

“I view embalming as something that’s very dignified and respectful, and an act of caregiving,” she says. “As the embalmer, you get to wash someone’s hair for the final time, clean their nails. You have the opportunity to restore them to their original appearance and you’re always prioritizing honoring their dignity as human beings and honoring a life well lived.”

Embalming is the process of sanitizing, preserving, and restoring a human body after death, Bilstein explains.

It is one of the most common options for temporarily preserving bodies after death, often with the goal of making the body suitable for “public viewing, long-distance transportation, or for medical or science purposes, such as anatomical research”, as per the Funeral Consumers Alliance.

“Many people think embalming is legally required for every funeral, or that it preserves a body permanently,” says Dr Camelia L Clarke, NFDA spokesperson and president at Paradise Memorial Funerary Corporation. “Neither is true.”

Embalming temporarily slows natural changes, she explains, and its purpose is to “give a family time to gather and, if they wish, to see their loved one”.

Embalming is not the only technique that can be used if families wish to view the deceased. Refrigeration is also an option, says Brad, a funeral service educator and creator of Fun Funeral Facts, who asked that his last name be withheld – this is less invasive and involves fewer chemicals, meaning it can be seen as a more environmentally friendly option.

But because it preserves the body for longer, Bilstein explains that embalming is often required for public viewings, transporting a body across state lines, international flights, and viewings of remains that are considered infectious (such as those with Covid or influenza).

PaperworkWhen a deceased person arrives at a funeral home, the first steps are bureaucratic, explains Clarke.

“We confirm their identity, review the information we’ve received, and assess their condition,” she says. Funeral directors must also obtain authorization from the family before embalming.

SanitizingThe deceased is then transferred to an embalming table, undressed and washed with disinfectant soap, says Brad. Clothing and jewelry is set aside and catalogued to be returned to the family.

During cleaning, an embalmer covers the deceased appropriately. “Dignity and respect is our primary concern,” says Bilstein.

Feature settingOnce a body has been embalmed, it becomes more difficult to move facial features, Bilstein says. So an embalmer does what is called feature setting beforehand – making sure the eyes and mouth are closed, and arranging the face and body so they look peaceful.

The body is positioned as it would be in the casket, Brad says – legs straightened, and hands crossed over the abdomen. A block is usually placed under the head to keep the head and neck in place.

Setting the face is more involved, explains Bilstein. To keep the eyes closed, embalmers may use glue or plastic eye caps – silicone discs with small spikes on their surface that hold the eyelid in place. The mouth is usually sutured closed with string or wire.

If instructed by the family, the embalmer will shave any facial hair. “Embalmers also like to remove any downy hair on the face because it helps makeup sit more naturally later,” Bilstein says.

Arterial embalmingThere are two primary components to the process, says Bilstein: arterial embalming and cavity embalming.

A chemical solution is mixed in an embalming machine – a device that pumps chemicals through the body.

Embalming fluid is generally made up of formaldehyde, water and a variety of other chemicals. The industry’s use of formaldehyde, a colorless, flammable gas known to be carcinogenic to humans, has long been controversial, but so far, no alternative has been found that is equally effective or affordable. To protect themselves, embalmers wear personal protective equipment (PPE) and work in rooms with multiple ventilation systems.

In arterial embalming, Brad says, an embalmer selects one of the deceased’s major arteries (usually the common carotid artery in the neck) to introduce the solution, and a vein (usually the internal jugular vein in the neck) to drain blood from the body. A tube connected to the embalming machine is inserted into the artery, and embalming solution is pumped through the body’s vascular system. This solution displaces blood, which is emptied through the selected vein.

The process is finished once tissue is firm and evenly colored, Brad says.

Cavity embalmingFor cavity embalming, a sharp, pen-shaped instrument called a trocar is inserted into the abdomen, pelvic and chest cavities, and attached to a device that sucks out fluids. Then the trocar is used to inject a highly concentrated form of embalming fluid into the same cavities. Holes from the trocar are plugged with a trocar button, made of plastic.

Finishing touchesTo complete the process, all incisions are sutured closed, hair is washed and brushed, and the body is disinfected again with soap and water. The deceased is transferred from the embalming table, dressed in a hospital gown and covered with a sheet, Bilstein says. Embalmers often apply moisturizer to the decedent’s face and hands because the embalming process is so dehydrating, says Bilstein.

Finally, the embalmer cleans and disinfects the area, and writes a report. All in all, the process usually takes about one and a half to three hours depending on the condition of the deceased, though complicated cases can last much longer.

“Embalming has its limitations,” says Bilstein.

She often compares the procedure to surgery. A standard case, without complications, is like a minor surgical procedure. A case involving major physical trauma is more like a major surgical procedure – the work is more invasive and involves more steps.

For instance, Bilstein says, if facial bones need to be rebuilt, this may involve reconstructive work with glue, wood or plastic.

Sometimes, damage makes arterial embalming and viewing impossible. “I had to have that tough conversation with a family,” Bilstein says. Bilstein sees much of her role as protecting families as they grieve, which means being realistic with them about what she can accomplish.

But there have been instances where she’s seemingly made the impossible possible.

“I’ve had cases where the family didn’t think a viewing would be possible, and I spent hours and hours on the case, and they were able to view and have an open casket,” she says. “Those are really rewarding cases, when you can give a family that opportunity to see their loved one.”

British and Irish governments ‘should negotiate paramilitary disbandment in Northern Ireland’

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:17:54 GMT

Report finds ‘window of opportunity’ for formal process involving loyalist and republican groups

The British and Irish governments should engage with paramilitary groups in Northern Ireland to negotiate their disbandment, according to a report.

A “window of opportunity” exists to establish a formal transition mechanism for loyalist and republican groups, provided certain conditions are met, it said.

The Independent Report on Paramilitary Group Transition to Disbandment, commissioned by both governments and published on Tuesday, said groups should not receive financial rewards for engaging in the process.

Fleur Ravensbergen, a Dutch conflict resolution expert who authored the report, said in Belfast: “I have concluded that there is sufficient merit in and support for a formal process of paramilitary group transition.”

Ravensbergen said she found “significant willingness to engage” among paramilitaries during a year-long scoping exercise.

She added: “There was limited support for the term ‘disbandment’ as the endpoint of a transition process. However, objections to disbandment appeared to be less about what transition should achieve and more about the wording.”

Paramilitary groups were expected to fade after the 1998 Good Friday agreement, but some endured and evolved into lucrative enterprises involved in drug dealing, extortion and coercive control.

Agreeing a transition process was more important than the terminology used to describe disbandment, said Ravensbergen, a lecturer in conflict resolution and governance at the University of Amsterdam.

She said: “I believe that the risks of the persistence of paramilitary structures, continued drift and unmanaged fragmentation outweigh the risks associated with attempting a structured and time-bound transition process. Inaction is not a neutral option. My consultations suggest that a window of opportunity exists to pursue further progress, but that this may weaken over time.”

Chris Bryant, the Northern Ireland secretary, thanked Ravensbergen and said the government was committed to ending paramilitarism.

Bryant said: “While these groups may pose as protectors of their communities, they are largely engaged in criminality including drug dealing, extortion and intimidation, blighting the very communities they perversely claim to protect. Their continued influence is a stain on our collective conscience.”

He said the government would consider the report and liaise with authorities in Dublin before responding to the proposed transition mechanism.

He added: “It is evident from the report that the implementation of any process will face challenges and will need the support from across the political community in Northern Ireland.”

Naomi Long, Northern Ireland’s justice minister and a member of the Alliance party, criticised Ravensbergen’s appointment as an interlocutor last year, saying engagement with paramilitaries and criminal gangs risked giving them a veneer of legitimacy.

Long said at the time: “The idea that paramilitary groups can transition into law-abiding entities has long since moved beyond the point of credibility. They cannot continue to be treated as if they are genuinely committed to reform – that moment passed long ago.”

The report did not identify individuals or specific organisations because discussions were held on a confidential basis.

It said: “The nature, extent and impact of paramilitary influence vary considerably between paramilitary groups, communities and geographical areas. However, it is clear that residual paramilitary structures continue to cause harm in some communities.”

Ravensbergen said a transition mechanism would need credible monitoring and verification of progress and robust law enforcement.

She declined to comment on the recent standoff between the Orange Order and nationalist residents at Garvaghy Road in Portadown, saying it was outside the report’s remit. There is speculation that renewed tension over the Drumcree parade may boost paramilitary recruitment.

Loves Trump, lies and conspiracies: Katie Zacharia is the perfect presidential press secretary

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:14:58 GMT

The Maga member believes the 2020 election was stolen and seemingly her new boss is saving the world from a cabal of satanic paedophiles. She’ll fit right in then

Poor Donald Trump. His (third) wife seemingly can’t bear to be near him and his (fifth) press secretary recently abandoned him to be with a baby she had only recently met.

“She decided she loved her children more than she loved Donald Trump,” the president lamented in August when Karoline Leavitt decided to step down a few months after giving birth. “I’m very upset about this. She has to go home and spend time with her children. That does happen on occasion with some people – when they love their children.”

Apparently, Leavitt loves her children and Fox News, because, in a highly predictable turn of events, the 29-year-old has got a gig there now. But don’t worry too much about the president: he’s found himself a new woman to attack the press and act as his mouthpiece. On Friday, Trump announced that he’d appointed Katie Zacharia, previously a communications adviser for the Trump Media and Technology Group, as the new press secretary. Unlike some of Trump’s other lackeys, Zacharia has government experience: she was once a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson. Her most important qualification, however, is her fealty to King Trump. “She has an unblemished record of support,” Trump said in his announcement. “She is … a devoted fan and member of Maga!”

While you’ve obviously got to worship the president to get a top comms role with him, there are a few other job requirements. Not least a willingness to embrace what former Trump adviser Kellyanne Conway called“alternative facts”. Zacharia gets full marks in that department. Last year the press secretary, who once worked for an anti-abortion advocacy group, claimed on X that the abortion medication mifepristone “is connected to the manufacturer of the deadly gas Zyklon B, used in the World War II concentration camps”. While there is a tenuous corporate connection which conspiracy theorists have tried to play up, mifepristone was developed in the 1980s by a French company.

The origins of mifepristone aren’t the only alternative facts Zacharia is fond of. She has echoed Trump’s big lie that the 2020 election was “stolen” and used her Truth Social account to promote the QAnon conspiracy theory, which posits that Trump is saving the world from a cabal of satanic paedophiles. She’s also promoted Pizzagate, the baseless theory that Hillary Clinton and her 2016 campaign chief, John Podesta, were operating an underground child sex-trafficking ring from a Washington DC pizza shop.

While Zacharia scores highly when it comes to devotion and unhinged theories, I suspect that she’s going to need to ramp up her public hatred of Joe Biden if she wants to stay on her boss’s good side. Biden is dealing with stage four cancer and mostly staying out of the public eye, but Trump still acts as if he’s running against the man. According to a recent Reuters analysis, Trump has invoked Biden’s name about 900 times this year. And not in a pleasant way.

Beni Rae Harmony, 24, who is Trump’s new assistant press secretary, seems to suffer from the same Biden Derangement Syndrome afflicting the president; indeed, it might be part of the reason she got the job. A Christmas 2021 photo of Harmony wearing a “Fuck Joe Biden” T-shirt while holding a rifle recently did the rounds online. The White House subsequently defended Harmony, calling her “a trusted voice for the Maga movement”.

Beyond bashing Biden, another helpful quality for a Trump spokesperson is a fondness for insults. White House communications director, Steven Cheung, whom Trump reportedly refers to as “my sumo wrestler” probably leads the pack there. He’s forged a shock-jock style comms strategy and endeavours to be as crass as possible. Cheung has told the former secretary of state, Mike Pompeo, to “shut his stupid mouth”, labelled senator Jon Ossoff “the biggest cuck loser in politics”, and described the former FBI head, James Comey, as “one of the dumbest motherfuckers in human history”. He’s also fond of calling people “retards”, recently directing the slur at CNN host Erin Burnett.

Cheung’s rhetoric would get a lot of ordinary people fired. But it has made him a fixture in Trumpworld: he’s been with the president in various capacities for a decade now. That’s rare for Trump, who cycles through staff. If Zacharia lasts even a year in her new role, meanwhile, I’ll be surprised. With a (very likely) disastrous midterm election approaching, she has her work cut out and will need all the alternative facts she can find. Zacharia has also admitted that she is probably not even the best person for the job. “President Trump does not need a spokesperson,” Zacharia gushed on X last month. “He is his own best Press Secretary.”

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

A return to a biennial Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) cycle is expected to be confirmed at Caf’s executive committee meeting in Abidjan next month after Motsepe surprisingly announced the U-turn last week – 10 months after the decision was taken to hold it every four years. That move is said to have wide support within Africa, but several sources have said there has been a weakening of trust in Caf’s leadership, with some questioning Motsepe’s management.

Most national association presidents are said to have been unaware Motsepe intended to announce the proposed change to Afcon’s frequency until the issue was raised at a strategic conference in Cape Verde last week. Motsepe confirmed he was not intending to stand for re-election for a third time when his term expires in 2029 and pledged Africa’s “unconditional support” for Gianni Infantino’s re-election as the Fifa president in March on the “unanimous” behalf of all 54 of Caf’s member associations.

It is understood Infantino remains extremely popular in Africa even though there are 10 to 15 member associations who would consider voting against him, as revealed in August. Motsepe’s potential rivals for the Caf presidency are believed to be attempting to gain Infantino’s approval should the South African billionaire be persuaded to step down early.

They include Eto’o, the former Barcelona and Inter striker, who is the president of Cameroon’s federation and a member of Caf’s executive committee, Ahmed Yahya of Mauritania, Côte d’Ivoire’s Yacine Idriss Diallo, and Souleiman Waberi, a Fifa council member from Djibouti who has been charged with embezzlement and money laundering. He has denied the allegations. Other candidates may emerge from southern Africa.

Sources indicate that Infantino could hold the key to whether Motsepe continues. The other option would be to challenge Motsepe through Caf’s statutory mechanisms, which say an extraordinary general assembly can be convened after a written request from at least two-thirds of the members of the executive committee.

Infantino is thought to have fallen out with Motsepe after Motsepe allowed the Somali referee Omar Artan, who was denied entry to the United States for the 2026 World Cup, to take charge of Uefa’s Super Cup final in August amid growing tensions with European football’s governing body. However, sources have indicated their relationship has improved in recent weeks as Infantino has sought to solidify his support in Africa.

Motsepe promised annual distributions of about $700,000 (£528,000) from Caf to each association at the conference in Cape Verde – an increase of $500,000 – and is understood to have increased payments to executive committee members for attending meetings from $150 to $350, and to have introduced for them an annual bonus payment of about $8,000.

Football regulator chair insists he will resign if politically pressured over Manchester City

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:00:18 GMT

Kogan says he has faced ‘absolutely no political pressure’

Regulator wants deal on redistribution through leagues

The chair of the Independent ­Football Regulator (IFR), David Kogan, has said he will resign if he faces any political pressure on how to respond to Manchester City being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules over a nine-year period, insisting “my independence is absolute”.

Kogan could remove City’s Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) should the damning verdict of an independent commission be upheld at the end of an ongoing appeal process. ­Concern had been raised, however, that the proximity of City’s ­ownership to Abu Dhabi’s rulers could trigger a political intervention by the UK ­government and an immediate test of the new regulator’s powers.

Those concerns have been rebuffed by Kogan. “Our independence is absolute and my independence personally is absolute,” he said. “I [have] made it very clear … any form of political interference on the way we operate is going to result in my resigning from this role, and I stand by that completely. And, just to be crystal clear, we’ve come under absolutely no political pressure whatsoever on this or any other topic.”

Kogan was speaking on Tuesday at the launch of the long-awaited State of the Game report, a document that lays out the financial challenges facing the English football pyramid. The City case has cast a huge shadow as the regulator prepares to introduce a new licensing regime for clubs later this season. “We have powers within the legislation that allow us to review not only owners and directors and senior executives, but also whether those owners are fit and proper ­people to run clubs going forward,” said Kogan, describing the process by which the regulator might intervene.

“That process is reliant on us ­having very detailed knowledge and information, which requires a ­certain amount of investigation. Then we would take judgments based on the legal advice that we then receive.”

Should a club owner ultimately be found to have failed a “fitness” test related to “integrity, honesty and financial soundness”, the regulator could force the club to be sold. “We deal with issues of this type much more frequently than you might realise because we are constantly looking at clubs,” Kogan said, stating if any decision by the regulator became the subject of legal action then clubs would be asked to foot the bill through a funding levy.

The acceleration of revenues among the Premier League’s biggest clubs is one of the key findings in the State of the Game report. The highest earning top-flight club currently earns 605 times the revenue of the lowest earning National League club. At the same time, spending has increased at all levels of the game, with 94% of the 116 clubs under the regulator’s regime posting a financial loss in 2025-26. In one particularly eye-catching statistic, the report found 11 Football League clubs recorded costs that exceeded their income even once player wages had been stripped out.

Kogan argued that a number of external factors that fall outside the regulator’s purview are affecting the game, including the expansion of the club calendar, the regulation of ­players’ agents and the recent rise in interest rates. However, he argued that one key measure – the agreement of a redistribution deal between the Premier League and EFL – could unlock change immediately.

While Kogan accepts the Premier League’s argument regarding the need for parachute payments due to “colossal” drops in revenue caused by relegation, he believes they have had a “distortive effect that’s grown over the years”. Kogan said that if a deal was done that reduced parachute payments but increased the amount going to all clubs then “that will go some way towards looking at the ­distorted effect”. Once that money was distributed, he said, “you’re going to see a softening effect going through down the 116 clubs”.

The Premier League welcomed the publication of the report, arguing: “It recognises what English football has built – the world’s most popular league, the leading second tier, and a pyramid of unmatched depth.”

The league argued that a recent offer of financial redistribution to the EFL – understood to amount to £320m per season – “meets the ­objectives the IFR has set out in its report” and said it “remains ­committed to concluding a long-term partnership with the EFL that is fair, generous and ­balances the interests of all clubs”.

The EFL said the report’s findings “reinforce the EFL’s longstanding position that English football generates sufficient revenue to sustain both a successful Premier League and a thriving pyramid” and it remained “committed to working constructively with the Premier League and the regulator to secure a financial settlement in the interests of the whole game”.

Meanwhile, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport, Lisa Nandy, said the stark figures covered in the report had “blown the doors off the game”. She urged football authorities to “consider these findings for the good of the game, for the fans, and for the communities of which they are so often the bedrock”.

Brexiters can’t cope with the fact that Putin was cheering them on

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 15:21:02 GMT

Russian meddling probably didn’t affect the referendum result – but the Kremlin’s motives for wanting to undermine the EU still matter

Russian territorial aggression against Ukraine didn’t feature much in the Brexit referendum campaign. It made headlines briefly when Boris Johnson blamed Moscow’s 2014 annexation of Crimea on the European Union.

According to the Vote Leave frontman, Vladimir Putin’s land grab was a consequence of Brussels making foreign policy “on the hoof” and having “pretensions to running a defence policy”.

The logic of that position was that Kyiv had no right to choose its own allies and that European democracies should never have supported Ukrainian aspirations to escape submission to Moscow. It is the appeasement fallacy: if only the west acquiesced to Putin’s conviction that Kyiv is a Russian city and that Ukraine is not a proper country, he would not want to suffocate his neighbour’s independence.

That notion is refuted by all the evidence of campaigns to coerce countries deemed by the Kremlin to be errant possessions since the collapse of the Soviet Union.

When Nigel Farage repeated the EU-provocation theory of the Ukraine war during the 2024 general election campaign, one prominent defender of Ukrainian sovereignty described the Reform UK leader’s assertions as “ahistorical drivel” and “Kremlin propaganda”. That stalwart friend of Kyiv was one Boris Johnson.

There is nothing unusual about Johnson contradicting himself. His talent as a political communicator came from the ability to hold whichever view was expedient to him in the moment and, for the duration of that moment, appear to hold it sincerely. In a more generous reading, he rose to the occasion of Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, understanding events in their proper geopolitical perspective (and with access to classified intelligence reports), which afforded a different reading of Putin’s motives.

In 2016, his focus had been wilfully myopic. The goal of maximising Eurosceptic votes meant reaching for any argument that presented Brussels in a negative light. If that involved narrating the cause of a conflict on the other side of the continent in warped terms that matched the Kremlin story, so be it.

Putin despised the EU for his reasons; the leave campaign despised it for theirs. Johnson was not minded to interrogate whether that alignment of enmities discredited his cause.

This is the context in which Andy Burnham’s recent assertion that Russia meddled in the referendum needs to be understood. The prime minister said it was inconceivable, given all the evidence of Kremlin interference in elections around the world, that the toolkit of subversion would not have been deployed in support of Brexit.

That is not a controversial claim to anyone with a glancing awareness of Russian foreign policy and the means by which it is pursued – the swarms of bot accounts flooding social media with falsehoods; dirty money channelled to extremists; industrial dissemination of conspiracy theories and stoking of intercommunal tensions to undermine social coherence, deplete trust in democracy and make it less functional.

No candidate who was knowingly complicit in that process will admit as much. But even those who were unaware that their cause was boosted by Kremlin troll farms have incentives to deny it. No one wants their heroic victory recast as useful idiocy in service of a hostile power.

Conservatives have called Burnham’s intervention “dangerous and divisive”, which could be interpreted as a denial that interference happened or just as a preference that it not be mentioned to protect delicate pro-Brexit sensibilities.

Farage’s feelings were certainly hurt. He called the prime minister a liar and described the whole thing as a “Russia hoax” – the formula Donald Trump applied to well-substantiated allegations that his 2016 presidential campaign got a helping hand from Moscow. The Reform leader can’t be too surprised by the idea of Kremlin influence in British politics. His party’s former leader in Wales is serving a jail term for taking bribes from Russian spies.

The backlash forced Downing Street to clarify that the prime minister didn’t mean to cast aspersions on the legitimacy of the referendum result. That is the right position when there is no way of knowing what impact, if any, foreign meddling might have had. The views that interference happened and also that the leave campaign would have prevailed anyway are compatible.

Some remainers might seek comfort in the idea that Britain’s democracy was hijacked and diverted through clouds of Russian-induced false consciousness to the wrong destination. The banal truth is that the Eurosceptic side won enough arguments and voters made their choice freely.

Brexiters didn’t need any outside help to turn latent anti-immigration sentiment into active hostility to free movement across European borders.

The Russia dimension is more relevant when it comes to a geopolitical argument that the pro-European side failed to land. In June 2016 it was hard to make the peril of strategic isolation for Britain, self-exiled from the club of European democracies, no longer confident in the transatlantic relationship, seem vivid or imminent.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Trump’s first presidential election was five months away. The full extent of his scorn for the US’s allies and his admiration for authoritarians would not be clear for years. His propensity to behave like a private client of the Putin regime can still shock, even if it no longer surprises, as with the sanctions-busting deal he struck last week to import billions of dollars of Russian diesel.

The hope, entirely vain, is to depress pump prices and assuage voter frustration ahead of midterm elections in November.

On top of the cash infusion for the Kremlin’s war effort, Trump added a bonus of rhetorical venom for Volodymyr Zelenskyy, calling for regime change in Kyiv. He blames Ukrainian targeting of Russian refining capacity for rising global energy costs because his narcissistic ego resists the truth – that his war in Iran has been a disaster for the US and a boon for its enemies. The fact that Russia is an Iranian ally, providing Tehran with intelligence support to resist US military pressure, is no impediment to Trump’s commercial collaborations with the Kremlin.

The exact character and motive involved in that relationship may never be elucidated. But there is no need to seek out hidden levers of influence that may not even exist when publicly available data paints a full enough picture.

Trump and Putin are two greedy despots who recognise no boundary between national interest and self-enrichment. They see law not as a restraint on government but as an instrument to be wielded by powerful leaders against perceived enemies. Their approach to domestic politics is gangsterish, based on networks of patronage and tribute. Their view of foreign affairs is imperial, based on the belief that strong states have natural title to territory in their immediate vicinity, and that big countries can trade in the fate of smaller ones like casino chips.

It is as obvious to Trump that Moscow has a seigneurial right over Ukraine as it is that he should be allowed to decide who governs Venezuela and who sells its oil.

That ethos leads inevitably to competition for resources where rival spheres of influence meet and, if there is no international framework for resolving that competition, to war. This is the lesson, learned the hard way in the 20th century, that became the foundational idea of the European project – the principle of swapping nationalistic rivalry for mutually beneficial cooperation within a common framework of law. That is why Putin and Trump cannot understand the EU and why they hate it.

And that is why the error of Brexit is more pronounced today than it was when the question was put in a plebiscite, and why Burnham is right to draw attention to the fact that Russia had a preferred side. The prime minister is also right when he says that rejecting the possibility of restoring closer ties with the EU would be “a dereliction of duty”.

Many falsehoods were propagated in the referendum campaign, but none greater than the leavers’ boasts of patriotism, when their agenda was certain to make Britain poorer and weaker. A decade into the error, there is no patriotism in pretending that Brexit has worked or in crying betrayal when anyone suggests a reversal. Isolation from the rest of Europe is the result that Britain’s enemies wanted in 2016. Sticking to that path is the route they would choose for Britain again today if they had a vote.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

Did Ukrainian strikes on Russian datacentres reduce online disinformation?

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 15:13:26 GMT

While some viral online graphs suggest less bot activity, Zelenskyy’s claims of improved social media discourse do not entirely pass muster

Over the weekend, Ukraine carried out at least three airstrikes on datacentres belonging to the Russian search engine company Yandex. Reports suggest at least two of these datacentres took significant damage, with Telegram footage appearing to show one on fire. Yandex acknowledged the strikes, and Russian media reported that several websites appeared affected by the downed datacentres.

On Monday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy suggested the strikes had dampened Russia’s massive disinformation operation, saying: “It suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social platforms. There was less hate, less division and fewer provocations.”

It is a commendable hope, but experts say the Ukrainian president may have overstated his case.

Probably not. While a few graphs went viral on social media suggesting there had been a big decline in activity from Yandex bots, those graphs are unrelated to Russian disinformation.

“Our platforms are still monitoring Russian social networks across the world and there is no discernible change in their posting patterns,” said Amil Khan, the chief executive of Valent, a tech startup that tracks disinformation.

Khan and his team track about 40 disinformation networks around the world, from the UK to Australia to Syria, and monitor what narratives they put out and how publics respond to them. They have seen no drop in the volume of posts from these networks, saying: “Yandex datacentres have no practical connection to social media bot farms.”

Yandex is a search engine which also hosts websites and bots. Data from Cloudflare, which monitors worldwide internet traffic, shows a marked decline in activity from bots associated with the Yandex network on 8 October and 11 October, corresponding to the dates of two of the strikes.

The independent Russian news outlet Meduza reports that a number of websites in Russia are down: major banks, retailers, sports apps and Yandex’s services such as Yandex Go and Yandex Eats. It suggests the damage took out a large part of Yandex’s operation and could take months to fully repair.

Some online commentators have mistaken the Cloudflare data to mean that the decline in bot activity has led to a major drop in disinformation on social media. But this is not what experts have noticed.

“The term ‘bot’ can mean many different things,” said Michał ‘Rysiek’ Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert. “When Cloudflare data shows a precipitous drop in ‘bot’ traffic, that does not mean ‘automated social media troll accounts’, it means ‘software that makes automated web requests on a large scale.’” What Cloudflare picked up was a decline in activity from Yandex’s web crawlers. These are used by search engines to index websites and help users to find them, said Khan.

State-sponsored disinformation networks – the kind of “bots” a lot of people misinterpreted this as – could still be affected by the strikes, said Woźniak. “But those effects are going to be much more indirect.”

Those networks are far more distributed, and more resilient, said Ned Mendez, the head of research at Alliance4Europe. “Platforms will routinely flag traffic from datacentres as likely automated, so serious bot operations run more through distributed methods, such as residential connections and phone farms, that airstrikes can’t really knock out.”

“We can’t simply bomb the bots out of existence, however appealing that might sound,” said Mendez. “They aren’t really a single set of buildings that can be switched off.”

Khan said the Ukrainians could consider taking action against companies such as the Internet Research Agency, Yevgeny Prigozhin’s Wagner-linked troll farm that was engaged in influence operations until 2023. But another tactic could be to work with Europe to disrupt the supply chain and recruitment pipeline of private sector contractors used by the Kremlin.

Another tactic could be to pressure big social media companies to moderate disinformation on their platforms. Khan’s team has successfully worked with Meta to tamp down on inflammatory content in Sudan.

But, said Khan, the Trump administration would probably push back on this, hard. “I can see why blowing up datacentres is an easier option.”

‘Shocking and sobering’: UK bird populations fall to lowest level on record

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 15:08:25 GMT

Nearly half of species are in decline, with farmland birds and seabirds the worst hit, conservation bodies say

Wild bird populations in the UK have fallen to their lowest level since records began, figures show, with nearly half of species in decline.

Figures produced by leading nature conservation bodies for the government show that average populations across 132 native breeding species fell by 19% between 1970 and 2025, with farmland birds and seabirds the worst hit in recent years.

Prof Richard Gregory, the head of monitoring at the RSPB, called the overall findings “shocking and sobering”.

“Birds are indicators of the way we’re looking after the countryside and the world around us,” he said. “We’re losing the birds that people are so emotionally connected to and want to protect.”

Average populations of turtle doves have fallen by more than half in five years, showing no sign of the bird recovering from the brink of extinction. Tree sparrows, wood warblers and capercaillie were among the birds with the next biggest average annual decreases between 2019 and 2024.

Swifts, whose arrival for many marks the beginning of summer, have declined by about 25% in five years, an average of nearly 6% a year across the UK. Bullfinches fell at a similar rate nationally, and by an average of 11% a year in England.

Of the 132 native breeding species tracked, 45% have declined over the past five years, while just 27% have increased. In England, 55% of monitored species have declined.

Seabirds are the worst hit group, down by more than a fifth over the past five years. Dr Ailidh Barnes, who helps build the index at the British Trust for Ornithology, said avian flu had “decimated” species such as Arctic skuas and terns.

after newsletter promotion

The disease spread quickly, she said, because seabirds nested shoulder to shoulder, and each year a different species appeared to suffer. “There’s a lag of data collection and then data analysis, and now we’re actually seeing that effect coming through,” she said.

Farmland bird populations have decreased by 63% since 1970 and 12% since 2020. Defra attributes the long-term decline to changes in farming since the 1950s, including the loss of mixed farming (crops and livestock), increased pesticide and fertiliser use, and the removal of hedgerows.

Gregory said if the trend continued, the songs of farm birds such as skylarks and yellowhammers would become only “memories” of what the countryside used to be like.

“It’s a familiar story of declining farmland [birds],” he added. “That’s not showing any upturn. We need to do more there to get nature-friendly farming right and help support farmers.”

Despite the general decline, some populations are booming. Red kite populations have risen by 48% since 2019, and firecrests are up 300% over the same period. Gregory also highlighted the number of cranes “really coming back from extinction in the UK”, rising to 87 pairs nationally.

Gregory said these examples proved concerted efforts to save species worked. “We know the main drivers of change and we can bring about recovery, but we need to massively scale up our conservation intervention,” he said. “We need more funding to support these conservation measures and they need to be at a larger spatial scale.”

A Defra spokesperson said: “We are committed to the recovery and protection of our native birds. There are multiple pressures on wild bird populations, including avian flu. We are acting to protect them, from supporting farmers to manage their land in a way that benefits farmland birds, to working with fishers to prevent the accidental catch of seabirds.”

‘A tipping point of ickiness’: Welsh star Tom Rhys Harries on playing eyelid-snipping DC supervillain Clayface

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 14:58:35 GMT

He cut his teeth playing rock stars and pretty posh boys. Speaking from his LA home, the actor talks about landing his first blockbuster lead in the grisly DC horror. Will it be too shocking for comic book fans?

Exactly 13 years ago this month, Tom Rhys Harries was hanging by his ankles from a meat hook every night. Playing a teenage rock’n’roll idol abducted by gangsters in a revival of Jez Butterworth’s Mojo, Harries was fresh out of drama school and the only unknown in a cast led by Ben Whishaw and Rupert Grint. The Guardian’s Michael Billington likened him to “an embryonic Elvis”.

Now the 36-year-old Cardiff-born actor has the title role in Clayface, a violent DC Comics supervillain blockbuster set in Batman’s stomping ground, Gotham City. This puts him in the company of fellow Brits in the comic-book universe, such as Tom Holland (Spider-Man), Robert Pattinson (Batman) and David Jonsson, recently announced as the new Black Panther. “I felt ready to do this,” says Harries. “Had I been younger, I’d have been suffocated by the insecurity of wanting to do a good job but not having that quiet trust in getting there.”

Harries is speaking over video call from the beach-adjacent Los Angeles home he shares with his girlfriend, Amy Allen. She is the professional musician of the two: songwriter of the year at the Grammys two years running, no less, for her work with Sabrina Carpenter and others. It is Harries, though, who is giving rock star this morning, even all this time after Mojo, in his grey denim shirt with a silver chain against tanned skin and assorted silver rings on his fingers. Stadium-rocker pomposity, however, is in short supply. Standing up to shut the door, he draws attention to his fashion faux pas. “I’ve got a smart shirt on but then these,” he laughs, gesturing to his navy-blue shorts. “Party on the bottom, business on top. Classic Zoom.”

Harries has earned the right to relax. He spent three months auditioning to play the severely mutilated protagonist of Clayface for producers James Gunn (Guardians of the Galaxy) and Matt Reeves (The Batman). How did he stay sane all that time? “I didn’t.”

His character is rising star Matt Hagen, who has just received his first Oscar nomination when he sleeps with the girlfriend of a razor-wielding mob boss and pays the price. His face slashed to ribbons and his career in tatters, Matt’s only hope lies with scientist Dr Caitlyn Corr (Naomi Ackie) and her miracle serum. This restores his good looks and gives him the power to change his appearance at will but comes with unstable side effects. In one scene, his eyelids melt, forcing him to snip away at the resulting sticky mess with a pair of nail scissors. Described by Harries as “the film’s tipping point of ickiness”, it is a moment that will be triggering for any conjunctivitis sufferers and plain disgusting for everyone else.

Closer to horror than anything in the superhero canon, Clayface is a cross between Darkman, in which Liam Neeson is a disfigured scientist who creates synthetic faces, and The Substance, the Demi Moore gross-out satire on ageing, vanity and celebrity. Despite being a pretty-boy actor playing a pretty-boy actor, Harries shrugs off any personal resonance in his own film about losing face. “I’m not interested in the vanity of it.” His looks, he says, “just happen to be an aspect of my work”.

A perceptive actor he may be but it is his otherworldly appearance which grabs you: penetrating eyes, a square, sinewy face, defiant chin and floppy vanilla hair. What does he see when he looks in the mirror? “I don’t know, man,” he says, squirming at the thought of analysing his own appearance. It has been integral, though, to films such as the 2016 folk horror Crow, where he exuded a Bowie-esque alien quality as a woodland-dwelling teenage mystic. “A Bowie-esque alien quality,” he muses. “You’re not the first person to say that. It’s not for me to comment on. I would hit a creative roadblock very quickly if I got too mired in aesthetics.”

Bowie was also a reference point in Harries’s first film role in 2011. Not only was Hunky Dory, starring Minnie Driver as an inspirational teacher, named after one of the singer’s albums, it also boasted a scene in which Harries leads his classmates in a mandolin-and-brass-tinged rendition of The Man Who Sold the World. Screen International singled out Harries as the cast member who “may ultimately become the star here”.

He was oblivious to the buzz. “And yet I’ve got negative reviews seared into my mind.” Proving his point, he quotes one from his early days. “It said, ‘Newcomer Tom Rhys Harries is out of his depth’. I read that and thought, ‘I don’t know if I’m going to get out of bed today’.”

The son of two teachers at Welsh-language schools, Harries has his parents to thank for being “ahead of the curve” in getting him tested for ADHD at the age of seven. “I don’t think I would be doing this job if I didn’t have ADHD. I notice traits within myself that I think are fairly commonplace with [the condition]. If I’m interested in something, I will hyper-fixate on it. That’s born out of a kind of peacefulness in being able to zero in on one thing because it gives your brain a rest.”

School was a struggle. “I was very naughty. I can really see a fork in the road where, had I not been supported by teachers and mentors, my life could have gone in a different direction.” That realisation instilled in him the need to prove himself. “It’s about repaying those people,” he says.

He “fell into” drama school, aced the audition for Hunky Dory in his first year, went from Bowie to Elvis with Mojo and has been building his career ever since: he took posh-boy roles in the horror-comedy Slaughterhouse Rulez, where he was a boarding-school bully, and the TV kidnapping whodunit Suspicion, opposite Uma Thurman. He went wild as an Ibiza DJ who meets a nasty end in the Netflix murder mystery White Lines, then joined Ralph Fiennes and Juliette Binoche in The Return, a Homer adaptation which pipped The Odyssey to the post.

Still, he has never had a showcase like Clayface. The gooey, grisly special effects may be the main attraction but the movie would count for little without his notes of rage, torment and vulnerability.

There is no escaping the fact, though, that Clayface arrives at a precarious time for any comic book movie not featuring Batman, Spider-Man or the Avengers. Box office disasters such as The Marvels, Joker: Folie à Deux and Supergirl, Clayface’s recent DC Comics stablemate which is predicted to lose more than $100m, indicate that fatigue has set in.

On this matter, Harries’s glass is half full. “That’s what excites me about Clayface,” he says. “It is trying to do something different in a space that is asking for that. The medium needs a shake-up and I hope that people feel they can support the film purely on the basis that it will allow studios the confidence to experiment.”

It seems unlikely, in the wake of the costly Tom Cruise catastrophe Digger and the recent Warner Bros-Paramount merger, that studios will be in the mood to do anything but play it safe, irrespective of whether Clayface triumphs or tanks. “Who’s to say? No one would have expected Backrooms or Obsession to come out of nowhere and do what they did. It’s such an unknown quantity.”

Time will tell if Harries is any kind of industry prognosticator but a star he undoubtedly is. Face it.

Clayface is in cinemas from 23 October

Check the waistband – and beware sneaky jargon: the expert guide to buying clothes that last

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 14:00:05 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Should you look for French seams or overlocking? Is dry-clean only a red flag? And how do you spot quality when shopping online? We asked the pros

How to make your leather last a lifetime

Take a look at the outfit you’re wearing now: how many times have you worn each item? And how long have you had them? Just over 10 years ago, Eco-Age founder Livia Firth and journalist Lucy Siegle launched the 30 wears challenge to encourage people to buy clothes they would wear at least 30 times.

The 30 wears challenge is a great concept. As a journalist interested in sustainable fashion, I’ve enjoyed applying this rule for years and found the goal can often be surpassed, but with one proviso: clothing must be chosen carefully. The goal is only realistic if garments are of good enough quality to stand up to repeated wear. So, how do you know if your clothes really are well made? Does it mean you have to spend a fortune on them? Do you need to know the difference between a French seam and an overlock seam? And how can we judge clothing quality before buying if we are, like 37% of Britons, getting most of our clothes online? I spoke to experts to find out.

Ask anyone who knows about clothes how to check for quality, and they will always talk about seams. “A seam’s primary purpose is to give a piece of clothing shape, and crucially structural integrity,” says Leigh Morris, a sustainability and product development consultant. “A bad seam, either poorly constructed or poorly placed, is the difference between a piece of clothing that looks good, feels great, and lasts, or one that feels awkward, looks questionable, and starts to come apart way before its time.”

But it’s not necessarily about whether a garment has a premium French seam (which neatly hides raw edges) or a more affordable overlock one (a quicker technique that sews over the raw edges with loops of thread). Both types have their place so long as they are done to a high standard. “It’s very much about whether or not the seams are loose and you can just tug slightly at them to see if they separate easily,” says Andrea Cheong, a fashion educator and author of Why Don’t I Have Anything to Wear? “If the inside is as good as the outside, it’s a good indication we’re on the right track. Examine high-friction areas [that are prone to] splitting, like the crotch on trousers.”

“In good garment construction, certain inner details are reinforced and properly concealed,” says Vianna Chan, a textile technologist and content creator for the blog Styled by Science. “A quality garment reinforces areas that bear the brunt of daily movement, such as pocket corners and zips. Gently pull both sides of a seam. If you see dense stitches that hold firm, rather than individual threads stretching apart and letting the light through, that is a good sign. Fast fashion skips many of these steps because labour and materials are expensive.”

She explains that fast-fashion waistbands, which are often a folded-over fabric sewn on to exposed elastic, are something to look out for, adding that well-made full waistbands, which usually consist of a band reinforced with sturdy interfacing to prevent rolling and conceal raw edges, help spread tension across the waist. “Sewing in a full waistband takes more time [ie labour costs], and requires more fabric and thread. Because these details are not visible from the garment’s outside, they are the easiest place to take shortcuts,” Chan says. So don’t worry if you know nothing about sewing – just get used to turning your potential new clothes inside-out and giving them a gentle tug.

We sometimes think dry-clean-only labels are a sign of good quality clothing, but they can mean the opposite, because the simple act of washing might make the garment fall apart. Morris warns this is especially true for pieces that you would have in heavy rotation in your wardrobe, such as tops and jumpers. “Brands can often default to using ‘do not wash, dry clean only’ labels if the fabric used was primarily selected for look or effect and not for wear, or if rigorous testing was not undertaken in the development and selection process.” These labels place more responsibility for care on the wearer and give the brand more scope to argue that the garment was damaged by incorrect care, rather than badly made.

Of course, there are some items that should be dry cleaned. “Tailoring is a prime example due to the complexity of construction and components used,” continues Morris. It’s also worth considering how much you’ll wear the item in question, not least because constant dry cleaning is a pain, expensive, and not great for the environment. “Is it a special garment? Is it tailoring? Is it occasionwear?” adds Cheong. “Also, where did you buy it? Because if you bought it from [a high-street store], it’s unlikely to be such a fine premium material that you do need to get it dry cleaned.”

Beware of material deception, where marketing language can make a garment sound as though it’s made from something it isn’t. Natural fibres such as wool and linen can be more sustainable than some synthetics, and they can feel more premium and are often more breathable and comfortable to wear. That can mean – in my experience at least – you’re likely to wear them more often.

Sign up to The Filter

Get the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.

after newsletter promotion

Chan suggests that if a brand uses labels such as “silk like”, it may be trying to mimic the look and feel of silk while using a synthetic fibre such as polyester. “Other sneaky examples are: ‘wool like’, ‘linen feel’, ‘premium blend’, ‘natural feel’. None of these speaks to the actual fibre composition and is instead meant to mislead the customer into thinking they are getting something of higher quality. Always read the label as your source of truth.”

If, like me, you don’t live near a big city, or even a town with any fashion stores, you probably do most of your clothes shopping online. So how do you virtually turn clothes inside-out? “I think watching clothes and movement is really useful,” says Cheong. “How baggy is the lining? Does the skirt move properly? Does it bunch around the hips and the waist or the shoulders when the model’s moving?” If a brand doesn’t have videos on its website, try looking at its Instagram account. If available, read product reviews and always check the returns policy so you can send back anything that doesn’t pass your home inside-out test.

It’s also a good idea to consider the cost per wear of an item before you buy it. This is calculated by dividing the cost by the number of times you expect to wear it: for example, a £30 T-shirt worn the suggested 30 times would cost £1 per wear. The longer your clothes last, the more you are likely to wear them, so even an expensive £200 cashmere sweater would cost just under £1.70 per wear if you wore it once a month for 10 years (I have one such sweater).

I haven’t shopped on the high street for nearly eight years; instead, I choose to buy from smaller, independent brands and those that produce in limited batches. These types of brands often have a wealth of information about their supply chains, to the point where they boast about the wonderful factories and artisans who make the clothing. In fact, you may even see pictures and videos of the production processes on their websites and social media feeds: a great indicator of quality. Many will add reassurance that their skilled workers are being paid fairly. They may also be using natural fibres with certifications such as the Global Organic Textile Standard, or cotton sourced through schemes such as the Better Cotton Initiative. All this may mean you pay a little more. But in my experience, buying less and wearing more evens out the cost in the long run.

If you’re unsure how the clothes you want to buy are made, drop the brand an email or social media message to ask. I have done this many times; it not only weeds out brands that don’t cut the mustard – in turn saving me money – but also builds my trust in those I’ll buy from in the future, albeit less frequently than in my fast fashion days.

Hannah Rochell is a journalist who specialises in writing about – and experiencing – a slower, more sustainable lifestyle, which she documents on her Substack Slowette. This involves everything from switching to eco-friendly cleaning products and advocating for dehumidifiers instead of tumble dryers, to shopping exclusively at responsible fashion brands and learning to sew

Could I make six figures from my couch? Influencers said yes – so I tried

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 14:00:04 GMT

I was seduced by creators hawking passive income hustles. Like the language used in MLMs, it seemed too good to be true

A very specific kind of content began taking over my social media feeds at the end of last year.

I had just finished a short-term contract and returned, with some reluctance, to the financial masochism of freelancing. As I mourned the end of steady paychecks and paid days off – as well as finally having enough money for regular haircuts – I couldn’t tear my eyes away from the glow of the screen.

A typical video starts with an ordinary-looking woman doing ordinary things: typing on a laptop, sipping coffee, perhaps doing some light cleaning. Bright, optimistic music blares in the background.

Then text stretches across the frame: she has made thousands of extra dollars each month, working just a few hours a day from the comfort of her home.

Sometimes the woman – and it’s almost always a woman – speaks directly into the camera. She was able to quit her job and spend more time with her family thanks to her side hustle! It allowed her to pay off debt, cover her mortgage and travel, all while setting her own hours! And with her tips and tutorials, you too can begin making money like her.

Across the screen come promises like:

“How to make passive income online …”

“How to earn daily with your phone …”

“Side hustles for women …”

“Lazy girl side hustles that have made me over $100K …”

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

The gospel of making money on the side, answering to no one but yourself and with no prior training or special skills, has gone global. As of October, Instagram alone had 8.5m posts tagged #sidehustle and 25.6m tagged #passiveincome, with content creators posting from kitchens in the midwest, beaches in New Zealand, country rambles in the UK and hammocks in Bali.

“It’s the perfect hybrid of labor and leisure, where the money comes in as you are going about your day,” said Brooke Erin Duffy, a communications professor at Cornell University who studies the impact of social media on creative work and labor. “The term ‘passive income’ puts an especially seductive spin on this. You don’t have to do anything and you just reap all of the benefits.”

These women were offering ways to make money that seemed doable: designing and selling stationery, earning commission on goods I already use, creating products with little to no overhead. The “passive” part would come in after a few hours of upfront work: you set up your hustle once, then sit pretty as the profits pour into your bank account.

With my financial future looking a lot more uncertain, I decided to put some of their hustles to the test. I went in with cautious optimism: I wanted to know how realistic these schemes really were, and whether I could actually make money from any of them.

What I found instead was what I believe to be the new face of multilevel marketing – and the future of scamming and getting scammed.

It’s easy to understand the allure of side-hustle content.

Plainly put, things are looking grim. In 2026, amid an affordability crisis, a few extra hundred dollars a month can be life-changing. It can mean paying down debt, being able to take a sick day or ordering a pizza when you’re too tired to cook.

But influencers rarely present side hustles as a response to global financial insecurity. They sell them as easy freedom, attainable without even getting out of bed. It’s easy to see why people buy in.

“On TikTok, I see reels that go insanely viral of just girls of all ages, being like, ‘how can I make money from home?’” said Erin McGoff, a career advice content creator who has more than 7m followers across different platforms.

I had a few rules for what I was and wasn’t willing to do. I didn’t want to put my face on any social media, and I didn’t want to use AI to create any products or videos.

Making and selling digital templates – probably the hustle that resurfaced the most during my nightly doomscrolling – checked all these boxes. The idea is simple: use the graphic design platform Canva to create invitations, planners or ebooks, then sell them on marketplaces such as Etsy. And according to the influencers, the earning potential is enormous:

“Use Canva to pay off your debt in under 45 seconds …”

“Canva is basically a money printer …”

“How Canva can pay your rent …”

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

I like pretty stationery and enjoy putting together E-vites centered on ridiculous party themes, so I decided to try it out and go all in with a boozy bachelorette aesthetic, heavy with bright colors and graphics of alcoholic beverages. I named my store GirlyGirlStationery and focused on putting together invitation templates that looked like a Barbie fever dream after a night of drinking pink prosecco.

But a professional graphic designer, I am not. I got overwhelmed quickly, second-guessing every design decision. I felt myself clenching my jaw trying to align my images and format my borders. In one instance, I had a listing up for several weeks before I realized that I had placed the goose illustration comically off center.

To make things worse, a quick Etsy search turned up thousands of templates that looked better than mine, many clearly using the same Canva artwork and styling. Some shops had more than 2,200 templates for sale; it had taken me eight hours to make eight and another five to fix them after realizing I had used Canva Pro elements that buyers would have to pay to download.

I made my first sale 12 days after I officially launched my Etsy store – an addictively giddy feeling that was undercut by the fact that I didn’t really make any profit.

I had kept the prices of my products low to drive upfront sales, with each template going for $2. Not taking into consideration the one-time $19 fee I paid to set up the shop, but adding in the processing fee, the transaction fee and the listing fee of $0.20 per listing, I made about $1.25 on that one sale.

In total for my first month on Etsy – about 23 and half hours of work – my net profit was negative 32 cents.

I grew up in the type of middle-class Massachusetts suburb where multilevel marketing (MLM) schemes had a foothold.

I remember listening to my mother complain each time she returned from what was supposed to be a casual social gathering but had turned out to be an acquaintance’s sales pitch for tupperware or cubic zirconia jewellery. After graduation, I watched from afar as a number of my former schoolmates began guilting their Facebook friends into buying “buttery soft leggings” and sisterhood-empowering mascara.

So when I started watching side-hustle influencers, some of the language felt immediately familiar, particularly in the way they present something nonsensical in a sensical way, making the aspirational seem easily achievable.

Take this Instagram video: “Instead of watching Netflix tonight, take 30 minutes, open Canva and create a digital product that you can sell 1,000 times a month for $17. That’s $17,000 each month.”

Yeah, OK – the math checks out. And I do watch a lot of Netflix. But wait, will I actually sell this product 1,000 times a month?

Most audaciously, some had found another way to monetize the hustle itself. If at first you don’t succeed, buy my masterclass, pdf, ebook or training program, they told their followers. Many of those products traced back to the same small ecosystem, with influencers spawning new micro-influencers who repeat the same scripts.

“There are thousands of accounts that are like ‘make money with Katie’, ‘make money with Marie’, ‘make money with Stephanie’, and they all are selling $7 courses,” said McGoff, the career advice content creator. “It’s a digital marketing or digital products course, but what the course does is it upsells you to a more expensive course and then that course just incentivizes people to sell the course.”

These courses immediately sent up a red flag for me. And yet, I reasoned, these women weren’t just trying to get me to buy questionable courses, nor were they dangling the prospect of private jets or luxury beach vacations before me. These weren’t get-rich-quick schemes, but a chance to make some extra cash without putting on a bra or changing out of my sweatpants. They boasted flexible hours that work around nap times and school pickups for mothers and homemakers who already feel exhausted. The upfront costs were minimal: all you needed was an internet connection.

I contacted Stacie Bosley, an economics professor at Hamline University who specializes in the MLM industry. She confirmed that, at face value, these side hustles did not meet the definition of an MLM.

In an MLM scheme, Bosley said, “you’re contractually buying the right to sell a company’s products but you’re also getting compensated for recruiting people and that compensation is not really tied to legitimate sales.” She continued: “It’s just sort of dressing around a pyramid scheme in that it’s really not about retail sales, but about recruitment.”

These side hustles don’t have one big bad overlord at the top of the pyramid. Each is supposed to be an independent venture: you make a product and sell it. Yet influencers promote them with the cultish zeal of Mary Kay saleswomen. With digital templates, that enthusiasm defies basic economics: if everyone follows their advice and starts selling Canva templates on Etsy, the market becomes flooded, making it harder for anyone to stand out.

“It’s a deceptive offer, that somehow you can just do this and that it can work for everybody without any acknowledgment of demand,” Bosley said. ***

I decided to branch out.

Next up was affiliate marketing, another popular hustle that met my personal rules. This one has you promoting a brand’s products through a personalized link that earn you commission whenever someone makes a purchase through it. It’s like a referral code, except you get paid instead of getting a discount.

The side hustlers kept telling me that I didn’t need to have a huge follower count or social media presence to become an affiliate marketer, with companies such as ShopMy, LTK and Amazon Associates making it easy.

But like the digital template scheme, it just didn’t make sense. Why would anyone bother to buy a product through me, with my hyperlink, if they didn’t know me?

I didn’t want to use my personal social media accounts, but influencers had a workaround: create a new account dedicated to affiliate marketing. Several recommended Pinterest, where you can post images linking directly to products, and DigiStore24 as the affiliate network that provides links to products you can earn commissions on.

Sadly, most of the products on DigiStore24 are the sort of garbage you would send to your spam folder: shady supplements, weird energy pendants and online courses on how to be a better lover. I decided to try my luck with a light therapy mask – the only product I do use on a frequent basis. I made three pins that all together got 79 impressions in their first six weeks – and no sales.

After a few weeks of nothing, I decided to try another affiliate marketing site, FlexOffers. com – and I was almost immediately rejected. The email told me I should get back in touch with them should I “later have more traffic sources”.

So I went directly to brands I knew. Sephora’s affiliate program directed me to Rakuten Advertising, where I applied to promote Wet ‘N Wild and Dr Brandt, this time using my actual Instagram account. Both applications were rejected the same day for failing the company’s social media network policy, with no explanation of what that meant.

That was when the logic of the side hustle economy began to come into focus.

Influencers had insisted that anyone could do this: no following, business experience or digital expertise required. But almost every hustle I tried seemed to demand precisely those things. “Affiliate marketing is a real way to make money, but it is far from a get-rich-quick secret and it is definitely not passive,” said McGoff.

What was much more reliable was the attention generated by talking about side hustles. Creators boosted engagement by asking viewers to comment words like “content” or “begin” to receive free prompts and tutorials, turning would-be entrepreneurs into hopeful followers. I watched one woman start a new Instagram account in May devoted entirely to side hustles. Six months later, she had more than 27,000 followers.

The hustle, increasingly, seemed to be selling the idea of the hustle. It’s the influencer as a possibility: if you work hard enough and follow their instructions, you too can quit your office job, be your own boss and make six figures for just a few hours of work a day.

The pyramid may look different, but by borrowing the tactics, psychology and promises of MLMs, it feels like a pyramid scheme all the same.

“What they’re selling, it’s the same as MLMs,” said Mara Einstein, a media studies professor at Cuny Queens College and author of Hoodwinked: How Marketers Use the Same Tactics As Cults.

“They’re selling a dream.”

And yet, not everyone in this space is a scammer.

On one end, there are grifters and creators who aren’t fully honest about their earnings and partnerships. Waleed Khan, a 24-year-old financial consultant in Calgary who is reviewing various side hustles, said he discovered that one person promoting the “clipping” side hustle – when you make money by breaking down popular videos into clips and posting them on to YouTube shorts – was actually the founder behind the clipping website he was instructing viewers to use for the scheme.

And on the other end, there are people who really do make these hustles work.

After giving birth to her son, Tricia Orme, a 38-year-old mother of two in Washington state, started exploring print-on-demand. And she was “really bad at it” at first, Orme said. “My designs were terrible.”

But as she kept going, she found a hole in the market. She needed a way to show customers what her designs would look like on clothing without having to photograph models wearing each product herself. So she began using AI to generate stock images of people in blank clothing, then placing her designs on to them.

Thus, she became the @mockupmama. The digital products she sells are the stock images she created on AI, so that others pursuing a print-on-demand side hustle have ready-made mockups on which to display their products.

After making $146,578.22 in Etsy sales over the course of three years, she has turned her focus toward mentorship and teaching how to sell and market digital products.

“I am such a firm believer that if you have more than you need, build a longer table, not a higher fence,” she said. She has had about 300 people buy a $150-250 course from her and has about 155 active students who pay $19 a month to be in her private coaching group.

She is, by all accounts, successful – and that shouldn’t be a surprise. Success stories will happen because once you take away the social media, these hustles are basically a combination of sales and marketing – trades as old as time itself. Digital products, be they print-on-demand T-shirts or silly stationery, is just art you make on a graphic design platform.

But not everyone is an artist, or talented at sales or marketing. Orme, for example, had worked in corporate retail and had an understanding of the marketplace before beginning her venture.

“It’s like dating apps,” Einstein said. “Almost everybody knows at least one or two people who met through a dating app. So you keep pointing to them like, ‘keep trying, you can do this too.’”

“Part of their job is making it look easy,” said Duffy, the Cornell communications professor. But in reality, success in these spaces is a combination of “pluck, luck and the algorithm”, she said.

Over six months, I tried to launch five different side hustles. I made just two sales and spent more than $200 on Etsy fees, a Canva subscription and eRank, a tool Orme recommended for identifying popular search terms and boosting sales.

Khan, the Calgary content creator, also didn’t make much from digital templates. The only big profit he’s made so far is the C$600 he got for using AI to create websites for small businesses – and that only happened when he got off the internet and put in real world effort.

“The claim was you can make $15,000 a month doing this,” he said. “I made these websites. I called 20 or 25 local businesses and calling didn’t work. Eventually I went in physically to these businesses, to 10 or 15, and only two of them said yes.”

I had difficulty finding others struggling with their side-hustle journey, as this is not a space with a big audience for failure – but it’s very clear that Khan and I are not the only ones out there.

And then there’s the question of what all these hustles are putting out into the world.

Every day, new accounts pop up, promising new ways to make money: using AI to copy bestselling coloring books, or churning out slop videos for YouTube views. Etsy, once a haven for handmade crafts and original work, is now awash with generic templates and AI-generated goods.

I thought I had escaped the MLM trap: no boxes of garbage to store, no friends to guilt into buying it. But the garbage is still there. We’ve just moved it out of our homes and garages and on to the internet.
