Man killed by tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park named

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 13:44:01 GMT

William Chapman was pronounced dead at scene on Saturday after scaling fence and entering enclosure

A man killed by a tiger at a zoo in South Yorkshire has been named locally as William Chapman.

Chapman scaled the fence and entered the enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster on Saturday afternoon. Witnesses described seeing Chapman, who has not been officially named by police, walking up to a 200kg male Siberian tiger, named Altai, which attacked him.

The incident lasted only a couple of minutes and Chapman, who is believed to have been in his 20s, was pronounced dead at the scene shortly after.

Videos in which onlookers urged him not to approach the tiger and to “play dead” during the attack were shared online in the aftermath, as well as a number of AI-generated fakes. Police advised members of the public to avoid sharing them. They said the man’s family was being supported by specialist officers.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park was evacuated on Saturday and remained closed for a fourth day on Tuesday.

Dan Swaine, the executive director of place at Doncaster council, said: “As the relevant licensing authority for the Yorkshire Wildlife Park, I can confirm that, in line with our statutory duties, the council has launched a health and safety investigation.

“We are also working with multiple agencies, including the police and health agencies, and are supporting the Yorkshire Wildlife Park in response to the incident. At this time, we won’t be commenting further on the individual or the investigation and we ask that the privacy of those involved is respected at this difficult time.”

The park said staff were receiving specialist support and that Altai, an endangered tiger, would not be euthanised.

Wildlife and zoo experts told the Guardian it was unlikely the wildlife park would have been able to prevent the incident.

Amy Dickman, a professor of wildlife conservation and the director of WildCRU at the University of Oxford, said: “I would not conclude that there was a major issue with zoo safety – the harsh reality is that it is virtually impossible for zoos to stop people who are very determined to breach safety measures.”

Campbell Murn, a lecturer in conservation science at the University of Reading, who until recently sat on the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs’ zoos expert committee, said: “It’s simply not possible … at an attraction like Yorkshire Wildlife Park that gets hundreds of thousands – if not over a million – visitors a year to keep an eye on everybody all the time.”

He added: “If a determined thief wants to get in your house, they’re going to get in your house. You can mitigate risk to a certain point but there’s sometimes no stopping events from happening, unfortunately.”

A spokesperson for the Born Free Foundation, which campaigns to phase out zoos, called for an “urgent review” into “how the man managed to enter the enclosure and what happened next”.

Josh Hazlewood reminds Australia of his worth with six for 49 to see off South Africa

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 13:28:17 GMT

After every stunning Scott Boland performance of recent years, many of them in place of an injured Josh Hazlewood, a reasonable ­question does the rounds: why isn’t Boland the automatic pick in the Test side, and why does Hazlewood take ­precedence when fit? In truth, ­Hazlewood has given a dozen years of answers, but on the fifth day of the ­Durban Test he provided one more reminder with a career-best six for 49, overcoming South African resistance to bowl them out for 206 and seal an Australia win by 214 runs.

Boland is good enough for a full-time spot, and may have been influential if picked. But in the side selected, Hazlewood was essential as South Africa blunted his colleagues. In a noticeable dip given his brilliant past few seasons, Mitchell Starc had radar issues: better around the wicket, though without the swerving reverse swing from his last visit to the ground, but over the wicket he often went too steeply across the right-handers, or down the leg side.

Pat Cummins bowled well but did not produce danger in the second innings, his only blow being self-inflicted thanks to Tristan Stubbs’ loose drive. Nathan Lyon got some bite, and his overs cost nothing, but he was defended well and went wicketless. Three times, Australia needed something from somewhere. Hazlewood kept delivering.

It had started on the fourth ­evening, when Aiden Markram and David Bedingham looked completely comfortable, when Hazlewood bowled the perfect nip-backer length to hit Bedingham’s pad so plainly in front that the batter walked off without challenge. From a tough 73 for one, Australia produced a rush that made it 86 for four.

The next morning, South Africa resumed control. Markram is a fourth-innings specialist, with two hundreds against Australia in three prior attempts, and looked ­immovable. Wiaan Mulder defended with perfect compactness and clarity. They scored enough to avoid ­stagnation, but did not play unnecessary shots. Occasional balls tested them, including another nip-backer that nearly took Markram’s off stump, but they gave every appearance of being able to bat for a draw if bad light brought an early close.

After 25 overs of toil on the day, Australia needed something. And it was not just a matter of Hazlewood getting lucky with a catch down the leg side. Bowling with a ball that had seen 66 overs, he brought in a leg slip to open up another mode of dismissal while targeting the pads. Mulder saw that line and wanted to flick square. A little reverse movement kept it ­tailing towards leg stump. So his flick became an inside edge, and Alex Carey took a one-hander diving left.

Skill had broken the most stubborn stand, one of 32 overs and 69 runs, with Mulder having batted more than two hours for 29. That ­opening allowed Matt Renshaw to get a flirty edge from a decidedly unstubborn Kyle Verreynne in the next over. Then, another stretch of obstinacy. Markram was in a zone, footwork precise for the most ­reliable defence, collecting the odd single like a prisoner does bottle caps to keep himself from going mad. Marco Jansen allowed ­himself to clobber loose balls, but did his best to be good.

Another 17 overs, another rise of concern for Australia about an early finish. Another Hazlewood spell required, this time with a new ball. The one that nips back. This time, the length perfect. Jansen on 35, trying to defend on the front foot, the faintest gap, and the ball through to off stump. Enter Simon Harmer, county pro gnarled as a ti-tree, a couple of first-class tons and 36 fifties to his name. Exit Harmer, three balls later, edging a horrible lifter. Hazlewood had five.

At eight down in the 85th, with 201 on the board, the double strike was when Markram’s resolve ­dissolved. He inside-edged Starc in the next over, having batted two minutes shy of six hours for his 75, and will surely have more of a say in this series. Hazlewood had Anrich Nortje caught at midwicket to ice both the game and his personal cake.

In the process, he jumped up a significant stretch of the Test wickets list: passing Yorkshire legend Fred Trueman on 307, local boy Morne Morkel along with West Indies spinner Lance Gibbs on 309, and the fast and the furious Brett Lee on 310, levelling Indian pair Ishant Sharma and Zaheer Khan on 311. In Australian terms, with three more wickets to pass Mitchell Johnson, Hazlewood would have ahead of him only Dennis Lillee, Glenn McGrath, and Shane Warne, along with his three current colleagues. Fitness pending, next week we could see four of Australia’s top seven wicket-takers in the same team. But this is fast bowling. Fitness also says that Boland, with 82 wickets to his name, will be needed soon enough. As in 2018, Australia leave Durban with a series lead. This time they need to keep it.

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 12:16:55 GMT

African Grand Prix will take place at new track near Kigali

Stefano Domenicali: ‘Today is a landmark moment for F1’

Formula One has confirmed Rwanda will join its calendar, ­having ­concluded a 10-year agreement for the meeting on a ­purpose-built ­circuit, with the first race set for the early 2030s. It will mark the first time F1 has raced in Africa since 1993.

The meeting, to be known as the African Grand Prix, will be held on a circuit in Bugesera, 40km south of the capital, Kigali, and constitutes a successful conclusion to the sport’s long-held ambition to return to the African continent, which Lewis ­Hamilton has championed.

F1 last raced in Africa at Kyalami in South Africa in 1993 and the seven-time world champion Hamilton has been outspoken in his belief that it should return, working behind the scenes to facilitate it.

“For the past six or seven years I’ve been fighting in the background to get a grand prix, sitting with stakeholders and asking the question: ‘Why are we not in Africa? There’s one on every other continent, why not Africa?’” he said this year.

The Rwanda track will be designed by WurzDesign, run by the former driver Alexander Wurz, but no ­specific date has been set for the first race, with F1 only stating the “early 2030s”. That timescale allows for it to be built and then authorised to full FIA – the governing body – Grade 1 status, with a rendition of the circuit indicating an intent for it to flow across the natural contours of the landscape.

South Africa – which hosted its race in East London, now known as KuGompo City, from 1962-66 before it moved to Kyalami in 1967 – was also in the running to host a race amid a booming fanbase in the country. F1, however, went with the proposal from Rwanda and its long-term commitment. The new race is being backed by the government of Rwanda and the Rwanda development board, who intend to develop the venue as a destination not only for motorsport but for promoting economic growth, including hosting events, ­conferences and entertainment.

The country has recently invested heavily in hosting sporting events, including cycling’s road world championships, cricket’s Women’s Challenge Trophy, the 2023 Fifa congress and the Basketball Africa League.

In 2024 Rwanda hosted the FIA prize-giving gala, at which the country’s president, Paul Kagame, announced the intention to bid for a grand prix.

The country has, ­however, attracted accusations of ­sportswashing, notably with Amnesty International forcefully criticising the Rwanda tourist board’s sponsorship of Aston Villa, saying: “The country is prolific in arbitrary detention, torture and the repression of free speech.”

Kagame welcomed the return of F1, believing it would prove inspirational across the continent. “Rwanda is proud to host the Formula One African Grand Prix, and to share this moment with more than 100 million fans across Africa,” he said. “Many of them young people who deserve to see the sport at home and to see themselves in it: as engineers, technicians, entrepreneurs and, one day, drivers.”

The F1 chief executive, Stefano Domenicali, insisted the agreement represented a broader long-term commitment between F1 and Rwanda.

“Today is a landmark moment for Formula One,” he said. “With Rwanda joining the calendar from the next decade, our sport will race in every inhabited continent. This is about much more than hosting a grand prix. Together, we can create lasting economic and social benefits through tourism, investment, skills development and local business growth, ensuring the positive impact of this event is felt for generations.”

South Africa, meanwhile, still ­harbours hope of bringing a grand prix back to the country, with its sports minister, Gayton McKenzie, reacting to reports Rwanda would be given the nod last week by posting on X: “Remember though that one country, Italy, has had two F1s a year, and some react like a ­continent of 55 countries can only get one. Rightwing extremists increasingly likely to consider terrorist attacks, MI5 chief says

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 12:00:14 GMT

Extremists with anti-migrant opinions are becoming increasingly likely to consider carrying out terrorist attacks against immigration centres and asylum hotels in the UK, the head of MI5 has warned.

Ken McCallum said a shift from radicalised rightwing sentiment to violence was “the most marked trend” in the spy agency’s caseload over the past year, contributing to a rise in the overall UK terror threat level.

The comments formed part of a wide-ranging annual threat update in which the spy chief indicated a more aggressive Iran had threatened other military bases in the UK, as well as being behind the incident at RAF Fairford late last month.

He also warned of the potential use of AI by hostile states and terrorists, including to possibly develop a novel bioweapon – while adding that MI5 would create a new AI Threat Assessment Centre to distinguish fact from fiction.

On the evolving extreme rightwing threat, McCallum said there had been an increase in cases where “extremist versions of anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievance are tipping into terrorist intent”, such as planning attacks on migrants and Muslims.

A number of aggressive anti-migrant protests have been held this autumn by the far-right Patriot Platform at Portsmouth and Dover, while racially and religiously motivated offences are running at record levels.

McCallum said young people were particularly likely to gravitate towards extreme rightwing terrorism, and at one point this year the Security Service was “investigating a radicalised … 13-year-old in the UK”.

A year ago, he added, a 16-year-old from Inverclyde received a 10-year prison sentence after he pleaded guilty to planning mass murder by firebombing a Muslim centre in Greenock.

There was a “concerning trend of violence targeted at political figures, religious or community groups”, McCallum said, as demonstrated by the killing of the former minister and Reform UK spokesperson, Ann Widdecombe.

Iran, he said, was trying to expand hostile activities in the UK and now had “ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites”, including the RAF Fairford airbase in Gloucestershire.

Five men from London drove to Whelford, a village next to a base used by the US air force, in three white vans shortly after midnight on 27 September. They were released on police bail a day later after no bombs or explosives were found.

There was also a hint that Iran had sought to target other bases. “Fairford is not unique in the UK,” McCallum said, though he would not be drawn specifically on what other sites had been threatened, or the nature of the threat.

However, allies said his comments were not a reference to RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire, where two Latvians were found by police at 2am inside the perimeter of a base used for US and Nato intelligence operations in Europe. They were subsequently released on police bail.

Iran, though, still has a relatively low level of capability to match its ambitions. Tehran typically hired criminal proxies to carry out operations abroad, so any ability to target a military base “is really a function of the sophistication level of those criminals”.

On Thursday, Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, is due to meet his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon for a discussion where the issue of base security in the UK is almost certain to be discussed. A week after the Fairford incident, the US withdrew 12 B-1 bombers from the RAF base, which had been used to attack Iran in the spring and early summer.

MI5’s counter-Iran operation has led to more than 50 arrests in the UK in the past year, with much of Tehran’s increased aggression aimed at “British Jewish communities” including terrorist plots and arson attacks against synagogues, businesses and ambulances.

In an unexpected observation, McCallum said he was “particularly focused” on the risk of hostile states or terrorists using AI to generate new, deadly bioweapons, particularly if guardrails introduced by software companies failed.

Last month, Anthropic, the company behind Claude, warned that there were “five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development” – and said misuse could have serious consequences.

Liam Booth-Smith, head of Europe policy at Anthropic and a former chief of staff to Rishi Sunak, told the Commons business committee on Tuesday that there was a risk of real harm from the fast-developing technology.

“Without appropriate mitigations, it’s possible that real harm could be caused in the space of helping people to create biological or chemical weapons,” Booth-Smith said.

The MI5 chief added that AI could also be exploited by cyber hackers, to help terrorists refine their attack plans and even try to use “AI-enabled drones”, he said, and to easily produce “propaganda and radicalising material tailored to the individual”.

In response, MI5 would create a new AI threat assessment centre to bring together expertise from across government to carefully distinguish the reality of the threats generated by the new technology and advise both government and the wider public to “separate the bluster from the realities”.

Russia, the MI5 chief emphasised, remains “aggressor number one” as the Kremlin continues to lash out against the west with assassination plots, explosive threats and cyber-attacks that at times stop “not much short” of conventional warfare.

Moscow tried to interfere in the 2016 Brexit referendum with anti-EU coverage on RT and Sputnik media, and via troll social media accounts, but there was a big difference between “what may have been attempted and what actually resulted”.

The UK’s relationship with China was “multifaceted”, with MI5 focused on Beijing’s efforts to steal university research and intellectual property, and obtain political secrets about areas it was interested in.

Overall, threats from hostile states had quadrupled in the last decade and now were running on par with MI5’s counter-terrorism mission. “We have again entered a new era of national security,” he said.

The secret to a non-cloudy chicken stock

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 12:00:03 GMT

Don’t cook it too quickly – and skim, skim, skim, says our expert culinary panel

Why is my chicken stock always cloudy?Ryan, by emailFrom broths and risottos to sauces and braises, there’s no question that a good, flavourful stock will stand you in good stead. “It’s an underestimated kitchen job,” says Adam Byatt, chef/owner of Trinity, in southwest London, and author of Trinity: The Cookbook, which is published next week. “I love stock: it’s wholesome and fruitful, frugal and delicious.”

Ryan’s clarity issue, Byatt says, is “only ever caused by cooking the stock too quickly or by allowing the fat to boil back into the base liquid”. So it’s crucial to take things low and slow. You will also need a pan that’s “big and heavy enough to give the bones enough room for movement, as well as a very fine sieve for straining the stock”.

On to the actual making, and Alissa Timoshkina, author of Lozhka, goes in cold. She puts chicken legs, drumsticks or a leftover roast chicken carcass in a large pot, adds her stock veg – onions, carrots, celery, garlic, say – and aromats (bay, parsley stalks, peppercorns, for instance), then covers the lot with cold water and brings everything very slowly to a boil. She then turns down the heat and leaves it to cook on a very gentle simmer. In the event of that carefully made stock going a bit cloudy, Timoshkina would seek to mollify that by straining the lot through a fine sieve and stirring in a tablespoon of lemon juice, which has the added benefit of being “great for flavour, too”.

Lloyd Morse, chef and co-owner of The Palmerston in Edinburgh, meanwhile, likes to simmer the bones first, “shoogling them occasionally”, to bring more of the scum to the surface: “You really need to skim the life out of it.” It’s only at this point that he adds the veg: “And keep skimming that top layer,” he says, adding that it’s important to be aware that “the more agitation or the hotter the pot gets, the cloudier the stock will be”.

Essentially, “if nothing is ever actually boiled, Ryan’s stock should be nice and clear”, says Louis Lingwood, head chef at Osteria Vibrato in London, who cooks his chicken stock “on the lowest possible heat for a whole day”, before discarding the bones and leaving the stock to sit until all the fat rises to the top. Skim that off with a ladle, then reduce the stock very slowly.

Lingwood has another trick up his sleeve to guarantee a clearer stock: get it in the freezer. “Defrost it through a sieve lined with muslin (or through a lined perforated tray), and the stock will be crystal clear.” Speaking of the freezer, freezing stock in ice-cube trays, then whacking them in a sealed container, is a welcome manoeuvre for those occasions when only small quantities of stock are required.

Of course, Ryan could make his life a whole lot easier by simply cooking his stock in the oven, Morse says: “My top tip is to make it in an oven-safe dish, such as a Le Creuset [other brands are, of course, available], then pop it in the oven overnight to cook super slowly,” by which he means about 90C. “The indirect heat makes the clearest stock possible, plus, when you wake up, you’ll have a lovely smell in the kitchen.” Convenience food at its best.

I’m a pediatrician. Loss of human connection is the biggest threat to kids, not AI

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 11:00:56 GMT

Amid worries about children’s relationship to tech, the solution is often spending more time talking openly with each other

We have become obsessed with the idea that screens are destroying human connection.

The evidence seems to be everywhere. Each week headlines warn of teenagers addicted to phones, a loneliness epidemic and the dangers of AI. The release of The Social Reckoning leads us to ask, “How bad were those guys at Meta?” and then ultimately wonder, “How bad am I if I still use Instagram?” In our day-to-day, we observe workers eating lunch alone while scrolling and friends choosing online games over offline gatherings.

But what if we are focusing on the wrong problem?

The greatest threat to connection may not be technology itself. It may be our growing unwillingness to curiously, thoughtfully and openly communicate about the role technology plays in our lives.

As a pediatrician, this issue often manifests in my clinic. Parents arrive with worries about their teens’ screen time. The parent will demand that their child “fess up” and reveal how many hours they waste on their phone every day. The atmosphere is immediately charged. The teen becomes defensive. The parent is frustrated.

I often suggest that we start somewhere else.

I ask: “Can you share a little about what you do when you are using technology? What do you enjoy? Are there things about your technology use you are worried about and willing to discuss?”

The answers are not usually what people expect. One teen tells me about the friendships she maintained on social media after moving to a new town. Another shows me videos he created to promote his school’s upcoming play. One shares how digital design tools are changing the fashion industry, so she is trying to learn about them now. Another quietly admits that gaming has become so consuming that it feels stressful.

As the conversation unfolds, something changes. The tension in the room eases. Parents relax. The teen patient might even smile a few times. We talk about strategies, relationships, stress and health.

What began as an argument about a device becomes a bigger conversation about health, relationships and life itself.

It often feels that our conversations about technology have become trapped in a false choice between two extreme camps. One camp is made up of the pro-tech enthusiasts, thought to embrace every new device or platform. The other camp is composed of preachers of digital abstinence.

The result is a polarized debate dominated by blame, shame and moral judgment. Instead of asking how technology affects our relationships, our sleep, our work, our wellbeing, we argue endlessly about whether technology is “good” or “bad”.

I was reminded of this recently during a community event focused on digital media. The event included a youth panel with several brave adolescents, willing to speak to an audience of their teachers, community members and parents. I asked the adolescents a question: could you describe a positive conversation you had with a parent about technology?

Every single panelist shook their head.

“I’ve never had that,” one teenager said, uneasily eyeing her mom who was sitting in the front row. The other panelists agreed.

It was a striking moment. Parents routinely talk their children through setbacks in sports, clubs, friendships and school. They listen, ask questions and offer support. Yet when it comes to technology, many conversations begin and end with warnings, criticism or fear.

Sign up to TechScape

A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives

after newsletter promotion

Why is this?

For years, parents have been barraged by alarming headlines about screen time and mental health. Many parents worry there is probably only one right way to approach technology, and they’re failing miserably. Parents are also navigating the necessity of using their own devices for work, home and communication.

The real anxious generation just might be parents.

So how do we fix this? The solution begins with curiosity. Parents can ask what interests their children have online, and why those interests matter. Parents can ask their kids about what questions or worries they have about their tech use, and share some of their own concerns. If a parent missteps by scrolling cute cat videos and delaying dinner, they can acknowledge it and make it a teachable moment for themselves and their kids.

Because children do not need adults who have all the answers.

They need adults willing to ask questions.

These conversations matter because they lower the temperature of the debate. Once we move beyond panic and polarization, we can begin asking better questions on the societal level. How should digital platforms be designed to ensure safety? What obligations do technology companies have to children? What policies would support healthier digital environments?

If we want to preserve human connection in the age of social media and AI, the answer is not to simply spend less time with technology. It is spending more time talking openly with one another. The irony of the current moment is that as we worry endlessly about technology pulling us apart, it might be our inability to have conversations about technology that ultimately divides us.

Megan Moreno, MD, MSEd, MPH, is a co-author of Connecting: Raising Kids in the Digital World, published by the American Academy of Pediatrics on 13 October.

Yes, Britain’s railways are a mess. But is anyone sober enough to care?

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 10:00:04 GMT

Prosecco for the birthday party, Pimm’s for the horsey bunch, some cheeky Stellas for the short-haul crowd: it was all going down on my train the other morning

On Saturday I went to Liverpool with my youngest, and the overhead lines went down at Crewe, but also there were crew shortages across the land, so between the homophones and my lifelong inability to start listening to a train announcement until halfway through, I cannot tell you at what point this journey became a five-train, four-hour odyssey. All I know is what’s happening on every train, in every part of the country. The 7.48am is a calm and ordered cohort of people who think they know where they’re going and will be there soon. And from 9.04am onwards, everyone’s drunk, all the way to everywhere.

Between Rugby and Birmingham New Street, there was an incredibly festive crowd going to the Horse of the Year show, squishing real fruit into cans of Pimm’s, because it was breakfast time, and also because it was funny. But what were the horses going to make of all this? Because they’re quite short on appreciation for ludic pranking, and famously easy to frighten.

Between Birmingham New Street and Wolverhampton, there was a 40th birthday party with a load of mini-bottles of prosecco, and they were extremely charming and well signposted in some ways (for instance, how did I know it was a 40th? Because of the massive flashing deely-boppers saying “40”), but I still had so many questions. Why buy 15 tiny bottles, when you could get four regular bottles for a fraction of the price, and they would have exactly the same effect? What earthly state are you going to be in when you get there? Is there somewhere you could have a little snooze before your next appointment? Maybe things are different when you’re 40, but I dimly remember it, and it’s not that different.

Between Wolverhampton and Stafford, it’s only 13 minutes, so I was mainly awed by how many people could even be bothered to open a can of Stella. Stafford to Liverpool was a stag do, and it was brunch o’clock by now, so running up and down the carriage, yelling “Ay ay ay” in a fake scouse accent, dressed in a Brazilian flag, all fell under the umbrella “having a normal one”.

I abhor British exceptionalism, except on this one subject: exceptionally bad train network; exceptionally fun trains. Would recommend.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

One thing must now be clear to Andy Burnham. The rightwing press is on a war footing – and he’s the enemy

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 07:00:18 GMT

Farage was its champion, now it’s Badenoch – and the aim is the PM’s defeat at all costs

While the merits of a so-called Britannia shield to protect Britain from missiles and drones are debatable, the Conservatives’ proposal did achieve one thing last week: the very idea of the shield was used to anoint a political leader.

In a significant development, little observed amid the hullaballoo of news events, Kemi Badenoch’s uncosted, pie-in-the-sky plans to build a £10bn anti-missile system were enthusiastically heralded by the rightwing press. It was not just a matter of the plans themselves being lauded, even by outlets that must know them to be ridiculous. More significant is what it said about the champion chosen by these media organisations in their offensive against the Labour government and Andy Burnham.

The Sun splashed a smiling Badenoch across its front page with a banner headline calling her the “Iron Dome Lady”; the Express paraded her in a power suit and a union jack. The Daily Mail, meanwhile, hailed the Tories for seeking to “protect the nation’s skies” and sealed the plans with its “Don’t Leave Britain Defenceless” campaign stamp. Even wartime leaders could not hope for better, unquestioning coverage from battle-aligned, nation-rallying propaganda sheets.

The slavish Badenoch coverage is significant so soon after Burnham’s first conference speech as prime minister. It marks the moment when much of the rightwing press has returned to its traditional Tory-supporting ways after years of flirting with – and outright eulogising – Nigel Farage and his now scandal-hit Reform UK party. It also suggests a back-to-basics return to the economy as the chief battleground for this fight, and not the madder excesses of the war on woke that has recently consumed them.

The praise for Badenoch, who was also recently treated to an all-expenses paid trip to Greece to meet Rupert Murdoch and executives from the Sun and Times-owning News Corp, suggests that she has cemented a position as the rightwing press’s best political hope of beating Burnham.

The search for a suitable champion has assumed a growing urgency because the prime minister has so far proved hard to leave a mark on. “Red Andy”, the early attack line, has not been widely used since the June byelection in Makerfield. The Mail may have dubbed Burnham’s first conference speech “the most Left-wing speech delivered by a modern British prime minister”, but in recent weeks only the Telegraph’s Allister Heath has fired the “Red Andy” missile in a column that called plans for pension reform, a social care system and all talk of a return to the European Union, “mad, nasty and shockingly extreme”.

This coverage reminds Alastair Campbell of his early years advising Tony Blair when he was depicted either as a “useless Bambi or Stalin”, he tells me. “They can’t decide if [Burnham] is a useless Paddington Bear or red in tooth and claw,” says Campbell. “They just can’t work him out yet.” A member of the loathed liberal elite or outright Trot?

There are a few factors that are making it difficult for the rightwing press to get the full measure of their enemy – including Burnham’s trajectory from New Labour luvvy to working-class champion, the King of the North. Labour advisers also cite the fact that Burnham’s inner circle, in contrast to his predecessors, has also been relatively leak- and conflict-free, leaving rightwing combatants with fewer vulnerabilities to exploit.

This is the calm before the storm, of course, with Burnham’s opponents gearing up for the budget and the inevitable controversies on 28 October. “The press are probing his defences,” Tom Baldwin, a former Labour party adviser, tells me. “They’ll keep trying, of course, and the chances are that one of their missiles will eventually hit a target.”

Amid rising fuel prices, geopolitical uncertainty and concerns over jobs, the back-to-the-future nature of this debate – indeed the back-to-the-Tory-future nature of it – is hardly surprising. Burnham has assaulted shibboleths. He has vowed to reverse “40 years of failure” with his pledge to repeal Margaret Thatcher’s ban on public ownership of water companies, to abolish the Tory version of the right-to-buy housing scheme, and to restore a sense of common good to Britain. To the right, this is unconscionable. Dan Hodges in the Mail, praising Badenoch’s “best speech yet”, wrote that the country faces a choice between Burnham’s “unashamed 1970s-style socialism” and the Tory leaders’ “bold attempt to reappropriate and recondition Margaret Thatcher’s radical conservatism”.

Although the rightwing outlets fight a similar battle against Labour, they do so for varying reasons. Some of those are ideological, but commercial imperatives also fuel their fervour. The 1970s and 80s marked a golden age for newspapers, when millions of loyal readers gave them heft and profits. With sales and readership figures now at a fraction of their peak in the late 80s, the Sun (which claimed sales of 3.8m per day in 1987) and several other titles no longer publish their numbers, focusing instead on online reach. In dwindling markets, the strategy is to stay competitive by aligning with, or perhaps exacerbating, the prevailing wave of political populism.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The Sun has struggled more than the Mail with the shift online. It has also struggled more with Burnham because of its coverage of the 1989 Hillsborough disaster, in which it falsely blamed Liverpool supporters for a crush that killed 97 people. According to Baldwin, citing well-placed sources, Burnham may become the first prime minister since the Labour leader Jim Callaghan to refuse requests for exclusive interviews and articles in Rupert Murdoch’s biggest tabloid.

The right’s battle-camp has the additional problem that Burnham himself is proving quite a wily opponent. The prime minister spends 10 minutes a day with his social media team before posting to his nearly 1m followers on Instagram and more than 700,000 on TikTok. His short-form videos on fuel prices and the triple lock don’t seem to target younger voters, but they are a way of bypassing a negative narrative – or what Campbell calls “the madness of the rightwing press”.

Burnham could opt to go his own way, to ignore the hostile rightwing outlets altogether. But in a democracy, that would be no more ethical for Labour than it is for Reform UK, which has barred press critics. David Yelland, the editor of the Sun when it put Tony Blair on its front page with the headline “Is THIS the most dangerous man in Britain?”, tells me it would also be unwise. The power of the rightwing press is diminished, he says; they are “toothless tigers in a jungle full of new dangers – dangers as lethal for them as the rest of us, by which I mean AI and what comes next”. But, “the truth is the Tory press still has influence over the political and media classes … it can still set the weather”.

And as we know from famous battles past, the weather can be a decisive factor. The side that copes with it best usually wins.

Jane Martinson is an academic and Guardian columnist. She is a board member of the Scott Trust, which owns the Guardian Media Group, and writes in a personal capacity

Athletics wishes it could scrub the women’s marathon world record – what can be done?

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 07:00:17 GMT

Ruth Chepngetich’s failed doping test, five months after she obliterated the record in 2024, left the sport deeply uneasy but powerless to act

When Ruth Chepngetich annihilated the women’s marathon world record in Chicago two years ago today, NBC’s commentators compared it to the moon landing. “Bring it on Neil Armstrong!” cried one. “She has done things in this sport that we have not seen,” said another. “Unbelievable!”

That was a word others reached for too after the Kenyan had crossed the line in 2hr 9min 56sec, a time that not only smashed the world record by 1min 57sec, but her personal best by a staggering five minutes. Afterwards she was asked by Robert Johnson of Let’s Run what her response was to those who believed she must be doping. “People must talk,” she replied. “I don’t know.”

We know a lot more now. Because five months after that epic run, Chepngetich’s star came crashing down to earth. First she failed a doping test. Then she was banned for three years. These days people in the sport talk about her reluctantly, like a family member who has joined a mysterious cult. Yet her world record still stands because she passed a test after the race itself.

What should we think of this? What are we allowed legally to say about this? And what, if anything, can be done about it?

A couple of weeks ago, I spoke to Brett Clothier, the head of the Athletics Integrity Unit, which prosecuted the case against Chepngetich, to ask about her world record. “It is not satisfactory, to be frank,” he admitted. “But the world anti-doping code is pretty clearcut on the rights athletes have, even if they’re found guilty of a doping offence.”

That much is true. But while legally Chepngetich was clean when she broke her world record, the fact it stands surely damages the sport’s credibility.

True, there are plenty of highly suspicious records from the 80s and early 90s, given what we know about state-sponsored doping behind the iron curtain and in China. And if you believe Florence Griffith Joyner knocked more than half a second off her 100m and 200m times in 1988 by doing 5,000 sit-ups a day and drinking water, I have some magic beans to sell you.

Griffith Joyner, of course, never tested positive. But before her death aged 38, her fellow American sprinter Darrell Robinson claimed in a paid interview with the German magazine Stern that he had sold her human growth hormone for $2,000.

He also alleged that she had told him: “If you want to make a million dollars, you’ve got to invest a couple of thousand.” Yet as much as Flo-Jo’s records make us uneasy, they are seen as coming from a bygone and more lawless era.

Also, what makes Chepngetich unique is that no other athlete has been hit with a lengthy ban so soon after a world record.

The Kenyan’s defence for being 20 times the legal limit of hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) in her system? That she had taken her housemaid’s medication after feeling hot and having a rapid resting heartbeat. It was, the AIU noted, a “hardly credible” explanation.

The AIU also found screenshots on Chepngetich’s phone about the banned drug testosterone and “messages related to unidentified third parties working on ‘programs’ possibly related to doping”. The Kenyan has insisted that she has never used testosterone and the messages were from a group chat, but they hardly inspire confidence either.

So what can be done? The short answer, having spoken to the World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada), is very little. As a Wada spokesperson pointed out to me, removing her results before her positive test “in the absence of any evidence or reasonable inference that the athlete was doping before or at the time of the earlier results, might well breach a number of legal principles including proportionality and human rights.”

Sign up to Sport in Focus

Our picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown in

after newsletter promotion

But what about Lance Armstrong, who was stripped of his Tour de France titles despite not being convicted of breaking any doping rules while competing? Could this not apply here? Not according to Wada.

“He had procedural avenues open to him to contest the sanction but ultimately chose not to use them,” a spokesperson told me. “That makes his case a relatively weak precedent for establishing how far retrospective disqualification could legally go.”

One idea I floated to various experts was the idea that athletes could be asked to sign a social contract, which pledged they would accept losing their world record if they tested positive within a year of that world record or winning an Olympic medal.

In theory, one anti-doping expert put it to me, it was possible to do this. But he felt it would require everybody – from sports federations and governments to athlete bodies and human rights groups – to buy in and to agree to change the Wada code to allow retrospective punishments. And that is not going to happen.

At least track and field can point to many significant victories over doping in the last decade, given that Chepngetich is one of 317 elite Kenyan athletes the AIU has caught since it was set up in 2017. Many sports pay lip service to catching cheats. Athletics actually does. And the AIU does it on a modest budget of $11.9m (£9m) a year.

There are also positive signs that prominent athletes realise more must be done when it comes to anti-doping. Before Sabastian Sawe set his men’s marathon world record in London, for instance, his sponsors, Adidas, paid $50,000 for extra testing. Nike did the same for two of their athletes, Jacob Kiplimo and Brigid Kosgei, before Chicago.

Sawe’s agent, Eric Lilot, wants to go further by making his athletes sign a contract that will require them to give up any money still owed to them if it is shown they intentionally tried to dope. All that points to brighter days ahead, however much Chepngetich’s record makes us feel queasy.

In Liverpool I saw the tough choices Louise Casey faces on social care – starting with who will pay?

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 05:00:15 GMT

Preparing her first report on England’s social care system, the peer says ‘everything is on the table’. This should include older people’s wealth, rather than taxes on younger workers

Residents with advanced dementia lined the day room, glazed stares or sleeping mouths agape, with that terrible human vacancy everyone most fears for their own end days.

This was Millvina House in Anfield, Liverpool, which I visited with Louise Casey, who is heading the commission on social care in England, last week. Here is a snippet of what she saw: an angry man jolting into life, shooting out his arm at her and bellowing: “Out! Get out! Get out!” A young care assistant went to stroke his back and calm him down. It’s a hard job, and part of it is watching for warning signs of aggression, one of dementia’s dreadful symptoms. “People don’t want to know,” Casey said, “but if you are born, you will die. Chances are you will need care, and dementia is the biggest killer.”

In her travels she has been appalled by the standards of social care she has found in some places, with so many people getting far too little help. The evening before this visit, she had been out with care workers attending to people at home. She said she had come away “profoundly, deeply shocked”. She had photographed an elderly man with diabetes, swollen legs and a stroke affecting his left side, who was unable to open a bottle of water. He had no relatives nearby. “He couldn’t afford more care, so he’d just cut their visits by half.” Then there was a woman with early dementia and an untreated, infected stoma bag, which she said had looked “so sore”.

Casey’s shock at this “hidden misery” was matched by her admiration for care workers: “Only young girls, going into unknown homes, paid just £6.50 for a half-hour visit; it’s grim. But they are so patient.” She noted they were being paid about £4,000 a year less than if they had become healthcare assistants in the NHS. With better care, Casey thinks many more people should stay in their own homes – indeed, most would prefer to. “Even at four visits a day,” she said, it would be cheaper than residential homes such as Millvina House.

Millvina is a good symbol for the tangle of problems facing Casey. It is rated “requires improvement”, struggling out of a troubled “inadequate” past and hoping the results of its latest inspection will be better. The nursing home used to be privately run but was put into special measures after the Care Quality Commission (CQC) reported a lack of staff, shortage of medicines, unlawful restraint, dangerous neglect of residents with diabetes, incorrect doses of antibiotics and doubts on adequate feeding and hydration. After gaining interim control in July 2024, Liverpool city council officially took it over in September 2025, fearing its collapse would mean the loss of 60 much-needed beds – in the previous two years, 187 beds in Liverpool had already been lost. Its sister home, Brushwood, has also been insourced back to the council: here, the CQC found dirty baths and toilets, staff using disrespectful and dehumanising language, agency staff who didn’t know residents’ names and multiple safeguarding failures.

Casey urges insourcing to council or voluntary services: “If it’s public money, it should mainly be publicly run.” She wants to stop private-equity owners profiteering from care homes at one end, but at the other she sees services barely surviving unless better-off residents subsidise those on too-low state funding.

Now council-owned, Millvina costs a lot more to run at a better standard, the council leader tells me. Local authority staff are better paid – something private providers, contracted to cut costs, have little incentive to match. That was the logic behind Margaret Thatcher’s privatisation of social care, but perversely the state ended up with a far higher bill. To force councils to privatise, central government paid for those entering a private residential home, but not if they used domiciliary care or council-owned care. The result was an explosion of people entering private residential care instead of staying in their own homes. The state’s bill for nursing homes and residential care shot up from £20m in 1979 to £459m in 1986. That misguided privatisation is likely to feature in Casey’s imminent report outlining the sector’s history. Expect a brutal description of its current state.

Soon comes Casey’s first of several reports, this one on finance, which will lift the lid on where wealth resides. Overwhelmingly it is older people who have most wealth, a foundational fact underpinning whatever Casey’s final plans will be for a national care service. The people needing the care are better able to pay for it than working-age taxpayers. Expect that generational truth to shape her conclusions.

Lest some misunderstood Andy Burnham’s promise of universal free care at the point of use, it is unlikely that better-off people will be significantly freed from their current residential payments, which amount to £14bn. That contribution can’t be magicked away into general taxation, though liabilities could be capped.

Creating a fair system for elderly people may be easier than solving the inadequate state of care for working-age adults in need of support, which absorbs nearly half of councils’ care costs (Casey is writing separate reports about this). But political heat focuses on older people using family inheritances on care, a situation unresolved as nearly 30 years of forgotten social care commissions, white papers and select committee inquiries gather dust.

“Everything is on the table,” Casey says. Does that include Burnham’s own 2010 plan, in which everyone with capital would pay in a lump sum on retirement (or a lien on their home) and thereafter get free care? “Everything.” She and the government are examining a care plan by Steve Webb, a former Liberal Democrat pensions minister, for auto-enrolment of 1p in the pound on income tax for over-40s, politically saleable as people can opt out.

What of the clash with Burnham’s devolution plans? Some councils with similar profiles of deprivation, disability prevalence and median income provide up to twice the care of others, reports the King’s Fund. Voters want power devolved to councils – yet they hate an unfair postcode lottery between localities.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Look at the conflicts Casey faces: public v privately run services, taxpayer funds v family payments, the NHS v council funding for different disabilities, and local v national standards.

Her report will also collide with Tory inheritance tax promises to the rich. The right to pass on property to family is at the heart of passionate feelings about people being obliged to sell homes (that they will no longer use) to pay for residential care. Should young working people, many unable to afford a home themselves, pay more taxes so others can pass theirs to their children? A third of first-time buyers rely on the help of family. The wealth gap is worsening, as the Institute for Fiscal Studies reports a “growing importance of inherited wealth” for some, while others will get next to nothing.

Casey wants to set off an alarm on the miserable quality of care she finds, but her fiercest fight may be over inheritance and generational justice. How will she cut through these political knots? It’s easy to believe her when she replies: “I will do what’s right, however controversial. That’s it.”

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

Lobbying, lawyers and a media blitz: the fight to kill the Church of England’s £100m slavery compensation fund

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 05:00:15 GMT

Some of Britain’s wealthiest financiers, including Sir Paul Marshall, have given a platform to critical coverage or are linked to its leading opponent

“This is virtue signalling,” said Nigel Biggar. “These are elites who are trying to demonstrate that they are being progressive.”

The target of his scorn was one that has obsessed him for years: the movement to pay reparations for the slave trade, and specifically the Church of England’s plan to spend £100m atoning for its involvement.

“I’ve got north of 100 parish churches in my constituency, many of them crumbling,” added Katie Lam, an up-and-coming Conservative MP and immigration hardliner.

Lord Biggar, a retired professor, Conservative peer and Anglican priest, was speaking alongside Lam last September on a Spectator podcast named after his latest book, Reparations: Slavery and the Tyranny of Imaginary Guilt.

Since the church’s commissioners – who manage the church’s endowment – announced in 2023 that they would set up the Fund for Healing, Repair and Justice to make amends for the church’s involvement in the transatlantic slave trade, Biggar has led the backlash.

In doing so he has gone from fringe voice to one of the most widely published proponents of revisionist theories about colonialism and the British empire.

Dozens of articles have been published against Project Spire, as the fund is known in the church, many by Biggar and people who share similar views, in publications including the Spectator, the Daily Telegraph, the Daily Mail and the Times.

Lam has led opposition in the House of Commons, asking questions of ministers and in December coordinating a letter from 27 MPs and peers to the incoming archbishop of Canterbury, Sarah Mullally, accusing the church of “legally dubious vanity projects”.

The media blitz has paid off so far, paralysing the church and stalling the fund well beyond its planned launch date of 2024. The church admitted in July it also faces a legal challenge – which could add years more delay.

Yet little attention has been paid to the lobbying campaign against Project Spire – and how it has become a cause célèbre within the broader rightwing ecosystem. The Guardian can reveal how some of Britain’s wealthiest financiers, including Sir Paul Marshall, are linked to the man at the heart of the campaign to kill the church’s fund.

The multimillionaire co-founder of the hedge fund Marshall Wace has given Biggar and his movement a powerful platform via his stable of media outlets, which spans the Spectator magazine, the broadcaster GB News and the comment website UnHerd.

A devout Christian, Marshall also funded several rightwing lobbying groups and organisations linked to Biggar to the tune of hundreds of thousands of pounds.

It all appears part of the libertarian financier’s significant efforts to reshape the Church of England – and wider society – in line with his own worldview.

In 2007 Dr Rowan Williams, the then archbishop of Canterbury, set in train a reckoning for one of Britain’s most venerable and staid institutions when he said the church should consider slavery reparations for its historical role in the slave trade.

It signalled Lambeth Palace’s determination to atone for those failings – from its distant past to the present day.

His successor, Justin Welby, reaffirmed that commitment. “I’m ashamed of our history and I’m ashamed of our failure,” said Welby, a former oil executive turned priest, in 2020. “There is no doubt when we look at our own church that we are still deeply institutionally racist.”

In 2019, the church commissioners ordered research into the endowment fund’s origins and links to the slave trade. Its initial findings, published in 2022, revealed the funds partly originated in Queen Anne’s Bounty.

Queen Anne’s Bounty, which was founded in 1704, invested significant sums in the South Sea Company, which traded in enslaved people – trafficking about 34,000 enslaved Africans. The South Sea Company also received numerous benefactions from individuals such as the slave trader Edward Colston, who were linked to, or who profited from, transatlantic chattel slavery and the plantation economy.

Subsequent work by historians on the newly digitised Register of British Slave Traders has revealed how C of E clergymen financed the Royal African Company (RAC), which trafficked more African men, women and children than any other single organisation in the history of the slave trade.

In January 2023 the commissioners published a 25-page report on the endowment fund’s links to the slave trade, employing forensic accountants at Grant Thornton. It declared its intent to set up a £100m fund to invest and generate returns to support communities most affected by African chattel enslavement. Money would come from the church’s endowment, now valued at £11.6bn.

An independent oversight group was formed to steer the Fund for Healing, Repair and Justice, which the commissioners hoped would attract external investment to grow to a £1bn pot. “It is now time to take action to address our shameful past,” said Welby.

Bishop Rosemarie Mallett, the chair of the oversight group, said: “We believe that, like the mustard seed of the parable, the fund will grow from small beginnings towards an expansive future, inspiring imitation and constructive atonement for enduring evils.”

It was part of a wider examination into Britain’s links to slavery: the statue of Colston had been toppled into Bristol harbour in 2020, and institutions from the Bank of England and insurance market Lloyd’s of London to the royal family were delving into their past.

But the church was not ready for the backlash that the fund would provoke.

“The church commissioners always anticipated pushback,” said a source connected to Project Spire. “But it was unprepared for the intensity and persistence of the campaign waged by critics and media associated with wealthy City hedge fund executives.”

Among the first opponents was a Church of England vicar who appeared on GB News days after the fund was announced in January 2023, to say it would put parishioners off donating to the church. “We keep hearing that there is no money left,” he said.

“And now suddenly, they’ve found £100m down the back of the sofa, to pay for this. You can imagine how I felt.”

A torrent of similar views has followed, with significant coverage in media organisations that are owned or backed by Marshall.

The Spectator, which Marshall bought in 2024 for £100m, has hosted repeated criticism, including one piece by Biggar entitled “Wokery is a Christian heresy”, and another by its assistant editor Madeleine Grant, which described the fund as “deeply unpopular, based on questionable history and law”.

GB News, the TV channel that Marshall co-owns with the Dubai-based fund Legatum, hosted Biggar for an interview in which he labelled the C of E’s plan “completely irrational and wilful self-flagellation”. Biggar, the former regius professor of moral theology at the University of Oxford, has been at pains to state that “racial prejudice is wrong”, and slavery is “abhorrent”. But his criticism of Project Spire has been unrelenting.

UnHerd, the commentary website Marshall co-founded in 2017 with former Times journalist Tim Montgomerie, has run pieces with headlines such as “The Church of England’s reparations plan is unchristian”. Marshall’s son, Winston Marshall, has hosted Biggar twice on his YouTube show, with episodes such as “The Inconvenient Truth About Reparations and the Slave Trade”.

Other rightwing publications and organisations have also weighed in. The Critic, a magazine founded by the hedge fund tycoon and Brexit backer Jeremy Hosking, has run seven articles critical of Project Spire, including by Biggar and Lam. None have been supportive.

In 2025 Policy Exchange, the right-of-centre thinktank, published a 58-page paper titled The Case Against Reparations: Why the Church Commissioners for England Must Think Again. Again, Biggar was one of the authors.

Critics claim parishioners are similarly opposed to Project Spire, citing a poll of 500 churchgoers by Merlin Strategy that received widespread coverage in January. An initial story in the Sunday Telegraph reported a key finding: that 61% might withhold donations if the fund went ahead and money was “unavailable for the support of parishes”. The story was widely followed up, including by the Daily Mail and BBC.

But the coverage failed to mention the results of another similar question in the poll: “If the national church decided to commit £100m of its endowment to slavery-related ‘reparative justice’, would this increase or decrease the amount you would normally con[tribute?]”

This time 61% said they would either maintain or increase their contributions, compared with 34% who said they would reduce their contributions.

Nor did the stories mention who paid for and commissioned the poll: Biggar. Merlin said it sent the results of the poll to Biggar but had no further involvement in its dissemination. Biggar declined to answer questions about the poll.

The Guardian understands the Telegraph story was based on a press release sent by Lam that omitted details including Biggar’s involvement and the finding that 61% would maintain or increase their donations. Lam did not respond to repeated requests for comment.

The church has said money for Project Spire will not be diverted from parishes, and that funding for churches and clergy has risen by 36% to £1.6bn for its current three-year period, versus the prior period.

Marshall, who was a substantial donor to the Brexit campaign, has become one of Britain’s most prolific philanthropists. Armed with almost £490m in assets, the Sequoia Trust, a charitable trust he supports and chairs, backs a range of causes close to his heart, including in the Church of England.

The Guardian recently revealed how he has given at least £13m to Holy Trinity Brompton (HTB), an evangelical church in Knightsbridge in central London that seeded the popular Alpha course, and the Church Revitalisation Trust (CRT), via Sequoia, between 2018 and 2025.

He also provides significant support to organisations where Biggar is heavily involved, many of which are on the frontline of the culture wars.

In May last year the hedge fund tycoon delivered a 48-minute lecture at the University of Oxford on his reflections as an “accidental media owner”. The event was organised by a little-known charity, the Pharos Foundation, which Biggar co-founded in 2023 and of which he is a trustee. It funds the work of young academics “pursuing civilisational or heterodox research in a climate of free inquiry”.

Biggar founded Pharos with another academic, Prof David Abulafia, and the fund manager and Conservative party donor Neil Record. Record has described Pharos as part of a “resistance movement” in academia, fighting back against the “cancellation” of debate around subjects such as “DEI/EDI; climate change; the genetic role in intelligence; trans rights; and colonial history”.

Pharos are “innovators and disruptors, and you fight the fight for freedom”, Marshall told the Oxford audience. “Therefore you do everything I like and want to support”.

Accounts for Pharos show that Sequoia gave it £700,000 in 2024 and 2025. At least 10 Marshall Fellows appear on Pharos’s website, studying subjects including the British empire and ancient Greece.

Biggar, who is a paid “fundraising ambassador” for Pharos, declined to say how much he receives for the role.

Another prominent City figure, George Robinson, the co-founder of the hedge fund Sloane Robinson and a Conservative party donor, is also a trustee of Pharos, and charitable trusts linked to him have given it at least £500,000.

Robinson said he was “not aware” of the campaign against Project Spire and is not involved. He said that Biggar’s opposition to the church’s fund was done in a personal capacity and “has nothing to do with Pharos, which is an educational charity”.

Biggar was also a speaker at the recent Alliance for Responsible Citizenship (Arc) conference in London, which brought together rightwing voices from across the globe. Marshall funded the launch of Arc in 2023 with a £1m donation, followed by £2m last year, and he co-owns it with Legatum. Biggar is a director of a subsidiary, Arc Research, for which he said he receives no payment.

Sequoia also gave £890,000 to Policy Exchange between 2020 and 2023.

Biggar was involved in a similar storm that engulfed another British institution several years ago. In 2020 the National Trust published a 115-page report that unravelled its properties’ links to slavery and colonialism. Biggar was reportedly the inspiration for a lobbying group called Restore Trust which was set up to oppose the charity’s so-called “wokeness”.

Pharos backer Record was also linked to Restore Trust, appearing on its “meet the team” page until his resignation in 2024. Record, a veteran City currency trader, is also a prominent backer of anti-net zero organisations, chairing Net Zero Watch.

Biggar mentored James Orr, the influential Christian academic and former adviser to Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, who was recently caught in a funding scandal. Orr told a Jordan Peterson podcast in 2021 that they spent a “few happy years” together at the University of Oxford’s McDonald Centre for Theology, Ethics and Public Life, which Biggar founded and Orr joined in 2014.

Biggar also has links to the hard-right party Restore Britain. It cited Biggar’s writing on rights and the legal system in a 2025 paper justifying its flagship policy of mass deportations. He was among the people thanked in the acknowledgments “for trusty friendship or helpful conversations”. Biggar said that he has “no formal relationship” with Restore and is a member of the Conservative party.

Biggar has written repeatedly for the website History Reclaimed. It was founded by academics including Robert Tombs in 2021. Tombs said that it “exists to correct historical errors and falsehoods, and that is why we criticise Project Spire”. History Reclaimed says none of its authors are paid and it receives “no financial support from any political party or organisation”.

Uncertainty now shrouds the fund. Mullally has reaffirmed the church’s commitment to it, including on a trip to Ghana in July when she expressed “lament” for the Church of England’s involvement in transatlantic chattel slavery.

Members of the church’s General Synod, who gathered in York in July, heard that commissioners had faced “some of the most vile abuse and correspondence” over Project Spire.

The threat of a judicial review has further delayed an application to the Charity Commission to establish the fund in a new arm’s-length body.

No further details were given on the legal threat, but the Guardian understands it is being led by Bijan Omrani, a Daily Telegraph columnist and barrister, who has repeatedly criticised Project Spire. It is understood to centre on the church commissioners’ authority to disburse the money and whether it corresponds with its duty to support the Church of England and its parishes, and whether it allows the commissioners to spend its funds abroad. The Guardian attempted to contact Omrani via a webform on his personal website, but no response was received prior to publication. Biggar said he is not involved in the legal challenge.

Biggar said: “Given the universality of slave-trade and slavery – especially among Africans – up until the 19th century some Anglican and British involvement is unremarkable. What is remarkable was the unprecedented campaign to abolish both, led by evangelical Anglicans from the 1780s. Project Spire tears the Church of England’s role out of its historical context, exaggerates its guilt, and ignores its abolitionist leadership.”

Paul Marshall said: “I am not funding the anti-Spire campaign but I would be happy to do so. I believe the reparations project is naive and ill-judged and that the money would be better spent looking after the needs of the global Anglican Communion, including the many parishes in the UK struggling to make ends meet. And I think the majority of churchgoers would agree with that.”

Winston Marshall, Record, Hosking, Orr, Policy Exchange and the Pharos Foundation did not respond to requests for comment.

A C of E spokesperson said: “Addressing our historic links to African chattel enslavement is an act of Christian repentance, responsible investment and credible witness.”

Europe’s big election season is about to kick off. It could change everything

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 04:00:15 GMT

If far right nationalists gain power in four big countries simultaneously, we are in for a dramatic Trumpian tilt

When it comes to Europe’s economy or its peace and security, it is obvious that decision-making has to be done largely at the European level to be meaningful. Yet electoral politics is still conducted mostly at the national level. The silver lining of this mismatch is that from country to country in Europe we have governments with different political priorities and leanings. Unlike in the US, where one presidential election can radically change the entire country’s course, as we have seen so vividly under Donald Trump’s leadership, the same drama has not so far unfolded in Europe. This may be about to change.

Pedro Sánchez rolled the dice in Spain last week, calling a snap election for next month after an unholy alliance of the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox and Catalan pro-independence party Junts blocked his big housing reform package in parliament. If the socialist prime minister, hailed by progressives globally but demonised by Europe’s right and Trump’s US, loses his election gamble, Spain could fall into the hands of a conservative/far-right coalition, which is currently ahead in the polls.

In addition to Spain, France, Italy, Poland, Finland, Greece, Estonia and Slovakia will all head to the polls in the coming year. The four largest of these, France, Italy, Poland and Spain, could see far-right or nationalist populist parties either confirmed in power (Italy), returned to it (Poland) or elected for the first time (France and Spain). This could dramatically change the face of Europe.

Europe has been tilting to the right for some time, with far-right parties entering coalition in different countries at different times. Centre-right and far-right groups are now able to form a majority in the European parliament, coalescing in particular around an anti-climate and anti-migration agenda. But while this tilt has slowed European integration, its policy effects have not been as rapid and radical as those we have seen in the US under Trump.

This is because the rightward shift has so far not been homogeneous. In the Netherlands last year, Geert Wilders’s far-right Freedom party was punished at the polls and the liberals made a comeback. This year, Hungary’s slide into authoritarianism was halted, and is now being reversed, after Viktor Orbán was ousted in a landslide election. Most recently, in Sweden, support for the far right, which had backed the outgoing centre-right government, slipped. The opposition bloc, led by the Social Democrats, scraped a victory. So, while the rise of the far right is a continent-wide trend – Alternative für Deutschland’s recent victory in eastern Germany sent shock waves across Europe – it does not hold everywhere, at all times.

But if the coming round of elections were to bring Marine Le Pen to the French presidency, confirm Giorgia Meloni as Italian prime minister, possibly backed by a coalition even further to the right than the current one, return the Law and Justice party to power in Poland, and produce a conservative/far-right government in Spain including Vox, the face of Europe could change dramatically.

If all these countries, plus several smaller ones, elected far-right or nationalist populist governments, they would not reach a qualified majority able to steer the EU’s policy course. But they would form a blocking minority, putting an end to any ambition of deeper EU integration in such areas as finance, energy, defence and technology.

And it is not just a question of numbers. These far-right leaders would have a galvanising and radicalising effect on each other, propped up by Maga America and Silicon Valley’s algorithms. The common perception outside Italy is that Meloni has mellowed in power. To the extent that this is true, it is in no small measure because she has been surrounded by the likes of Emmanuel Macron, Donald Tusk and Sánchez, among others. If these leaders were replaced by the likes of Le Pen, Jarosław Kaczyński and Alberto Núñez Feijóo, backed by Vox’s Santiago Abascal, Meloni herself would act differently, more in line with her true political instincts. All this could trigger not simply a slow erosion of the European integration project – a muddling through with the unambitious agenda we have seen in recent years – but a hollowing out, if not an outright implosion. The EU as we know it would struggle to retain its purpose, especially if no agreement is reached on its next seven-year budget in the coming months.

The irony is that European political heterogeneity persists, but outside the EU it is not only Canada that wants more proximity. More importantly, the UK may have begun the slow journey of retracing its steps. It took 10 years for a British prime minister to call a spade a spade, publicly recognise that Brexit has done more harm than good and open the door to rejoining the EU, as Andy Burnham has now done.

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

It has taken a decade to remember the purpose of European unity and the emptiness of petty nationalism – just as Europe risks losing the memory of its dark past and teeters on the brink of falling apart. Now is perhaps the moment for the UK to remind its European neighbours what it means to be out there, all alone.

Nathalie Tocci is a Guardian Europe columnist
