I was kidnapped and held hostage for 977 days. Could I forgive my captors?

The Guardian Tue, 13 Oct 2026 04:00:14 GMT

At first the idea of mercy was something that helped me through the ordeal. But would real forgiveness be a form of Stockholm syndrome?

I knew Mohamed Tahlil as a gentle pirate who oversaw a team of guards during the first months of my life as a hostage in 2012. I had travelled to Somalia to report on the outbreak of modern piracy off the coast. On the 10th day, along a dusty road near Galkayo, in the centre of the country, I was kidnapped by pirates. For the next two and a half years, I was a hostage.

I spent most of my time on a thin, sweat-soaked foam mattress on the floor of a dusty room. The dim concrete prison houses changed, but the filth and the circumstances didn’t. Sometimes my captors moved me into the Somali savannah – where we camped in the open and slept on the ground – and for a six-month stretch, I was held on a hijacked tuna vessel, where I joined 28 fishers from east Asia who had been captured about three weeks before I was placed on board. (They had captured me on land, but they were a pirate gang, organised to capture ships at sea.) In each location, pirate guards would sit around with AK-47s and listen to the radio, or else chew khat, a narcotic plant.

Tahlil was a skinny, almost cheerful man who spoke little English and swept the junk-littered yard of his unfinished prison house with a grandmotherly calm. When he came into my room, he would give me his snaggletoothed smile and teach me a few Somali words (for “sun”, “cloud” and so on). He carried rifles but never threatened to shoot me. Tahlil did not seem particularly tough – he would cook and wash dishes alongside lower-ranking guards – but he commanded respect. I thought of him as a low-ranking guard leader in the vast school of clan pirates in central Somalia, who ranged from foot soldiers to a handful of top bosses, warlords who travelled with armed escorts. Tahlil said the men who had captured me were the “bad group”, while he and his guards were the good group. He promised to keep me safe in “his” house until the real pirates negotiated the ransom. I heard this kind of thing all the time in Somalia.

The “bad group” of rougher and fiercer guards was led by a squat man with rotten teeth named Ahmed Diriye. I had understood Tahlil and Diriye as team leaders of the “good” and the “bad” – so it surprised me when, one day, I saw both men squeeze into the front seat of a crowded SUV to visit some random part of the Somali bush, laughing and joking in the seat like old friends. It would be years before I understood how wrong my impression of Tahlil had been.

During my years in captivity, I was usually kept alone. I was beaten on multiple occasions. I saw a friend of mine being tortured. I was frightened most of the time. I was also livid – at my captors, and at myself, for getting kidnapped.

For two separate periods I had access to a short-wave radio, and I could listen to whatever programming came into range. One day, on the BBC World Service, I heard a story about Abraham Lincoln. He supposedly gave a speech during the US civil war in which he referred to southerners as fellow human beings who were simply in error. A Yankee woman criticised his meekness and wondered if southerners were not mortal enemies of the union, who ought to be destroyed. “Why, madam,” Lincoln replied, “do I not destroy my enemies when I make them my friends?”

I resisted this story at first. I wasn’t interested in edifying tales of secular saints. I lived through most of my days in a state of quiet fury.

In September 2014, after 977 days as a hostage, I finally walked free. Two months later, back home in Berlin, I received a Facebook message. It began: “hello michael i am ur friend mohamed”. The author was Tahlil.

Had it come from any other pirate, I would have dumped this message in the digital garbage can. But I was curious what Tahlil could want. He wrote: “I am happy u r out of bondage” and wished me a “happy and joyous life”. The message raised my temper. He was trying to ingratiate himself with me, to dissociate himself from the “real” pirate gang, and pretend we were all OK. After 32 months of horror he still thought I would believe his fairytale about “good” and “bad” pirates in Somalia.

I did not lash out. I wanted information. During the sporadic, long-running conversation that followed, I asked Tahlil to shore up my memories and correct my sometimes blurred impressions of the most squalid phase of my life. He gave names. He sent pictures. He answered questions, not always honestly. He helped me research a book about the ordeal, The Desert and the Sea, which took two years to write.

Of course, Tahlil did want something. He must have known that asking for cash wouldn’t work, since my family, friends, benefactors and various magazines I’d worked for had together sent $1.8m in ransom money to Somalia to have me released. But in the spring of 2015, he asked to come to the US. “I live in constant fear,” he wrote, “and I have no one to help me … I am left with only two options: to flee the country illegally or to continue living this way.”

At the time, the FBI had an open investigation into my kidnapping, and I had informed them about my ongoing online conversation with Tahlil. I was not about to help him immigrate. But it did sound as if he might cooperate with the government. So if I were to help Tahlil come to the US, it would be to help the FBI arrest him upon arrival. For a journalist it’s no small thing to participate in an operation with the feds, but when the pirates took me hostage, they converted me from a journalist to a kidnapping victim, and I felt that the ethical line had already blurred.

I was conscious that Tahlil was not the most important man to throw in jail. On the other hand, piracy is organised crime, and I hoped that a smaller boss, under pressure of evidence, might cough up dirt on his higher-ups. I wanted the right people to be punished. But I knew it was a gamble, in both practical and moral terms.

The FBI set up an operation to lure Tahlil to New York, where he would be arrested. “If you have second thoughts about all this,” one agent told me in the fluorescent-lit Manhattan field office one afternoon, “just let us know.” He meant that once Tahlil was arrested, any question of punishment or forgiveness would be out of my hands. The FBI would have a case to prosecute, and my one-time jailer would be subject not to my sense of right or wrong, but to US law.

In the summer of 2018, the FBI made covert arrangements for Tahlil and flew him to New York City, where he expected to stay in a hotel for two weeks. There was no promise of payment, but I helped lure him with a fake story about the hotel and “final factchecking” on the book. He, in turn, acted vague about his purposes in America. He seemed to vacillate between hope and despair. He would regularly check in to see if his visa and plane ticket were ready. Sometimes he would say he wondered whether he might get arrested. But he never seemed too interested in seeing me. I think we lied to each other for weeks.

On 10 August 2018, when he landed at JFK airport, the FBI arrested Tahlil. The agents said he seemed genuinely surprised. I hoped he would accept a plea and help the Bureau arrest one of the top pirate bosses, such as Mohamed Garfanji. Garfanji was an infamous figure in the state of Galmudug who had tortured my friend Rolly Tambara, an elderly hostage from Seychelles, by dangling him from a tree by his ankles and beating him with a bamboo cane. Garfanji also threatened to sell me to the terrorist group al-Shabaab. I have not forgiven him.

By November, three months after his arrest, Tahlil had still not cooperated, and I was having profound second thoughts. If the full weight of the US government came down on the shoulders of a seemingly gentle and low-ranking boss like him – and no one else’s – the whole operation would seem pointless and cruel. In late 2018, the New York Times published a short article about the case. “I’m not as happy as you might imagine that he’s in jail”, I told the journalist.

In the comments beneath the article, readers wondered whether I had “Stockholm syndrome”. Some people could not understand how a former hostage could wish anything short of savage vengeance on his captors. He must be hypnotised; he must be traumatised; he must be out of his mind.

But forgiving your captors is not the same thing as “Stockholm syndrome”. Not even close.

In my first few months as a hostage, my companion in captivity was Rolly Tambara, a 69-year-old fisher with tattoos on his forearms and a dry but unwavering sarcasm. He spoke English in a French-inflected island pidgin. He knew how to be a hostage, having been at it three months longer than me. At this point in my captivity I was still charged with a hair-trigger rage, and he would try to calm me down. Whenever our guards acted in an arbitrary or cruel manner, he mumbled, ironically: “We are the devil, Michael. And they are like God.”

He was right. The first thing a criminal needs to clarify once he has you under his violent control is that he is right, and you, by definition, are wrong. As hostages, we lived in a world turned on its head, and the consequences of rejecting its hierarchy could be lethal. “Within a matter of hours, the hostage is treated like an infant and has a kind of regression to infantile emotions,” the influential psychiatrist Frank Ochberg has said. “They can’t eat, they can’t talk, they can’t use a toilet, they can’t move without permission. To do it risks death and they accept the feeling that ‘this is the giver of life just like my mother was’.”

Ochberg was talking about Stockholm syndrome. The term has its origins in a six-day hostage standoff that followed a failed bank robbery in Sweden in 1973. The robber, Jan-Erik Olsson, took several employees hostage at a bank in Stockholm, using a knife and a submachine gun. He demanded freedom for an incarcerated friend, a great deal of money and a Ford Mustang for a getaway car. One captive was a 23-year-old stenographer named Kristin Enmark, who seemed to empathise with him from the start. The Swedish authorities met most of Olsson’s demands within a day. By this point, Olsson had been joined by a friend; when he asked if they could drive away with two hostages – to reduce the chances of the cops shooting him dead – the answer was no. Enmark, during a phone call from inside the bank to Swedish prime minister, Olof Palme, said that she and another woman genuinely wanted to leave with Olsson and his friend in the Mustang. “We are more afraid of the policemen than these two boys,” she told a journalist in another phone call from the bank.

Enmark seemed angrier with her own government than with her kidnappers. This posture mystified both Swedish authorities and the general public. But a psychiatrist named Nils Bejerot – who had worked as a negotiator for the Swedish government – told journalists that all the hostages suffered from a syndrome that led victims to stick up for their abusers. He called it “the Norrmalmstorg syndrome” after the bank’s location on Norrmalmstorg Square. To the rest of the world it became “Stockholm syndrome”.

It wasn’t until the following year that the term took hold in the US and beyond. Patty Hearst, the 19-year-old granddaughter of the newspaper tycoon William Randolph Hearst, was taken from her Berkeley apartment by a far-left gang called the Symbionese Liberation Army (SLA). Two months later, Hearst appeared on a bank surveillance video as “Tania”, threatening customers during an afternoon heist in San Francisco. “Up, up, up against the wall, motherfuckers!” she hollered. People wondered if the privileged daughter of a rich American publishing family had lost her mind. Was she brainwashed? Acting under duress? Had she started to work for the SLA? (She had.) Did she have Stockholm syndrome?

After Hearst’s arrest in September 1975, a famous defence lawyer named F Lee Bailey took up her case. He wielded the term “Stockholm syndrome” to keep her out of jail. It didn’t work in the courtroom, but she went free after 22 months because of a commutation by President Carter. Bailey’s headline-making arguments in the Hearst case are the main reason that people all over the world know the phrase “Stockholm syndrome”. But it’s never been listed in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, because evidence for it has never been clear enough for a formal definition.

Whether or not the term is valid, there is no dispute that the pressures on a hostage’s mind are real. Humans can have any number of reactions to absolute rule – rebellion, peacemaking, sympathy, obedience, rage – and no single response is “wrong” in a short-term crisis. Hostages who fall in love with their persecutors, convert to another religion, or identify with a gunman’s delusional notion of the world all give up their sense of self out of self-preservation. The mental strain has to resolve itself somehow.

What helped deliver me from my overwhelming sense of murderous anger, after more than two years in Somalia, was something I heard on the shortwave radio. It was a homily by Pope Francis about forgiveness. I was suffering not just from feelings of outrage, but also from a self-lacerating guilt about my own mistakes, which had led me to this miserable existence. I lived with a recurring urge to grab one of the Kalashnikovs and shoot either the pirates or myself. “How many of us perhaps deserve condemnation!” said the pope, adding that a person’s sins were like the stars at night. “We look at the sky, so many stars, but when the sun comes in the morning with so much light, the stars are no longer seen.”

This homily woke up a dormant Catholicism within me – not the whole system of belief, but a living river of feeling. I did not have road-to-Damascus conversion, and I wasn’t about to sit down with the pirates for an earnest chat about guilt and reconciliation. But after thinking about the pope’s homily for a few days I noticed how bitterness and anger were acts of will, like suffering itself, and how a slight step backwards, an unhooking of the mind, could let in a flood of mercy and light. I did it in silence. But I found that this mental shift made it easier to smile at the guards in the morning when they delivered a Thermos of oversweet tea and unlatched the steel shutters on my window. Whatever else I was condemned to suffer, I came to see that rage and self-pity were not mandatory aspects of the sentence.

When people ask if that isn’t just a “version of Stockholm syndrome”, I argue it was the opposite: to forgive a persecutor helps maintain your sense of self. It isn’t the same as adopting a false view of the world, or identifying with enemy interests. It’s a cool-headed resolution that dissolves the need for vengeance.

In retrospect, Enmark understood how strange her state of mind must have seemed to others. When the bank robber came up with the bright idea of shooting another hostage through the leg – promising not to hit any bone – Enmark tried to convince the hostage that it might turn out fine. (“But Sven, it’s only in the leg,” she said.) In an interview many years later, she pointed out that she was in a situation where “all your values, the morals you have, change in some way”. But in a matter of days she had found a working survival mechanism. It’s worth noting that in spite of the criminal’s lunatic threats, no one died in this standoff. Enmark found the right tone to handle an erratic, narcissistic gunman for almost a week.

When it was over, the gunman couldn’t believe he was the captive, sentenced to a decade in jail. “It was the hostages’ fault,” he later complained. “They did everything I told them to do. If they hadn’t, I might not be here now. Why didn’t any of them attack me? They made it hard to kill.”

In February 2019, six months after they had picked up Tahlil at JFK, the FBI arrested a Somali-American citizen named Abdi Yusuf Hassan in the frozen parking lot of a Starbucks in Minneapolis. In Somalia, he held a formal title, minister of interior of the state of Galmudug, where I was kidnapped and held. Hassan had lived between the US and Somalia for years.

The FBI believed Hassan had made off with about $250,000 of the ransom money that had been paid to release me. After that, he had retreated to Minnesota, which left the pirate bosses in Somalia to argue about the remaining cash. (Five ranking bosses died in a shootout over the ransom after I was gone.) I pieced this story together in vague outline when I wrote The Desert and the Sea, but after Hassan’s arrest in Minneapolis, and particularly after the trial of Tahlil and Hassan, I started to see there were whole dimensions of my case that I knew nothing about.

Both men were charged with conspiracy to kidnap an American, “terrorism” (in the sense that I was threatened with death in Somalia) and related firearms offences. Neither accepted a plea deal. They each faced 30 years or more, against a mountain of damning evidence.

I had rebuilt my life in Berlin and California, and I was anxious to get the trial over with. It should have run for two weeks in the spring of 2020, but Covid and other unexpected troubles delayed things until February 2023. By the time it finally came around, I was sick of hearing cliches about pirates as “protectors of the Somali coast”, and I wanted to see some semblance of official justice.

In court, Tahlil looked well-fed and wore a Covid mask. Hassan had grey in his hair. My job on the witness stand was to tell the story of my captivity as I remembered it, from start to finish. The defence objected a handful of times, first at my constant use of the word “seems” or “I had the impression …” and then, sharply, at a comment I mumbled into the microphone: “A lot of this is impressionistic.” All I meant was that it was difficult to know absolute facts in Somalia while I navigated that world as a hostage, without my glasses. But the judge agreed that I should stick to facts, rather than trying to interpret them for the jury.

It was cathartic to tangle with defence teams on the witness stand. A lawyer for Tahlil, Steve Lynch, spent part of his cross-examination asking me about guards at Tahlil’s house. “The dozen or so men who were in the house,” he said, “some of these men did not appear to have military training; is that right?”

“It was always hard to tell about military training with the guards,” I said, trying not to use Lynch’s own word “appear”.

“But some of them seemed to be, you know, people who were fishers – right?” he suggested. I felt a bolt of outrage, because the pirates I met were overwhelmingly not fishers trying to protect their livelihoods. That was propaganda, repeated by well-meaning journalists in the west from the moment pirates had made headlines in 2005. In the 1990s and early 2000s it had an element of truth, but by the time they were hijacking oil tankers and cargo ships, pirate gangs no longer consisted primarily of poor fishers defending the Somali coast from illegal fishing vessels. They were clan soldiers with Kalashnikov training – poor men who needed jobs, certainly, but still members of brutal organised criminal networks.

I leaned into the microphone and said, low and clear, so no one in the courtroom would miss it: “Absolutely not.”

“Let me ask you this,” he said. “Did some of the people who were there … did they seem to be relatively simple people?”

“They were clan soldiers,” I said.

Not what the defence wanted to hear. Other witnesses echoed this point during the two-week trial: most pirates were clan soldiers, not simple fishers. The witnesses were Somali spies, informants from the ranks of local Galmudug police or the pirate network itself. One key witness told the court that Tahlil was more sophisticated than the cheerful guard leader he had played around me. In fact he was a captain in the Somali army, the witness said, and he ranked as a mid-level boss in the pirate network.

After the trial, as I read the 2,000-page court transcript, Tahlil came into focus. He’d spent a surprising amount of time on the hijacked tuna vessel, out of my sight. The ship, called the Naham 3, was a long-line tuna vessel run by owners in Taiwan and Oman. It had been hijacked in open water near Seychelles, more than 700 miles from Somalia. (Territorial waters for any nation reach 12 miles out.) The ship was 50 meters long and had a vast maze of fish freezers in the hull, which, according to witness testimony, Tahlil had converted to an armoury. “Tahlil was responsible for collecting all those weapons at the end of the guards’ shifts and locking them overnight in the ship’s freezer,” said one US prosecutor, Gillian Grossman, in her summation, “which the pirates used as a sort of makeshift gun locker. Tahlil controlled access to those weapons. He was the only one with the key.”

Remarkable. This mass of information shifted my impression of him. I no longer thought of my skinny, mild-mannered Facebook informant as a minor boss. If he stashed weapons in the freezer hold, he was involved in the Naham 3 case, too. I doubt he had hijacked the ship, just as he hadn’t physically kidnapped me – but as an armourer he was responsible for all the pirates’ weapons, and in that sense he was also partly responsible for the long captivity of the 28 fishers held hostage on the ship. Twenty-six of them were finally released in 2016, having spent nearly five years as hostages. Two died in captivity.

It also turned out that Tahlil and Hassan were friends, although I had never seen them together. The feds had a binder full of Facebook correspondence and phone calls between them. The defendants called each other “brother” and “my friend”. But Tahlil seemed to acknowledge his own lower rank by using “minister” and “my respected leader”.

My urge to forgive Tahlil eroded like a salt statue in the rain. Not that anger or vengeance rushed back; but I was less interested in showing grace. The released fishing crew members that I spoke to had little interest in forgiveness. One Filipino, Arnel Balbero, wrote to me that he hoped “all of the pirates are put in jail … Because of them there’s a lot of dreams in life broken.”

As for Hassan, it came out in court that he owned a home in Galkayo just down the road from one of my prison houses. According to a pair of Somali witnesses, it was a hideout and a meeting point for some of the highest-ranking pirates I encountered. Alongside his work as the long-distance interior minister for the state of Galmudug, in his capacity as a local landlord Hassan found a way to profit from my presence in the neighbourhood by renting a house to my kidnappers.

I expected to hear some kind of plausible counter-narrative in court about Tahlil and Hassan. It never came. Both men argued that they had infiltrated the pirate gang with some hope of giving me comfort or helping me escape. If that were true, why had they not aided the FBI, never mind the prosecution team? Why did Hassan own a house in Galkayo that was full of ranking pirates? And how did Tahlil come to work as an armourer, responsible for every Kalashnikov I saw, every grenade launcher, every machine gun?

The Somali witnesses said Tahlil had reached out to me on Facebook because the top pirate bosses had paid a final, insulting compensation of $8,000 for his armoury services. He had felt stiffed. So he messaged me in 2014 and began to help me with my book, dreaming about a new life in the US. That made sense. I still felt a measure of pity for him that I didn’t feel for Hassan. I had learned some illuminating facts from Tahlil and convinced him to board a plane. After I absorbed the evidence against him, the Tahlil in my mind had become a less hapless, more calculating man, but I didn’t think he deserved a minimum sentence of 30 years.

Getting these punishments “right”, whatever that meant, felt important for the same reason that forgiveness on the floor of a filthy prison house had felt liberating. It was a form of agency. I had lost my desire for revenge, but not for justice. But, by this point, justice was out of my hands.

People talk blithely about closure, as if a criminal case in a bland federal courtroom can bring peace to the victim of a violent crime. I don’t think it can. You have to find peace on your own. The US Department of Justice did a tremendous job in prosecuting my captors, but psychological comfort wasn’t part of the deal.

On the day of his sentencing, in late 2024, I read out a terse letter for Tahlil in court. I asked Judge Allyne Ross to hand him less than 30 years if she could. “I know what it is to be held against my will,” I said. “I also learned mercy in Somalia as a means of survival … This is not the same as forgetting what happened.”

Tahlil gave a speech insisting on his innocence, insisting (still) that he had wanted “to help Michael”. Ross listened to everything. At last she handed out two 30-year sentences. Tahlil’s would have been lower if a minimum of 30 on one firearms charge were not strict law in New York state. For Hassan, given the weight of evidence, the 30-year sentence was “appropriately severe”, she said, “in contrast to Tahlil’s”.

Another of my captors, Bashko, had been arrested in 2021, this time by FBI agents and local police in Djibouti, a nation north-west of Somalia. He was sent to the US, where he faced similar charges in New York – involving conspiracy to kidnap, terrorism and firearms – but pleaded guilty for a lighter sentence.

I first became aware of Bashko as a lean and clever young gunman on the Naham 3 who wrapped his head in flamboyant turbans to keep the sun off. He was good-humoured and smart, a ground-level guard from start to finish. For two years, he guarded me almost every day with his Kalashnikov, sitting cross-legged on the floor of a given prison house. We used to hold long, sometimes entertaining conversations in fractured English and Somali during our sweltering prison-house afternoons. Our worldviews rarely lined up – he justified my captivity with the most violent, infidel-phobic verses of the Qur’an – but we had lively arguments.

If the poverty trap applied to any pirate I met, I believe, it applied to him. He did not fit the desperate-fisher profile, but he’d signed on as a foot-soldier because he was poor and had few other options. Bashko faced a sentence ranging from zero, or time served, to 25 years, and I saw no reason for him to spend a third of his life in jail. So I wrote a letter to the judge, emphasising his low rank.

“His willingness to talk and joke also made my captivity easier,” I wrote. “He ordered samosas for me as a snack. He mediated between me and more aggressive guards, and he sometimes arranged for me to sleep without chains. Once, in a fit of temper, I flushed the keys to those chains down the toilet, which I think caused him a little trouble.”

Bashko was sentenced in the fall of 2023. The judge gave a long assessment of the case. “There is a word for the inhumanity of Mr Moore’s kidnappers, all of them, leaders and followers,” said Judge Paul Engelmayer. “The word is ‘evil’. We don’t use that word often in courthouses, and we don’t use it often in criminal sentencing. It is reserved for the worst of the worst crimes. It fits here.”

He went on to say that my letter was not the final word. “A court can never subcontract its determination of the just sentence to a victim, whether the victim seeks vengeance or mercy.” But the letter perhaps had some effect. Engelmayer slashed Bashko’s maximum sentence from 25 years to 12 and a half.

I couldn’t be at the hearing in New York, but I was told that Bashko was agitated in the courtroom – and that he wanted to give me a “postcard”. His lawyers would be sending it to me, I learned. I was away at the time, and for a couple of weeks I imagined Bashko’s message would be a screed about how I had ruined his life.

When I returned home, I found a thick envelope, not a postcard. I opened it with some trepidation. It was a handcrafted greetings card with no language at all, no English or Somali, just a sliding pop-up contraption made of pink and white paper, which, when you opened it, unfolded into an eloquent flower.

After his trial, Bashko was moved to Leavenworth federal correctional institution in Kansas, and I tried to visit him while writing this essay. The bureaucratic system was sluggish and unresponsive, but we did manage to speak on the phone.

Bashko’s voice was deeper than before, and his English was now strong. He thanked me for writing to Engelmayer. “I know you were helping me, for real, Michael. I want to say I’m sorry … Bashir from 10 years ago? He’s different, for real. Before, I knew nothing. You remember?”

“I remember.”

“God bless you. Everything is good now,” he said.

It was strange, but he sounded excited, even happy.

“I can’t hate the jail. I know what I did before,” he said. “I did bullshit.”

I raised my eyebrows. In Somalia he had been full of doctrinaire, self-righteous religious beliefs. It sounded as if, in prison, he had arrived at some deeper revelation. “I told the judge: ‘I’m guilty.’ I say: ‘If you give me 30 years, I don’t care. If you give me 15,’ that’s what I told him. I said: ‘Judge, I did wrong. I’m sorry.’”

He had no chance of remaining in the US after his prison term. He wasn’t angling for anything in return. He was serious.

“Thank you, Bashko. You sound like a new man.”

“Your family, everything is good, right?” he said.

“My family is good right now, thank you.”

“I hope you can forgive me, please.”

I hesitated. I’d grown so used to not hearing confessions for this period in my life that I had no idea what to say. A forgiveness that had been completely personal, inward – a form of self-liberation – turned shy in the face of a spoken request. But the piece of mail he had sent was still on my sideboard; in fact I could see it from where I sat with my phone.

“Well, yeah,” I said at last. I cleared my throat. “Yes, Bashko.”

“Thank you, Michael Scott Moore.”

It cost me nothing to grant. I thought about Lincoln and his vaporised enemies. For the first time, I felt something had shifted out in the world – something beyond my own life had transformed because of this halting, doubting, uncertain trajectory of forgiveness I had been writing about for years – and it was more powerful, in its effects, than any project of vengeance.

Cornell Bans Fraternity Parties and Adds Sexual Assault Investigators

The New York Times October 13, 2026

Cornell Rape Investigation

Advertisement

Supported by

The expansive changes to campus life, including working closely with the state police, come in the wake of the national uproar caused by allegations of a gang rape at a fraternity house.

By Sharon Otterman and Debra Kamin

Cornell University has banned parties at fraternity houses for the rest of the academic year and will add experienced sexual assault investigators to work with its police force in response to a student’s allegations of gang rape in October 2024.

The university announced the changes on Tuesday as it tried to reassure students, faculty and alumni that it is addressing the ongoing crisis set off several weeks ago by the lawsuit filed by a former undergraduate, known as Jane Doe.

“We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action,” Michael I. Kotlikoff, the president of Cornell, announced in a letter to the campus on Tuesday. “Cornell must be a place where safety is not an open question.”

The lawsuit shocked the campus and nation not only because of its allegations of rape, but also because it put on full display how fraternity members exchanged Snapchat messages using crude and dehumanizing language to describe the woman and what was taking place.

The announcement on Tuesday aims to also address the social culture at Cornell that set the stage for the alleged assault, Dr. Kotlikoff said.

“I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community,” he said.

The most immediate change is a ban on all parties and social events in fraternity houses at Cornell for the remainder of the academic year, a sweeping measure on a campus where one-third of students are part of Greek life. Dr. Kotlikoff, in an interview on Tuesday, noted that since the pandemic, fraternity parties had been pushed even more to the center of student life.

“There is an issue, post-Covid, of what are the options for students in a town like Ithaca,” he said. “Many, many bars and venues went out of business and did not come back.”

The moratorium, which comes days before homecoming weekend, will allow for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether it can safely resume, Dr. Kotlikoff said.

“This is a step that we need to take at this point in time to force a reset,” said Anne Smalling, the chair of Cornell’s board of trustees, in an interview. “It’s incumbent on us to try and find other ways for these kids to engage in social settings.”

The campus will also enhance support for survivors of sexual assault, including by adding staffing to its civil rights office to help those who report incidents navigate what has been described as a complicated bureaucratic system. The university said that it would also work with the New York State Police to allow their “experienced, trauma-informed criminal investigators, who are independent of Cornell University” to investigate allegations of sexual assault, and to prepare “comprehensive investigative summaries for the appropriate law enforcement agency.”

Those changes seek to address some of the gaps in Cornell’s response that were highlighted by Jane Doe’s experience. Though she was interviewed at length by Cornell police in November 2024, the woman’s statement was condensed to a six-page summary for the district attorney that omitted a direct allegation from her stating that she was “100 percent certain” she had been raped.

The district attorney, Matthew Van Houten, decided not to prosecute. He also declined an offer from the Cornell University Police Department to review additional evidence, files obtained by The New York Times showed. In late September, after Jane Doe filed her lawsuit, he reopened a criminal investigation, which has since been taken over by Letitia James, the New York attorney general, at the request of Gov. Kathy Hochul.

None of the accused men have been charged with a crime, and all have denied wrongdoing.

On a deeper level, the reforms will try to address the social context of drug and alcohol abuse and attitudes toward women surfaced by Jane Doe’s allegations, Dr. Kotlikoff said in the letter.

Jane Doe, and several men whom she accused of assaulting her, drank alcohol and ingested ketamine at the fraternity house, the lawsuit said. She alleged that no one intervened to help her through the long night during which she said she was assaulted.

Cornell will enhance existing education and programming “to address the bystander effect and the duty of care we owe each other,” Dr. Kotlikoff announced. The university will also accelerate the implementation of other changes recommended by a 2025 task force on campus sexual assault, including a public health campaign about sexual violence and “expanded training for students, leaders and residential staff.”

Whether the changes will go far enough to address the anger on campus sparked by Jane Doe’s allegations remains an open question. Students have held protests, and the university’s faculty senate gave notice of a rare resolution of no confidence in the administration over the handling of the allegations.

Missing from the letter were any announcements of firings or personnel changes among Cornell administrators, or an explanation of why these steps were only being taken now, when university administrators have known about the gang rape allegations since 2024.

The letter also didn’t announce a pause on fraternity and sorority rushing for new students, as some on campus have demanded.

Despite the district attorney’s decision to not prosecute the case in 2024, Cornell’s Title IX office conducted a lengthy investigation in early 2025, in which it interviewed six of the seven alleged assailants and dozens of witnesses.

In the days after the alleged assault, some of the men coordinated to try to contain rumors about what had happened and sought to reassure Jane Doe that the gossip would blow over, text messages between the men revealed in the investigation showed.

After 12 days of hearings in May 2025, a panel of Cornell staff and faculty found sufficient evidence of sexual assault to expel two of the men and suspend two others. The three remaining men received lighter punishments, including having to study sexual harassment, social media use and bystander intervention, and write “reflection papers,” the documents obtained by The Times showed.

The fraternity, Chi Phi, was barred from campus, and its stately Tudor mansion remains closed.

Thomas Giuffra, an attorney for Jane Doe, praised the changes as moves in the right direction. While they come too late to protect Ms. Doe, he said, “these steps will hopefully go a long way to help ensure that there are no more Jane Does.”

In Ithaca on Tuesday, reaction to the news that there would be no more fraternity house parties this year was mixed.

A protest in support of Jane Doe at the Ithaca Commons opened on Tuesday afternoon with a round of applause for the ban.

“This happened because they were backed into the corner,” Ray Epstein, an event organizer, said of the university. “This is a step in the right direction.”

Others, interviewed on a quiet campus on the last day of fall break, said the ban did not make sense.

“Banning parties now doesn’t do anything to fix what has happened,” said Ryan Nazari, a Cornell freshman. He wanted additional consequences to focus more squarely on the accused men and university officials, rather than all campus fraternities.

“It is more of a punishment on the entire student body,” Mr. Nazari said.

Finn Clancy, a senior majoring in biology and society, thought the ban could prove counterproductive.

“It’s slightly naïve of Cornell,” he said, “to think that these parties won’t happen.” He said younger students might flock to Collegetown, the Ithaca neighborhood where he lives, for off-campus parties that are outside of the university’s purview.

Hurubie Meko, Zane Irwin and Mack Liederman contributed reporting.

An earlier version of this article misstated when a panel of Cornell staff and faculty held hearings for 12 days. It was in May 2025, not March.

We acknowledge mistakes in our reporting with corrections. If you spot an error, please let us know at corrections@nytimes. com. Learn more.

Sharon Otterman is a Times reporter covering higher education, public health and other issues facing New York City.

Debra Kamin is an investigative reporter for The Times who covers wealth and power in New York.

Pope Leo Found to Have Lung Cancer During Surgery, Vatican Says

The New York Times October 13, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The surgeons removed the lower lobe of the pope’s right lung after finding a cancerous nodule.

By Elisabetta Povoledo

Reporting from Rome and Vatican City

Pope Leo had a lower lobe of his right lung removed during surgery on ⁠Tuesday and was diagnosed with ​lung adenocarcinoma, a form of cancer, ​the Vatican said in a medical bulletin.

It said an examination of a nodule during the operation had confirmed the diagnosis, which it said had been “suspected by preoperative tests.”

The surgery itself lasted approximately 90 minutes, and the pope, 71, was in the operating room for about 3 hours. “The surgery was successful, and there were no complications,” the statement said.

The statement did not say whether the pope would undergo further treatment. A Vatican spokesman said that the statement spoke for itself.

Lung adenocarcinoma is a common form of lung cancer. Survival rates for it vary greatly depending on the stage of the cancer and a patient’s overall health. The information released about Leo thus far seems to indicate he has early-stage lung cancer, which is typically treated with surgery and tends to have a very high survival rate, said Dr. Sudish Murthy, a thoracic surgeon at the Cleveland Clinic.

The Vatican had said previously that Leo was expected to spend about a week recovering in the hospital after the surgery, and that all audiences with him would be canceled until Oct. 20.

The hospital has a 10th-floor suite that has been reserved for pontiffs since the papacy of St. John Paul II, but it is under renovation. The pope was resting in a nearby suite, the Vatican said. A Vatican spokesman said Leo had asked to eat supper.

The pope announced during his weekly blessing and prayer in St. Peter’s Square on Sunday that doctors had advised the surgical intervention after detecting a “very early-stage and well-localized” nodule during recent medical tests.

He had also said that he planned to travel to South America next month. A Vatican spokesman said that those plans had not changed. The pope had been aware of his condition when he spoke on Sunday, the spokesman said.

Leo, the first American pope, was elected to lead the Roman Catholic Church in May 2025.

Medical advances and increasingly effective drug therapies mean that a lung cancer diagnosis is no longer a death sentence.

“You can heal from a lung tumor,” said Dr. Lorenzo Spaggiari, a thoracic surgical oncologist at the European Institute of Oncology in Milan who is not part of the pope’s medical team. A patient of his once ran the New York Marathon after having a lung removed, he said.

“The important thing is to catch it an initial stage,” Dr. Spaggiari said.

The medical bulletin did not say whether any lymph nodes had been removed, but Dr. Spaggiari said that was standard procedure.

A Vatican spokesman said that postoperative and histological tests would be carried out in the coming days.

It is unclear whether the pope was ever a smoker. When asked, the Vatican declined to respond.

Dani Blum contributed reporting.

Elisabetta Povoledo is a Times reporter based in Rome, covering Italy, the Vatican and the culture of the region. She has been a journalist for 35 years.

Man Killed at Six Flags Struck Other Riders During Fall From Roller Coaster

The New York Times October 13, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The police identified the 42-year-old man who died at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday. The company said it was temporarily closing multiple rides in the U. S. and Canada as a precaution.

By Mark WalkerLaura ChungChristine Hauser and Rick Rojas

The police in Georgia on Tuesday identified the person who had died after falling off a roller coaster at Six Flags on Monday. The man, Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old from Atlanta, was ejected from the ride, witnesses said, and struck other patrons as he fell.

In a statement, the Cobb County Police Department said that Mr. Kariem was found “unresponsive and not breathing” when investigators showed up at the Six Flags Over Georgia amusement park in Austell, Ga., about 17 miles west of Atlanta, just before 4 p. m. local time on Monday.

Witnesses and employees described the fall to the authorities, who are continuing their investigation. Several other people were injured on the Goliath roller coaster.

Additional details about the death, as well as the number of people injured and their conditions, were not immediately available on Tuesday.

The episode has rattled Georgia. The Six Flags location is among the state’s largest and most popular theme parks, becoming over the past 60 years a fixture in the Atlanta metro area for recreational trips by families, schools and church groups. The park covers nearly 300 acres, with more than 40 attractions and a dozen roller coasters.

“We are all grappling with how something so devastating could happen at a place that has given generations of families such happy memories,” Lisa N. Cupid, the chairwoman of Cobb County’s commissioners board, said in a statement. Mr. Kariem was an information technology manager with Wesley International Academy, a public charter school that educates children from kindergarten through 8th grade, Atlanta Public Schools said on Tuesday. His online profile said he worked there for more than 12 years, including several years as a teacher.

“He was a cherished member of the Wesley International Academy and APS families whose presence and impact will be deeply missed by our students, staff, and all those whose lives he touched,” the statement said.

After the fall on Monday, Six Flags said that it had temporarily closed some of its rides in the United States and Canada as a precaution

A Six Flags representative said in a statement that park officials and the local authorities had responded immediately, but declined to describe what happened, citing the family’s privacy.

“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” the representative said.

Operators stopped the Goliath right after the fall, and video footage captured from a helicopter by WSB, an Atlanta-area TV channel, showed passengers stuck on the coaster, perched high above the park. Park officials had to climb up a staircase alongside the tracks and guide them down individually.

A representative of Six Flags said it had closed the ride there as well as eight similar attractions across the company’s parks, “out of an abundance of caution.” The company said the closures were temporary, though it did not provide details about when the rides would be reopened.

Goliath opened 20 years ago as a centerpiece of Six Flags Over Georgia. The ride ascends 200 feet and reaches speeds of roughly 70 miles per hour, lasting just over three minutes.

“It’s fantastic topography,” Walter Bolliger, the president and a founder of Bolliger & Mabillard, the Swiss engineering firm that designed the Goliath along with dozens of other coasters worldwide, told The Atlanta Journal-Constitution in 2006. “Goliath is the right combination of speed, height and airtime,” he added, referring to the climactic moments in the ride when riders float up in their seats. “It’s very comfortable, very smooth.”

In a statement on Tuesday about Monday’s roller coaster fall, Bolliger & Mabillard said it is investigating what occurred.

A passenger died on the coaster just a few months after it was opened: A 45-year-old man from Alabama had a fatal heart attack right as the ride reached its end, according to accounts from the time.

Six Flags said on Monday that it had temporarily closed the following rides:

Raging Bull at Six Flags Great America in Gurnee, Ill.

Goliath at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia, Calif.

Nitro at Six Flags Great Adventure in Jackson Township, N. J.

Leviathan and Behemoth at Canada’s Wonderland in Vaughan, Ontario

Fury 325 and Thunder Striker at Carowinds in Charlotte, N. C.

Orion and Diamondback at Kings Island in Mason, Ohio

Additionally, in Montreal, a spokeswoman for the theme park La Ronde said in a statement that it had shut down its own Goliath ride for a safety review. Six Flags sold the park this year to EPR Properties, a real estate investment company based in Missouri.

The tragedy on Monday at Six Flags Over Georgia happened less than a month after three people sued Six Flags and S&S Worldwide, a manufacturer of roller coaster vehicles, saying they suffered catastrophic brain injuries after riding X2, a roller coaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain amusement park in Southern California.

The lawsuits accused Six Flags of failing to adequately warn passengers about the risks to riders.

The X2 is a 200-foot-high roller coaster with seats that rotate independently as the train travels along the track, spinning riders by as much as 360 degrees. It reaches speeds of up to 76 miles an hour and sends riders through dives, flips and twists.

In court filings in an earlier case involving X2, Six Flags denied that the roller coaster had caused a rider’s fatal brain injury. The ride has been closed since July.

Christina Morales contributed reporting.

Mark Walker is a Times reporter who covers breaking news and culture.

Laura Chung is a Sydney-based reporter and researcher for The Times, covering Australia, New Zealand and the Pacific.

Christine Hauser is a Times reporter who writes breaking news and features.

Rick Rojas is the Atlanta bureau chief for The Times, leading coverage of the South.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

After a glide bomb killed his wife and younger daughter, Yevhen Ovcharov was determined to prevent other Ukrainians from dying the same way.

Yevhen Ovcharov at home with photos of his wife and youngest daughter. Credit...

Supported by

By Siobhán O’Grady and Liubov Sholudko

Visuals by Johanna-Maria Fritz

Reporting from Kyiv, Sumy and the Carpathian Mountains in Ukraine

The 500-pound Russian bomb first appeared as a tiny blip on Yevhen Ovcharov’s live military map: a red speck gliding over the Ukrainian border and above the villages beyond.

Then he saw it hurtling toward his hometown, Sumy.

Yevhen was a Ukrainian soldier deployed 300 miles from home, on the eastern front. It was 9:45 p. m. on July 3 when he reached for his phone.

His wife, Nataliia Ovcharova, answered quickly. Don’t worry, she told him. She and the girls were fine and happily walking home from the park. Their 13-year-old, Veronika, was trailing slightly behind with a friend. Their youngest, Milana, who was 5, was beside her.

At 9:46, the call was cut off.

Yevhen called back once, twice, three times.

For six minutes, he heard nothing.

At 9:52, his phone rang. It was Veronika. She screamed that she was covered in blood. Milana, she said, was lying completely still on the ground.

“No one is helping,” she sobbed. “Dad, please come save us.”

Yevhen ran outside and jumped in a car to start the four-hour drive home.

This summer was Ukraine’s deadliest and most violent period since the first weeks of Russia’s invasion in 2022. Russian attacks killed more than 1,100 Ukrainian civilians from June to August, according to an estimate by the United Nations. Another 7,000 were wounded.

Russia preyed on Ukraine’s air-defense shortages, bombarding cities far from the front line with waves of drones and ballistic missiles that it knew Ukraine could not intercept.

Yevhen had been sent to fight in the eastern region of Donetsk, but his hometown in Ukraine’s northeast was the center of another Russian military push. Russia terrorized residential areas there with drones and glide bombs that it produces in large quantities.

Glide bombs have leveled cities across the country’s eastern and southern regions for years. The only way to stop these World War II-era weapons is with planes that shoot Russia’s fighter jets down before they drop the bombs. Ukraine still does not have the means to do that. In July, Russia launched a record 8,300 glide bombs. And at 9:46 p. m. on July 3, one landed in Sumy.

Veronika was 8 years old when the war started: old enough to understand that everything was changing but young enough that her parents still protected her from what they could.

Still, she could see how much her mom worried about her dad, a career police officer who was fighting in the infantry. Nataliia often asked Veronika to pray for him. As the oldest daughter, she told her, she had a special bond with her father. This was an important responsibility for Veronika, who often felt left behind by the attention on her sister, who was just a baby when Russia invaded.

“She was stressing a lot,” Veronika said of her mother. “When Dad was not reachable on the phone, she was panicking.”

Veronika didn’t worry like that. She got used to the explosions and the hum of Russian drones and the years that passed without her dad, who kept deploying to different parts of the front line.

When he had time off, Yevhen would come home and walk with her and Milana to the park for ice cream. Once, he arrived with a kitten he had found, a striped male with folded ears, whom he had named Max. The girls fell in love.

Veronika was growing up fast and took care of Milana while their dad was away and their mom expanded her beauty business, using the third bedroom that would one day be Milana’s to style women’s eyebrows and lashes.

The more time the sisters spent together, the less their age difference seemed to matter. “I could still talk to her about anything,” Veronika said. Milana was small but fiercely protective of Veronika. Once, she even threw a phone charger at a boy she saw bullying her sister. Veronika felt proud.

In May, Veronika turned 13. War or no war, she was thrilled by the idea of her first teenage summer: the freedom to roam the neighborhood with her large friend group. Her dad’s scheduled time off in July. The photo shoot her mom had booked for when they would all be together again. The trip they planned to a water park three hours away.

It would be Milana’s first time going anywhere. The girls couldn’t wait.

Yevhen got into the passenger seat of his friend’s car. While one friend drove, another, in the back, told him to hold on despite his panic.

Yevhen called everyone he knew in Sumy as they drove. The story about his family’s whereabouts kept changing. They were here, they were there.

It was past 2 a. m. when he arrived at the hospital. He rushed to the front desk and asked for the mother and daughter brought in a few hours before. The receptionist told him they weren’t there.

He ran outside and saw an ambulance.

“What happened to the woman and child who were wounded tonight?” he asked.

“They died,” the driver replied.

Veronika cut through the woods, slipped through a fence and walked down the bank of the shallow river until she reached a large rock. It was gray and smooth, with a curve that made it feel almost like a chair.

It had been two months since her mother and sister died, and she was 600 miles from home, the farthest she’d ever been. The sky was bright, and the mountains stretched into the sky.

The police had sent her and her father to this property nestled in the Carpathian Mountains a few weeks earlier. It was where Ukrainian police families like hers — with relatives who were wounded, dead or in need of a rest — could start to recover. There were no air-raid sirens, no explosions, no threatening hums from drones.

Veronika found the spot in the river on her own, when she wandered away from the wood-paneled building and the psychologist who kept asking how she felt. Away from the gym where her dad was always working out to manage his grief, and the pile of stuffed animals they had brought from home that reminded her of her sister. She returned to it nearly every day.

Veronika couldn’t think too much about her sister. When she did, her vision blurred, her heart pounded. She felt sick. She had learned that this is what doctors called a panic attack. She’d had three since that night in July.

The days passed slowly. She had visited the tourist markets and waterfalls and even climbed the tallest mountain in Ukraine, where visitors left messages for friends and relatives killed in the war.

But she was lonely and bored now. She wanted to go home.

She returned to scrolling on her new iPhone, the one she secretly wished for on this trip and that her dad bought her the very same day. She clocked 18 hours of screen time on it in a single day, most of it on TikTok. She tucked an AirPod into her right ear. She didn’t bother with the left ear: She hadn’t been able to hear out of it since the blast.

There was a necklace in her pocket, one that her mother had given her on her 13th birthday in May. She had not taken it off until the week before when a boy at the retreat pulled the chain and snapped it. She still wanted to keep it close to her as she waited for it to be fixed. The charm was thick and round and had words engraved along the edges.

“Dream, Act, Love. Daughter, you can do everything. I’m proud. I love you — Mom.”

While Veronika would sneak away to the river, Yevhen split his time between the gym and the psychologist’s office on the third floor. He made protein shakes to regain some of the strength he had lost to grief. He insisted sometimes on dragging Veronika away from her phone and taking her for hikes.

He didn’t want to sit still. When he sat for too long, he remembered too much, and ugly thoughts surged to the front of his mind. The thoughts told him that there was no point in living, that there would be no justice for his family.

The psychologist was helping him learn to push these thoughts away. To make plans instead. He was only 38. He knew he had to forge a path forward.

The first days after the deaths had been a blur of rage and stress. Yevhen broke the news to Veronika at the hospital and then slept by her bedside. Her legs and arm were pocked with bits of Russian shrapnel that later would cover her in purple scars. Her left ear drum had exploded from the shock wave.

At home, he took a blue Stitch stuffed animal that Milana had loved and stuck it in his bag. He decided to carry it with him everywhere.

He also searched for the police officer he heard had tried to save Milana. He wanted to ask him: Did you really do everything you could?

They met at the scene of the strike. The officer, Dmytro Zuienko, told Yevhen that he had been on a patrol and rushed there just after the explosion. He and a colleague performed CPR on Milana for 15 minutes, even after others moved away, afraid that another strike might be coming. Milana’s face, he told Yevhen, was stuck in his mind for days.

The officer went home that night, he said, his clothes soaked in blood, and told his wife that a girl had died in his arms who was only a few years younger than their own daughter.

Yevhen knew the officer was telling the truth. But he couldn’t forget the words Veronika screamed that night: “No one is helping.” If he had been there, would he have gotten to Milana faster than the officer? He couldn’t stop himself from asking that question again and again.

A few days later, Yevhen walked again to the spot where Natalia and Milana had been killed. He had dreams of transforming this road into an alley that would honor children killed in the war. But on this day, he planned only to leave candles at the makeshift memorial that neighbors and friends had built.

The sidewalk was covered with impact marks. The windows on the grocery behind were still boarded up. Flowers and stuffed animals adorned a broken tree.

When Yevhen looked up, Mykhailo Fedorov, the defense minister at the time, was walking toward him. Mr. Fedorov was in Sumy on that July day and had asked to visit the place where he heard a Russian glide bomb recently killed a mother and child.

Neither knew the other would be there.

Yevhen introduced himself, and the two men embraced. Yevhen’s story devastated Mr. Fedorov, who also had a young daughter. Both saw the chance meeting as an opportunity: Maybe Yevhen’s new mission could be to tell the world what happened to his family, to show everyone why Ukraine needed more air-defense systems, more planes. Maybe Yevhen could stop this tragedy from happening to anyone else.

They exchanged numbers. Later, at the police retreat, Yevhen thought about this idea constantly. It motivated him to stay alive.

Yevhen and Veronika left the mountains overnight on Sept. 14 and drove through winding roads in darkness. By morning they were in Kyiv, standing outside the children’s hospital where Aliona, one of the friends Veronika was walking with on July 3, was still a patient.

Aliona was 16. Russian shrapnel had maimed her legs. She’d already had 20 surgeries, and more were planned. Her doctors said she might never walk normally again.

Veronika burst through the door. She and Aliona held each other. Yevhen hugged Aliona’s mother, Iryna. They were old friends who shared another heavy grief: Iryna’s husband had died from cancer while Yevhen was on the front line.

“I missed you,” Aliona whispered to Veronika. “I want to go home.”

The girls compared scars. Veronika gave Aliona a teddy bear she had chosen from the mountain market and showed her the necklace the boy broke. Aliona tried to fix it. “I loved your mom,” she said when she read the charm’s message. She took a deep breath and covered her face with her hands.

The conversation turned back to the night of July 3.

Iryna was the first one there after the attack, she told Yevhen. She ran through dust and debris and found two men tying tourniquets around Aliona’s legs. She was sure her daughter was dead. She screamed. And then Aliona blinked. And when Iryna looked up, Veronika was standing there watching, her legs bloody, her face confused.

Veronika interjected to remind Iryna about her jean shorts. “They were bloody halfway up, if not more,” she said. “My sneakers were completely covered in blood, and my socks were covered in blood, too.”

“Veronika — imagine — she gets up and sees all of this. Everyone and everything,” Iryna said. “Aliona was lying facing upward, so she didn’t see it.”

As her mother talked, Aliona started to cry. Veronika did, too. In the next bed over, another teenage girl, wounded in a different strike on Sumy, sat and listened silently.

That afternoon, after Mr. Fedorov stopped by the hospital in Kyiv to visit Yevhen and the girls, and after a doctor checked Veronika’s ear and made plans for a future surgery, Yevhen and Veronika started the drive back to Sumy.

Yevhen’s mind was racing with plans. Mr. Fedorov, who had been fired in July but remained deeply involved in defense issues, suggested that morning that Yevhen should speak to officials in Sweden.

The Swedish government had promised jets to Ukraine to help shoot down planes before they could launch glide bombs, he said. Maybe Yevhen’s story could drive home the urgency and help the planes arrive sooner.

Yevhen agreed. It would the first step in his mission.

In Sumy, he and his daughter returned to an apartment that was too quiet and still. A pile of toys lined the back of the couch. Milana’s dollhouse sat nearby on the floor.

In Yevhen and Nataliia’s room, Milana’s bed was still pushed up against her parents’, the word “Princess” printed on its footboard. Yevhen took Stitch out of his bag and placed it on Milana’s pillow.

Veronika ran outside. She hadn’t told her friends when she would be back, and she decided to surprise them.

She hid behind a car, one hand on her mouth to muffle her giggles. She tilted her head to listen with her good ear and caught the sound of a faraway hum. “Is that an F. P. V.?” she asked. Satisfied it was not a Russian drone, she settled back into position.

Then she saw a group coming. She jumped out from her hiding place and onto her best friend, Uliana.

Just like that, Veronika was 13 again. She pulled a stuffed sheep she had bought in the mountains from her pink backpack and shoved it into Uliana’s hands. She showed off the new pink shorts and Nike sneakers her dad had bought her in Kyiv and held out her new iPhone. Her friends looked at her things with a hint of envy. No one talked about why she had been gone. At home, Yevhen retreated to the room where he had arranged a shrine to his wife and younger daughter. He lit candles, touched their photos and bowed his head in prayer. In the room next door, Veronika and Uliana were now planning a sleepover. They squealed and giggled and ignored the Russian drones packed with explosives that buzzed just outside their window.

The next day, Yevhen stood in the cemetery, tidying Milana and Nataliia’s graves.

So many toys were piled up from visitors paying their respects that some had started to fall to the ground. “Daughter, Daddy loves you,” he whispered. “He doesn’t forget about you.”An explosion shook the city. “They probably hit the checkpoint behind us,” Yevhen said, barely looking up. He touched the signs above the graves with his wife’s and daughter’s names and then, crying, kissed them. He thought again about his new mission.

“Let the world see what Russia did to my family,” he said as he walked to the car. “I want to tell Europe and the United States that our kids also want to live.”He looked back at his wife’s and daughter’s graves. “They also wanted to live.”

On Sept. 21, Yevhen and Veronika drove west again, back to Kyiv.

They boarded a morning train to Budapest, where they spent one night before they caught a flight to Stockholm. Mr. Fedorov had arranged the trip, and a Ukrainian businessman, Oleh Horokhovskyi, paid for it.

The Swedish defense minister had agreed to meet them. They were going to describe to him what happened to their family. They knew that sharing their story would not change its ending. They wanted to tell it anyway.

Thank you so much for reading this article about Yevhen and Veronika. I first heard of them in July, when I saw that a girl lost her mother and younger sister in Sumy. I wanted to follow what grief looked like for a teenager still living through the war. Then I learned her father was a soldier. My colleagues and I spent a lot of time with Yevhen and Veronika, watching them navigate the aftermath of this tragedy. We were profoundly affected by their love for each other and desire to protect each other from their own versions of grief. We also saw how Yevhen sought a mission and Veronika sought some return to a sense of normalcy, and how those two realities somehow clashed. I’m happy to answer any questions about our reporting process and about the family. They both were very open with us and grateful to share their story and worlds with us, which made this story even more intimate.

Nataliia Novosolova contributed reporting from Kyiv.

Siobhán O’Grady is a Ukraine correspondent for The Times, based in Kyiv.

Tupac Shakur Murder Conviction Lands Man 40 Years to Life in Prison

The New York Times October 13, 2026

Tupac Shakur Murder Trial

Advertisement

Supported by

Duane Keith Davis was convicted by a jury of obtaining a gun and pursuing the rapper in a violent act of revenge in 1996.

By Julia Jacobs

A judge in Las Vegas on Tuesday sentenced a man to 40 years to life in prison after he was convicted of orchestrating the murder of the rapper Tupac Shakur in a 1996 drive-by shooting.

The murder of one of hip-hop’s most celebrated artists went unresolved for nearly 30 years until this past summer, when a jury found Duane Keith Davis guilty of arranging for the killing. At the three-week trial, prosecutors accused Mr. Davis, 63, of obtaining the gun used in the shooting and pursuing Mr. Shakur amid a gang war that had become entangled with a feud between East Coast and West Coast hip-hop labels.

The prosecution prevailed in the case despite a dearth of physical evidence or direct witness testimony about the people responsible for the drive-by shooting — shortcomings that long stymied investigators.

But for years, Mr. Davis had admitted to being involved in the killing, repeatedly taking responsibility in a memoir and in podcast interviews. After he was indicted on a murder charge in 2023, he said he had been making false confessions to profit from a connection to the notorious case.

The sentence means Mr. Davis is likely to die in prison.

“You don’t get to take a man from his family,” Judge Carli Kierny of Clark County District Court told Mr. Davis before handing down the sentence. “You don’t get to take his very life, his whole future from him and just walk away from it,” she added.

“Especially when that man is Tupac Shakur,” she said. “The world never forgot about him and his death, and neither did Las Vegas.”

Wearing prison clothes and shackles, Mr. Davis declined to address Mr. Shakur’s death when given an opportunity to speak.

“I’m going to appeal this case for sure,” he said, and demanded that the government return items the authorities had taken from his home, including photographs.

The judge handed down the sentence after emotional testimony from two of Mr. Shakur’s siblings, who described the immense pain that the murder had caused for their family.

“We lost something; our whole generation lost something huge,” said Sekyiwa Shakur, one of Mr. Shakur’s sisters, calling her brother the “promise of all of our grandparents.”

The state’s strongest evidence against Mr. Davis was his own statements, including a 2008 recording of him admitting his involvement to the police and interviews tied to the release of his 2019 memoir. He later disavowed the memoir and said he lied to the police to avoid prosecution in a separate drug case.

Known by the nickname Keffe D, Mr. Davis was depicted by prosecutors at trial as having been a powerful shot caller in California for the South Side Compton Crips, a gang that had ongoing hostilities with the Mob Piru Bloods. Suge Knight’s Death Row Records, which represented Mr. Shakur, relied on members of the Bloods for security, associating the label with an escalating gang war.

In September 1996, members of the Bloods and Crips ended up in Las Vegas for a Mike Tyson prizefight. A night of revelry descended into violence after the fight, when Mr. Shakur and Mr. Knight participated in a group beating of Mr. Davis’s nephew, Orlando Anderson.

According to prosecutors, that public attack fueled a brutal act of retaliation on the streets of Las Vegas.

Later that night, Mr. Shakur was in a black BMW driven by Mr. Knight when a car pulled up alongside them and someone inside opened fire. Mr. Shakur, 25, was hit four times and died in a hospital days later. The murder weapon was never found, nor was the car that Mr. Davis and three other members of the Crips were said to have been riding in that night.

Word soon spread in Compton that Mr. Anderson had been the person to open fire. But other accounts suggest it was Deandrae Smith, who had been sitting next to him in the back seat. Both men are now dead.

Christopher Wallace, the rapper on the rival Bad Boy label known as the Notorious B. I. G., was gunned down only six months later, turning the shootings into twin tragedies in hip-hop that long languished on detectives’ desks without any convictions.

“It took us 30 years,” Judge Kierny told Mr. Davis at the sentencing hearing. “But at this time, you are going to face justice for what you did.”

Julia Jacobs is an arts and culture reporter who often covers legal issues for The Times.

Worlds More Habitable Than Earth? They’re Out There.

The New York Times October 13, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Scientists believe there are planets outside our solar system where life is even more abundant and sustainable.

By Natalie Wolchover

Natalie Wolchover is a Pulitzer Prize-winning science journalist and the writer of “Other Worlds,” a new series about planets outside our solar system and the search for life.

A few years ago, in a lab in Berlin, the astrobiologist Iva Vilović was thrilled when she observed garden cress sprouting under a light designed to mimic a “K-dwarf” star — an orange-hued star that’s cooler and slower burning than our yellow sun. To her surprise, the cress grew even faster and taller than it did under simulated sunlight.

Her results suggested that photosynthesis, the process that supplies the energy for Earth’s entire food web, can happen on planets orbiting these orange stars. “K-dwarf light is a very, very interesting light source, and it should be considered, if not prioritized, for any type of search for extraterrestrial life, in my opinion,” said Dr. Vilović, now at the Leibniz Institute for Astrophysics in Potsdam, Germany.

In particular, alien life may thrive in the light of these stars on planets that are slightly larger than Earth, known as super-Earths. Scientists like Dr. Vilović believe super-Earths that orbit K-dwarfs might, in fact, be the liveliest places in the galaxy — perhaps even more suitable for life than here.

Scientists call these “superhabitable worlds,” planets that would allow carbon-based life to persist longer and become even more complex and diverse than on Earth.

A superhabitable world — as scientists imagine it — is about 20 to 30 percent wider and twice as massive as Earth, and is placed at the right distance from its star for water to flow on its surface. The stronger gravity of this bigger Earth would hold on tighter to ambient molecules than Earth does, giving the planet a thicker atmosphere and a warmer and more stable climate, fueling the growth of extraterrestrial plants and animals (or their equivalents). The super-Earth’s bigger iron core would erect a stronger magnetic field around it, better blocking cosmic radiation.

As for the superhabitable planet’s surface, picture paradise. An enlarged orb would be rounder and smoother than Earth, as its stronger gravity erodes continental shelves and fills in trenches. Water would spill evenly over its surface as shallow lakes and seas.

On Earth, tropical islands and shallow seas are among the most biodiverse habitats. Now imagine a whole world of balmy archipelagos and reefs. The islands would burst with biological activity, their diverse topographies and geographic isolation fueling explosions of distinct species. Light would reach clear to the seafloor, powering abundant alien algae and plants to feed a booming marine ecosystem.

As for that light, it might be the orange glow of the planet’s K-dwarf star.

It was in the 2010s when astronomers began contemplating planets that are a little bigger, and a little nicer, than Earth, and where to find them. The whole idea was spurred in part by a question from John Armstrong a professor at Weber State University in Utah, who asked in the comments section of an astrobiology seminar on YouTube: “Shouldn’t there be planets more habitable than Earth?”

That got another astronomer, René Heller, who is now at the Max Planck Institute for Solar System Research in Germany, thinking. In the quest to discover chemical signs of life on distant worlds, he thought, astronomers have focused on finding “Earth twins,” rocky, watery, Earth-size planets orbiting sun-like stars. But when it comes to hosting life, Earth may not be the ideal archetype. After all, the fact that we’re not located at a special place in the cosmos (that we revolve around the sun, not that it revolves around us) is what the Copernican revolution was all about.

“It occurred to me that currently, humanity is looking for Earthlike planets with the same anthropocentric bias,” Dr. Heller said. “Of course, Earth is special to us. But from a universal perspective, why should Earth be a reference?”

In fact, Earth is only marginally habitable. Most astrobiologists think water must be present on a planet’s surface for life to arise there, and indeed the first bacteria appeared on Earth almost as soon as water pooled on its cooling surface roughly four billion years ago. But if Earth were just 2 percent closer to the sun, that pooling wouldn’t have happened. Instead, all of Earth’s water would have boiled away. We got lucky. But our luck will run out. The sun is expanding and brightening. Scientists calculate that in another half-billion years or so, Earth will be too hot to sustain complex life like plants and animals.

For Dr. Heller, the hunt for more habitable worlds is about “finding out if we are alone, if we could have been found, if there’s someone to talk to,” he said.

“Although I am not, at least in my everyday life, a very spiritual person,” he added, “it’s nevertheless something that at least drives me — this question, Could there be someone?”

He contacted Dr. Armstrong, and together they wrote a 2014 paper introducing the hypothesis of superhabitable worlds, which the two envisioned as archipelago-covered super-Earths. They were proposing a new target for telescopes.

“Superhabitable worlds must be considered for future follow-up observations of signs of extraterrestrial life,” they wrote.

In the paper, Dr. Heller and Dr. Armstrong reasoned that cool, petite K-dwarfs would be better host stars for superhabitable worlds than sun-like stars because they burn through their hydrogen fuel more slowly and brighten much more gradually. Our sun has only five billion years’ worth of hydrogen left before it will suddenly balloon and redden, becoming a red giant that will engulf the Earth. K-dwarfs, by contrast, shine steadily for tens of billions of years. This means life on a superhabitable planet orbiting a K-dwarf has far longer to evolve into ever more complex life forms.

What kinds of life forms? We can only imagine. All we know is earthlings have grown increasingly complex and sophisticated over the past four billion years, culminating so far in human-level intelligence.

“K-dwarfs do seem to be everyone’s sweet-spot star,” said Johanna Teske, a planetary scientist at the Carnegie Institution for Science in Washington, D. C. Planets that can sustain liquid water sit closer to K-dwarfs than they do to sun-like stars, so they are easier to observe with telescopes.

Astronomers search for life on planets tens or hundreds of light-years away by looking for gases in their atmospheres that may indicate biological activity. Current instruments, such as the James Webb Space Telescope, are mostly capable of checking the skies of rocky planets that tightly orbit tiny red stars called M-dwarfs. So far, most of these planets have been revealed as bare rocks, stripped skyless by their aggressive, nearby stars.

Probing the skies of potential superhabitable planets — namely, super-Earths orbiting at the right distances around K-dwarfs — should become feasible in future. The first step is to find nearby candidates. Dr. Heller is a leader of the European Space Agency’s Plato mission, a space telescope launching in 2027 with the purpose of detecting potentially habitable planets, including super-Earths orbiting K-dwarfs. “We will probably find a few of them — maybe a dozen,” Dr. Heller said. “But we won’t learn much about them.”

Follow-up observations from other telescopes should reveal more about the chemical makeup of these planets’ skies. The Webb telescope might be able to investigate the skies of some potentially superhabitable super-Earths in the coming years. The Extremely Large Telescope, which measures 39 meters across and is currently under construction in Chile, will be capable of seeing more of them. Even more extensive and definitive observations will become possible with the Habitable Worlds Observatory, a NASA space mission planned for the 2040s.

For Dr. Vilović, the pursuit of superhabitable planets is, in part, “an idealistic dream of a world that has beautiful conditions that are not being influenced by humans in a negative way,” she said. She thinks it’s also about a “drive to find extremes” — the most extreme version of the kind of life we know and understand.

As for whether the dream is also a reality, Dr. Vilović feels good about the odds. “I like to believe that statistically speaking, in the realm of the universe, it is likely that life exists — especially on superhabitable planets,” she said.
