F. B. I. Disrupts Pyongyang Revenue Stream: North Koreans in U. S. Tech Jobs

The New York Times October 13, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

F. B. I. investigators worked with the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike to dismantle so-called laptop farms that steal American identities to earn cash for Pyongyang.

By Dustin Volz

Reporting from Washington

The F. B. I. last month disrupted a widespread network of American facilitators accused of aiding the North Korean government in securing remote information technology jobs that helped fund the reclusive country’s nuclear and ballistic weapons programs, U. S. officials said Tuesday.

The operation included the dismantling of more than 40 so-called laptop farms across Texas and the seizure of nearly 200 computer devices, the officials said, marking one of the largest efforts to date by U. S. authorities to block a key revenue stream that has helped North Korea evade harsh international sanctions and generate billions in cash in recent years.

The Justice Department separately unsealed indictments in Ohio on Tuesday against two U. S. nationals and 10 China-based North Koreans accused of committing identity theft to earn paychecks from unwitting American companies that hired them. Prosecutors said that scheme bilked 70 companies out of more than $3 million and ran from 2019 to 2025. The identities of two additional defendants remained under seal.

The moves were the latest by the United States in an intensifying campaign to try to cut off a stealthy and evolving digital threat from North Korea whose scale is not entirely clear but likely vast. U. S. intelligence officials in both the Biden and second Trump administrations have said the I. T. worker scams are a primary method of funding Pyongyang’s weapons program, alongside thefts of cryptocurrency.

North Korea is deploying “thousands of state-controlled I. T. workers to infiltrate companies in the United States and allied countries,” Brett Leatherman, the head of the F. B. I.’s cyber division, said in an interview. “Every one of these jobs is funding a stream for a nuclear and ballistic missiles program obtained with the stolen identity of an American and the trust of an American employer.”

The bureau worked closely with the U. S.-based cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike to identify and disrupt the network, Mr. Leatherman said. He added that the coordinated actions were an early example of the F. B. I.’s new cyber strategy, which was unveiled last month and promised closer collaboration with the private sector to target hackers in ways that impede or thwart malicious activity. The strategy is part of a broader effort across the Trump administration to work more closely with American companies to strike hackers with cyberattacks, a pivot cautiously welcomed by some security experts.

U. S. officials and cybersecurity analysts have said the North Korean I. T. worker scheme is among the most serious ongoing digital threats facing businesses today, and that it remains underappreciated as a risk. Adam Meyers, who oversees counteradversary operations at CrowdStrike, said the North Korean schemes to get hired for jobs have been “increasing both in prevalence and complexity.”

It is difficult to know how widespread laptop farms are in the United States, Mr. Meyers said, but noted that CrowdStrike identified an average of two new cases per day throughout the month of September — which is likely only the tip of the iceberg.

For more than two years, U. S. intelligence officials and cybersecurity researchers have warned that North Korea has been using stolen American identities — often acquired from compromised private information, like Social Security numbers, on the dark web — and artificial intelligence tools to get hired for remote information technology jobs at companies across the United States, Europe and elsewhere. Experts have said companies ranging from small start-ups to Fortune 500 firms have been victimized.

A crucial aspect of the fraud campaign is support from people in the United States who are recruited by North Korea to help bypass corporate security measures that detect fraudulent hires, according to investigators. Facilitators help enable the fraud by receiving and setting up work laptops at addresses that appear like legitimate residences to corporate human-resources teams. North Korean operators then use software to remotely tunnel into those laptops and work on them, posing as Americans to the companies that hired them.

The appeal for facilitators is simple: jobs that look like easy cash and, at least at first, might not require much of them. “They get kind of hooked on it initially, and then more gets asked of them, and they’re kind of in too deep at that point,” Mr. Meyers said.

Mr. Leatherman said that the Texas sweep did not include any arrests of facilitators, but that authorities warned them they could face criminal penalties should they continue to assist with remote fraud. The decision stemmed in part from a desire to move quickly to upend the network rather than wait for prosecutors to file charges, he said.

Mr. Leatherman said the laptop farms often operate like a “mini data center” for the North Koreans, where one facilitator hosts dozens or even hundreds of laptops used to fill scores of jobs. A woman in Arizona sentenced last year to more than eight years in prison was accused of hosting dozens of laptops at her home to help North Koreans connect to more than 300 U. S. companies.

The tactics of North Korea’s I. T. worker army have steadily evolved to evade detection. That includes increased reliance on artificial intelligence to create fake résumés, videos and photos, and to navigate virtual job interviews, officials said. The fraudsters are also relying more on subcontractors in places like Pakistan and Nigeria to further obscure North Korean involvement, Mr. Leatherman said.

In an advisory released on Tuesday, the F. B. I. said the North Koreans were paying Americans and other Western accomplices to “perform a growing variety of identity and location obfuscation tasks” that included appearing on camera, participating in job interviews or meetings, verifying fraudulent identities, shipping packages, and even completing urinalysis tests or fingerprint submissions.

Dustin Volz writes about cybersecurity and intelligence for The Times. He is based in Washington.

The New York Times October 13, 2026

Houthi-Saudi War

Advertisement

Supported by

The Iran-backed militia threatened to attack the Saudi energy giant Aramco after the Saudi authorities issued an evacuation notice for an oil facility in the Yemeni capital.

By Ismaeel Naar

Reporting from Dubai, United Arab Emirates.

The Iran-backed Houthi militia threatened to strike multiple facilities belonging to Saudi Arabia’s oil giant Aramco on Tuesday and accused Saudi forces of targeting an oil company in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa.

The threat against Aramco was made soon after Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, a spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition that is fighting the Houthis in Yemen, told civilians to evacuate the site of al-Sabaha Central Station, an oil facility in Houthi-controlled Sanaa, in a post on social media.

Later on Tuesday, the Houthi-run television network al-Masirah reported that a Saudi airstrike had targeted the oil site, without elaborating. Saudi strikes on another oil facility in Hodeidah, in western Yemen, killed at least two people, Anis al-Asbahi, a spokesman for the Houthi-run health ministry, said on Tuesday.

It was not immediately possible to verify whether either of the sites had been hit, and the Saudi authorities did not respond to questions about the reported strikes.

It was unclear whether the Houthis would act on their threat against Aramco. The militia has targeted the company’s facilities before and has frequently hit Saudi oil infrastructure and tankers in the Red Sea since tensions escalated between the two sides in July.

Saudi warplanes have been bombing Houthi positions in Yemen in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government, which is fighting to retake territory seized by the Houthis last month.

Yahya Saree, a military spokesman for the Houthis, said in a post on social media that, if Saudi forces were to attack the oil company in Sanaa, then the Houthis would target Aramco's headquarters in Dammam, Saudi Arabia; the company's refinery in the capital, Riyadh; and King Khalid International Airport, also in Riyadh.

The Houthis struck the airport over the weekend, and an attack on Saturday killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300. It was the deadliest attack on a Gulf Arab country since the start of the U. S.-Israeli war with Iran, the Houthis’ primary backers.

On Tuesday, Saudi officials, during a cabinet meeting chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, vowed that the Houthis would bear the consequences for the “heinous attacks” on the kingdom’s airports.

The Houthis on Sunday accused Saudi Arabia of bombing an airport in the Yemeni capital, according to statements carried by the Saba news agency, which is run by the militia. The Saudi authorities have not commented on that assertion.

President Trump, in a social media post after the exchange of threats on Tuesday, said, “The Houthis are behaving very badly.” He said that he thought the militia had “learned their lesson a year ago when we bombed the HELL out of them.”

Though Mr. Trump condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia over the weekend, he has so far rebuffed the kingdom’s requests for U. S. support in fighting the militia.

The Houthi militia has been fighting the internationally recognized government of Yemen, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, since 2014. Saudi Arabia pledged to restore the government, declaring war on the Houthis and initiating a bombing campaign that triggered one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. A fragile truce agreed to in 2022 has unraveled in recent months.

Emboldened by regional instability, the battle-hardened Houthis have far less to lose against their more powerful, wealthier enemies, even as they imperil Saudi Arabia’s ambitions to transform itself into a global hub of business and tourism.

The Red Cross called for the urgent de-escalation of the conflict on Tuesday, warning that further escalation would be disastrous for tens of millions of civilians. “Civilians are paying an unacceptable price as a result of military operations in the Middle East,” said Mirjana Spoljaric, the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross.

Shuaib Almosawa contributed reporting from Sanaa, Yemen.

Ismaeel Naar is an international reporter for The Times, covering the Gulf states. He is based in Dubai, United Arab Emirates.

Trump Hands Victories to Putin, Who Offers More War in Return

The New York Times October 13, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

Russia has reaped a diesel deal and an increase in U. S. pressure on Ukraine as President Trump’s political needs align with his longstanding inclinations toward Russia.

By Paul Sonne

Reporting from Berlin

The wins for President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia came in rapid succession from Washington.

President Trump proffered sanctions relief for Russian diesel fuel. He publicly called for Ukraine to get a new leader. And he pressured Kyiv to stop a strike campaign against Russian oil facilities that has damaged the Russian economy.

Mr. Putin, in return, offered more war.

Minutes after Mr. Trump announced the diesel deal, the Kremlin reiterated Mr. Putin’s stance that he would not negotiate with Ukraine at the moment, because he remained angry about Ukrainian strikes during last month’s Russian parliamentary election.

The next day, Russia launched an attack on the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia that killed 22 people, including four children. It was the latest in a near daily drumbeat of devastating Russian strikes, which have dramatically increased the civilian toll in Ukraine as Kyiv sorely lacks air-defense missiles.

And Mr. Putin has signaled that he plans to escalate further, aiming to knock out Ukraine’s power and water infrastructure in what Ukrainians expect to be the worst winter of the war.

Mr. Putin is reaping his victories as Mr. Trump’s own domestic political needs align with his longstanding inclination to tip the scales toward Russia. With the American president focused on trying to bring down fuel prices before a difficult midterm election, he is pushing Kyiv to trade away its leverage for nothing in return.

Ukraine has said it would suspend its oil refinery strikes if Russia ceased attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities heading into the winter. But when Mr. Trump announced an “energy cease-fire” on Sunday, he meant only a suspension of oil refinery strikes in both countries, The New York Times reported. Ukraine has only one major oil refinery, and Russian strikes took it largely out of service in 2022.

Mr. Trump has promoted his energy deal with Mr. Putin as an example of how he is tackling America’s diesel challenge, which experts say is more attributable to the war with Iran. But it was seen as a betrayal by Ukrainian officials, undercutting years of Western efforts to starve the Russian war machine of cash.

It may not even do much to lower diesel prices. Economists have said the amount of fuel discussed is not enough to move the needle significantly.

“The U. S. president is focused on one thing, which is himself and his reading of the world,” said Alexander Gabuev, director of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center.

That reading, Mr. Gabuev said, includes Mr. Trump’s stubborn denial that his own decision to go to war against Iran caused fuel prices to skyrocket. “In his picture of the world, the Gulf war doesn’t play a role in the current diesel crisis, and there needs to be a magical solution with someone he is predisposed to, who is Vladimir Putin.”

Earlier this year, things were looking difficult for Mr. Putin. Expenditures on the war were rapidly expanding. Progress on the battlefield had slowed to a crawl. Global prices for oil, Russia’s top export, had slumped to around $60 a barrel.

Then Mr. Trump launched the war in Iran, alongside Israel. Oil prices jumped to over $100 a barrel. The vast use of air defense missiles by the United States and its Gulf allies in response to Iran’s attacks dried up the supply for Ukraine, leaving it increasingly vulnerable. With Mr. Trump looking for a way out, Russia’s longstanding relationship with Iran offered Mr. Putin a new calling card with Washington.

As the Iran war accorded benefits to Russia, Ukraine tried to limit Moscow’s economic gains with increasingly effective strikes on oil refineries — the campaign that Mr. Trump is now demanding that Kyiv end.

Kyiv’s systematic targeting of Russian oil infrastructure brought the war home to Russia as never before, causing lines at the pump across the country and forcing Russia, one of the world’s largest diesel suppliers, to suspend exports.

As Ukrainian strikes decreased production, Russia’s tax revenue from oil and gas for the first three quarters of the year fell by 17 percent compared with the same period in 2025, even as fuel prices rose dramatically. (A rise in the ruble and Russian domestic fuel subsidies also played a role.)

Now, the diesel deal could pour billions of dollars into the Russian economy. An extended suspension of Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries, if Kyiv agrees to one under the intense American pressure, could generate much more money.

The wins for Mr. Putin go beyond the diesel deal. Mr. Trump has also welcomed Russian ministers this year for Group of 20 events in North Carolina and Wisconsin, and he plans to host Mr. Putin in December at the G-20 summit in Miami. His administration is also negotiating potential business deals with the Kremlin, in what Mr. Trump’s team has cast as inducements to a peace deal.

The Russians want even more from the U. S. president, analysts say.

When Mr. Trump returned to office in 2025, Moscow hoped that the United States would cut off all support for Ukraine and force President Volodymyr Zelensky into a capitulation largely on the Kremlin’s terms.

Mr. Trump’s Oval Office blowup with Mr. Zelensky in March of last year made it seem as if Moscow’s dream was within reach. The Trump administration’s decision to halt weapons donations to Ukraine and suspend intelligence sharing stoked hopes even further.

But in the months since, U. S. intelligence sharing resumed. Mr. Trump brokered a deal for the Europeans to buy weapons from the United States for Ukraine. And U. S.-led peace negotiations fizzled as the Trump administration became distracted by the war in Iran.

Fyodor Lukyanov, a Russian political scientist who advises the Kremlin, wrote last month that Ukraine would be left with little defense if the United States completely ceased its military support.

“But Trump is unlikely to take that step,” Mr. Lukyanov wrote, “even if he were personally inclined to do so,” because a complete Ukrainian defeat would not win him any plaudits in the American political establishment.

Such a move by Mr. Trump might also invite more aggressive actions from Congress, particularly after the midterms. The Senate recently passed a Russia sanctions bill, named in honor of Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, with a veto-proof margin, though Mr. Trump retains the power to waive its provisions on national security grounds and will need to do so to import Russian diesel.

As Mr. Trump so far stops short of forcing Ukraine into a surrender, Mr. Putin is likely to continue his escalation, said Hanna Notte, an analyst at the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies and the author of a new book on Russian foreign policy called “We Will Outlast Them.”

She said of Mr. Putin, “It’s quite clear that his intention right now is to inflict a really, really nasty winter on the Ukrainians.”

Although Russian forces remain largely stuck on the battlefield, Mr. Putin has long believed that he can achieve victory in Ukraine by outlasting Kyiv and what he sees as its fickle Western allies, analysts say. He believes they will eventually pull back their extensive support of Ukraine as their own domestic problems mount, analysts say.

The French presidential election next year could usher in the far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who has advocated halting financial assistance to Ukraine. Chancellor Friedrich Merz of Germany is also under pressure from a surging far-right party that has pressed for ending support for Ukraine. And both Britain and France are struggling under huge government debts that are far more expensive to service at current interest rates.

“You could make the case that from the Kremlin’s perspective, the future looks better, more conducive to an outcome of the war that is closer to their terms,” said Sam Charap, a Russia analyst at the RAND Corporation. “You have to change that perception of the future, diminish that optimism, to affect their calculus.”

Paul Sonne is the Moscow bureau chief, leading coverage of Russia, the Caucasus and Central Asia. He is based in Berlin.

Kimberly Guilfoyle Resigns as Ambassador to Greece

The New York Times October 13, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Ms. Guilfoyle was asked to quit by the White House after a string of damaging reports, including that she had asked a Republican donor to pay off a credit card.

By Tyler Pager

Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned as the U. S. ambassador to Greece on Tuesday after the White House asked her to do so following a string of damaging reports, including that she had asked a Republican donor to pay off her credit card.

In response to a question from a reporter about Ms. Guilfoyle’s status, President Trump’s new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, said: “We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign. She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well.”

Mr. Trump said Tuesday that Ms. Guilfoyle “was doing a good job” but that he “didn’t like what I read.” The president also downplayed his connection to Ms. Guilfoyle, who was once engaged to his oldest son, Donald Trump Jr.

“She wasn’t a member of my family,” he told reporters before leaving the White House for Alaska. “She, I guess, dated my son a long time ago.”

In a lengthy post on social media, Ms. Guilfoyle said that her time as ambassador was “coming to an end” and that she planned to “vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.”

“I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service,” she wrote.

A donor, Eric Deters, first told The Wall Street Journal that Ms. Guilfoyle asked him to wire her $100,000 to pay off her American Express card just before her Senate confirmation hearing in July 2025. According to messages Mr. Deters provided to The New York Times, Ms. Guilfoyle promised to serve as his “ride or die in Trump world” if he sent her the money.

Ms. Guilfoyle was one of the first ambassadors to be nominated in the president’s second term. In Greece, she has been a highly visible ambassador, appearing on the cover of Vogue Greece and at parties around Athens. Ms. Guilfoyle told The Times last year that her active social life demonstrated her commitment to the job.

In her resignation post, Ms. Guilfoyle said she was proud of her work to expand American liquefied natural gas exports to Europe and strengthen defense and security partnerships with NATO.

In Athens, the reports of her potential conflicts of interest have generated exasperation.

“The fact that they would send someone like that here, with no tact or diplomacy skills, shows how low we rank in Trump’s priorities, how insignificant Greece is for them,” Maria Stefanou, a 68-year-old retiree, told The Times last week.

The resignation caps a remarkable rise and fall for Ms. Guilfoyle, a former Fox News personality. Decades ago, she was married to Gavin Newsom, then the mayor of San Francisco, and in 2004, Harper’s Bazaar predicted their marriage would be “one of the most glamorous political unions since Jack and Jackie.” They divorced in 2006.

Ms. Guilfoyle then became a legal analyst for CNN and ABC before joining Fox News. She was forced out of Fox in 2018 over questions about inappropriate workplace behavior. That same year, she started dating Donald Trump Jr. and working for a pro-Trump super PAC. The two were engaged in 2020, and Ms. Guilfoyle spoke at both the 2020 and 2024 Republican National Conventions. In May, the president’s son married Bettina Anderson, a Palm Beach socialite.

“While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end,” Ms. Guilfoyle wrote on social media.

Tyler Pager is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

We Know How to Fix Homelessness. Look at Denver.

The New York Times October 13, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

German Lopez

By German Lopez

Mr. Lopez is a writer for the editorial board.

Homelessness, all appearances to the contrary, is a long-solved problem. We know both the causes and the cure. You wouldn’t think that’s the case from visiting many U. S. cities. Stymied by political and financial hurdles, progressive bastions including Los Angeles, Seattle and Burlington, Vt., appear to have given up. They have surrendered public spaces to the homeless and their encampments to the point that it’s difficult to describe these spaces as truly for the public anymore.

Denver shows what happens when a city puts into place proven policies with determination and focus. Not only has it dramatically reduced homelessness, it embarrasses every other urban jurisdiction that has failed to deal with its Covid-era surge of homeless encampments. Other cities no longer have an excuse.

Denver has recorded the biggest recent drop in street homelessness among the largest U. S. cities, according to my analysis of local data. The city’s drop was roughly 13 times the national rate in 2025, the most recent year for federal statistics. Since 2023, Denver’s unsheltered population is down 64 percent. “What they’re doing is working,” said Samantha Batko, a senior fellow at the left-leaning Urban Institute, which is independently evaluating the city’s progress.

Since Mayor Mike Johnston of Denver took office in 2023, he has focused on getting unsheltered homelessness to zero. He has done so by using some fairly standard ideas. Police officers break up homeless encampments, warning that repeated violations could lead to arrest. With the help of social workers, the city connects those people to services and shelters. Crucially, it has expanded those services to ensure that officers and social workers have something to connect people to.

By successfully combining enforcement and social services, Denver demonstrates that cities don’t need to choose between those binaries. They should do both.

Politically, none of this is easy. On the policing side, progressives remain skeptical of using law enforcement to deal with what they see as largely an economic issue. On the housing side, the constraint is money. Building housing and shelters requires public and private funds that cities often don’t have and aren’t willing to prioritize over other spending and tax cuts.

Speaking from an office stuffed with Colorado memorabilia, Mr. Johnston said he wanted to go further. He laid out a vision to ensure that all people are housed and that public spaces are actually available to the public. “Our fundamental mantra when we started was our belief that all of our problems are solvable and we’re the ones to solve them,” he told me.

On a Monday afternoon, Mr. Johnston played tour guide. He wanted to show me the city’s new homeless shelters and how they differed from traditional facilities. We walked 10 minutes from City Hall — the mayor stopped to congratulate a wedding party on the way out — to a block of tiny houses known as Elati Village.

Each resident there gets a small house that offers a level of privacy not typical for homeless shelters. Valentino Ortiz, a former Elati Village resident and a transgender man, said privacy was important for his safety. He recalled a previous stay at a more traditional shelter. “The third day, I was already getting sexually assaulted,” he said. At Elati, “you have a beautiful tiny home to call your own. You have hot showers, you can cook your own meals and do laundry.”

Next, Mr. Johnston took me to The Aspen, a city-owned hotel. For residents, it is like an apartment complex. The rooms weren’t too different from places I’ve lived before. Mr. Johnston said he wanted the city’s shelters to feel like real homes — “a room of one’s own.”

As we walked through the building, residents told the mayor they finally had been able to get their lives in order. Staff at The Aspen and other shelters spend much of their time preparing people to leave. They help residents get the documents they need to find a job and permanent housing. They connect them to training, education programs and additional government aid, including housing vouchers and rent subsidies. Residents don’t face hard limits on how long they can stay, but providers are, under their contracts, evaluated on how many people they help get on the right path.

The goal is to keep people off the streets for good. To that end, the city still has to address the high cost of housing. Denver has enacted some reforms, but buying and renting a home remain too expensive for much of the poor and middle class.

Ana Miller, an organizer for the homeless rights group Housekeys Action Network Denver, criticized The Aspen for some of its rules and their enforcement, particularly the staff’s room inspections. She also panned the shelter’s provider, Urban Alchemy, which has faced criticisms in other cities for its unorthodox tactics, including its hiring of ex-convicts as staff members. Ms. Miller said Elati Village offers a better model than typical shelters, but she worried about resistance from neighborhoods to building more such communities. The neighbors living in apartments near Elati “literally point cameras at the community and watch them,” she said.

Still, the numbers speak for themselves. Mr. Johnston said that no one has declined an offer to move into one of the new facilities, and that they are consistently at or near capacity. The city’s biggest problem is how it can buy or build more places like Elati Village and The Aspen to meet demand.

Much of the tens of millions of dollars the city has spent on shelters was paid for through temporary federal funds that have expired. The Trump administration has also moved to cut housing subsidies across the country. The financial constraints have led some local officials to question whether the cost of the city’s efforts is worth the benefit. If that sentiment spreads, it could doom progress.

At 6:30 a. m. on Tuesday, I met with a Denver police squad to see the enforcement side of the city’s strategy. Officer Michael Nierenberg, who led the group, told me his goal was not to arrest people. Tall and imposing, he said the threat he presented was only an incentive to push people to get help. Social workers rode along.

Early in the patrol, we came across a tent. Inside, a couple slept with all their belongings scattered across the floor. Officer Nierenberg waited patiently as they woke up, and then explained the consequences of breaking laws against camping outside: a verbal warning, then a written warning, then a ticket or arrest. He started asking about the couple’s situation. They were from Texas, they said, and still had family there. They would like to go back, but they didn’t have the means to do so.

Officer Nierenberg told them to pack up their tent and that he would go see what he could do. He sat in his car, making calls and looking through his computer. After about 15 minutes, he came back with a bus ticket. The man, who identified himself as Chance, cried tears of joy.

We continued like this for the rest of the morning. Sometimes the encounters were less pleasant. One man told the officers, in colorful language, to go away. Other times, people were cordial. “It has been a typical morning,” the officer told me as we headed back to the police station.

Progressives tend to view the enforcement side of anti-homelessness strategies with disdain because it can involve criminalizing an economic or a mental health issue. At the same time, residents don’t want encampments clogging up parks and sidewalks. Progressive cities have tried to get around the dilemma by flooding the streets with social services, hoping that offers of help would get people on the streets to pack up. The reality, as cities have painfully learned, is that people often need a stronger push to abandon their tents.

The balanced approach has shrunk the number of encampments across Denver, the Urban Institute’s evaluation found. Between 2023 and 2025, the number of active encampments fell by nearly half. The number of large encampments, with 10 or more tents or structures, dropped by 91 percent. “It’s pretty much night and day,” said Anthony Mantelli, whose family runs the West Saloon and Kitchen in the city’s 16th Street Mall. “I close the restaurant four or five nights a week. I don’t deal with many issues at all.”

Mayor Johnston described his strategy through his perspective as a former school principal. “Your job is to keep everyone safe,” he said. “That means I love every single kid in the building. And if there’s one kid who’s making other kids in the building feel unsafe, my job is to either help him change his behavior or hold him accountable for it.”

I asked Mr. Johnston if it’s realistic to think a city as large as Denver can eliminate street homelessness. “I genuinely believe we can do it,” he said.

The next phase will be more difficult. Those who continue to live on the streets are much more likely to suffer from mental illness and addiction. They need more than a roof over their heads.

For this step, Mr. Johnston has begun an initiative that focuses on connecting people to mental health and addiction treatment. That will be hard to execute. Many of the sick and addicted are resistant to treatment, and getting them to accept help can require a kind of coercion and policing of low-level crimes that many progressives are uncomfortable with.

I came away from Denver convinced that the mayor’s focus and determination are the most crucial factors. I’ve seen this happen nationwide: Policies that work in one place fail in another because officials can replicate the law or the money, but not the leadership — the force of will — behind the original success.

But Democrats around the country should figure out how to copy Denver’s program. The party’s failure to tackle homelessness and public disorder more broadly has haunted it nationwide. It’s one reason the party is unpopular, even as President Trump has approval ratings in the 30s, leaving many voters with two options on the ballot they don’t particularly like.

“When you see a problem in front of you every day and nothing happens, your only option is either to blame your neighbor or to blame democracy,” Mr. Johnston said. Mr. Trump “has proved that if things are bad enough, Americans are open to both of those arguments.”

He added: “I think the opposite’s also true. If you can prove that there’s something hard to do and we work it out together and it gets better, you train people’s muscle memory to turn to each other — not to turn on each other.”

Mr. Lopez is a writer for the editorial board.

U. K. and Europe Recoil From Trump’s Diesel Deal With Putin

The New York Times October 13, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

Shocked by the U. S. agreement with Russia, which Ukraine has called “a gift” to President Putin, officials in Europe have coalesced around a cautious diplomatic message.

By Michael D. Shear and Jeanna Smialek

Michael Shear reported from London and Jeanna Smialek reported from Luxembourg.

European and British officials were stunned by President Trump’s unexpected announcement that he had made a deal with President Vladimir V. Putin to purchase Russian diesel fuel, which had been subject to American sanctions. But they were in a bind on how to respond.

The arrangement, which President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine called “a gift” to Mr. Putin, directly undercuts years of effort by dozens of countries — including the United States — to cut Russia off from the money that fuels Mr. Putin’s war of aggression in Ukraine.

Energy experts have said that the diesel agreement, if it goes ahead, could send some $4 billion of American money into the Russian economy.

Mr. Trump’s announcement on Friday afternoon of his “highly successful discussion” with Mr. Putin was all the more shocking in Europe as it came after Russia had conducted several brutal strikes in Ukraine, killing 22 people including three babies in an apartment block on Wednesday and at least 30 people in a bus on Thursday.

For European leaders, the dilemma over the past three days has been familiar: How to support Ukraine in a moment of acute diplomatic peril, without triggering Mr. Trump’s ire?

Complicating their response is the fact that Europe as a whole depended heavily on Russia for energy before 2022. And despite cutting purchases significantly since the invasion of Ukraine, several European nations continue to buy Russian natural gas — which does not yet face full sanctions — amid growing energy insecurity and limited supply.

Hungary and Slovakia, which have had pro-Russian governments in recent years, have continued to import Russian oil.

Both Mr. Trump and Russian officials highlighted the imports of Russian fuel to European nations over the past four years in the aftermath of the diesel announcement.

As European leaders scrambled for a response, they stopped short of directly criticizing the American president and coalesced around a single diplomatic message: We are not changing our own approach to Russia, and we stand by Ukraine.

On Saturday, Britain announced that Prime Minister Andy Burnham had spoken to Mr. Zelensky, noting that he had begun the call “by recognizing the last 24 hours had been difficult for Ukraine” — an oblique reference to Mr. Trump’s intervention — and had “reiterated his complete solidarity.” The statement added that Mr. Burnham would meet with Mr. Zelensky in the coming days.

A spokesman for the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, told reporters that the government was “standing by the sanctions decisions against Russia and is working together with its European partners on further sanctions.”

Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s top diplomat, began her comments to reporters on Monday with a conciliatory nod to the United States, before saying that the bloc was “continuing our path” of trying to keep Russia from enriching itself by blocking the sale of oil and gas on the global market.

“The U. S. is our biggest ally, but our message is clear,” she said while entering a meeting of foreign affairs ministers in Luxembourg. “If we want to end this war, the only way we can do this is by putting more pressure on Russia.”

Margus Tsahkna, the minister of foreign affairs for Estonia, was more blunt.

“We have had this kind of turbulence and also pressure from President Trump’s side to Ukraine before,” he said. “So we need to focus on what we can do.”

Mr. Trump responded to the European reaction on his TruthSocial site Monday afternoon.

“The European Union paid Russia 250 Billion Dollars for Energy, and the Fake News Media doesn’t want to get near that story,” the president wrote, possibly referring to European purchases of Russian oil since Russia invaded. “I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!”

Since early 2022, the European Union as a whole has imported 238 billion euros’ worth — about $266 billion worth — of Russian oil, coal and gas, according to a tracker led by the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air, a research group.

But the bulk of those imports were in the first year after the war began, as Europe worked to cut its longstanding reliance on Russian energy. Since then, the bloc has imposed sanctions and implemented phase-outs, and the European Union’s fossil fuel imports from Russia now stand at about €47 million of energy imports per day, a fraction of the nearly €800 million it imported on the peak day in 2022.

Russian natural gas, which is harder to replace than oil because of tight global supplies and because it is transported via pipelines or specialized terminals, has continued to flow to nations including Belgium, France and Spain. But Europe is tapering those remaining imports, and it is set to prohibit new long-term liquefied natural gas contracts from early next year.

Petras Katinas, a researcher at the Royal United Services Institute, a think tank, said that Europe had moved quickly to phase out Russian energy in some cases, as in the case of oil, while moving more slowly than many supporters of Ukraine would prefer in the case of natural gas.

But he said that overall, Europe had gone from being very dependent on Russian energy to cutting it rapidly, and he argued that European leaders were not being hypocritical in criticizing Mr. Trump’s diesel move.

“The drop is huge,” he said of Europe’s Russian energy use.

He added that the diesel purchases that Mr. Trump’s policy would permit were tiny in the grand scheme of things, saying that it was “more the political signal” that was significant.

Since beginning his second term, Mr. Trump has repeatedly indicated support for Russia’s positions over those of Ukraine. Before his re-election, the president promised to end the war in 24 hours and has on several occasions blamed Mr. Zelensky for the continued fighting.

“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does,” Mr. Trump said Saturday.

On Sunday, the president announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “ENERGY CEASEFIRE,” though neither side confirmed that such an agreement existed. Several European leaders on Monday welcomed such a cease-fire but noted that Russia struck Ukrainian energy facilities after the announcement.

For European officials, the latest example of the president’s go-it-alone diplomacy with Mr. Putin strikes at the heart of their attempts to maintain a consensus on opposing Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Nearly three dozen countries, including Britain, France and Germany, formed what they called the “coalition of the willing” last year to demonstrate their resolve in supporting Ukraine.

None of the countries want to engage in a direct military confrontation with Russia. Instead, they have focused on helping Ukraine acquire weapons to defend itself. And they have used economic sanctions designed to cut Russia off from its most lucrative exports.

On Monday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland urged the United States and other European nations to increase sanctions — not back away from them.

“This message must go out today from every capital, from Warsaw to Washington,” he said. “I am certain that our response in the coming hours, weeks and months will be one of full solidarity and determination on the part of the free world, all capitals and all political leaders.”

He added, in words that signaled a more complicated reality: “I very much hope so.”

Michael D. Shear is the chief U. K. correspondent for The New York Times, covering British politics and culture and diplomacy around the world.

Jeanna Smialek is the Brussels bureau chief for The Times.

War Collides With Saudi Ambition at a Gathering of Oil Powers

The New York Times October 13, 2026

Houthi-Saudi War

Advertisement

Supported by

The tone of the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh this week was defiant even as delegates were forced to redirect travel or address the audience from afar.

By Lisa Friedman

Reporting from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia

Outside Riyadh’s cavernous exhibition center, where hundreds of oil and gas executives gathered this week for an international energy summit, foreign diplomats received a warning of a potential missile bound for the Saudi Arabian capital.

Inside the hall, there was an urgent announcement: Attendees should please take their seats, because Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, the Saudi energy minister, was about to take the stage.

Saudi Arabia has faced a severe escalation of cross-border missile and drone attacks from the Iran-aligned Houthi militia in Yemen. Missile strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh have killed at least 17 people and injured hundreds. Saudi authorities suspended commercial operations at the airport until further notice.

The timing was hard to miss. Delegates to the WPC Energy Congress, which started on Sunday, were forced to reroute to other airports and even countries in the region. Some including the chief executives of Exxon, Shell, Chevron and BP canceled their scheduled appearances altogether.

Despite the threats, Saudi officials are working to convey an air of unflappable calm at the conference, which is scheduled to continue until Friday.

“The word ‘fear’ in the Saudi dictionary does not exist,” Prince Abdulaziz said defiantly on Monday.

The war in Iran, now in its eighth month, has upended numerous elements of the economic and security order in the Middle East. Ports in the United Arab Emirates that are linchpins to global trade were trapped behind what was suddenly a battlefront at sea. The sophisticated facilities in Qatar that produce the liquefied natural gas that powers large parts of Asia sustained devastating damage.

Few places were tested recently quite like Saudi Arabia, the region’s longtime oil producing leader.

The Saudis, as did other oil producers, lost much of their access to the Strait of Hormuz, their most efficient path to export oil to the world, when Iran started using force to control who could pass. When they redirected exports through a pipeline to the Red Sea, Iran-backed militia in Iraq attacked it.

Throughout, Saudi Arabia’s rulers, and its state oil giant Saudi Aramco, adapted to get crude out of the region. It was costly, but oil producers were minting huge profits because prices had surged.

But the strikes in the past days underscored the growing risks to not only Saudi Arabia’s projection of security in the region, but also the kingdom’s determination to become an increasing center of global finance.

Iran’s attacks have posed similar challenges to the Emirates and particularly Dubai, which has long been a safe haven for business in a volatile Middle East. Iran has launched hundreds of missiles and drones at Persian Gulf countries, which host several U. S. military bases.

Later this month, Riyadh is scheduled to be the host of what in many ways is an even more important event for Saudi Arabia: Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s annual investment summit. The conference, known as the Future Investment Initiative and sometimes nicknamed “Davos in the Desert,” typically draws world leaders, billionaires and executives. It brings financial firms hunting big-game projects as investment vehicles for their clients’ money.

The conference is a platform for Prince Mohammed’s ambitions to transform the Saudi economy. Known as Vision 2030, the program aims to diversify Saudi Arabia from dependence on oil into a global destination for trade, sports, technology, culture and tourism.

Organizers of F. I. I. said in a statement on Tuesday that the conference would continue as planned and promised “comprehensive security measures” including assistance with transportation.

But the consequences the Houthis wrought on the WPC Energy Congress this week were an urgent reminder of the risks facing the investment conference.

Darren Woods, the chief executive of Exxon Mobil, and Meg O’Neill, the head of BP, stayed away. Several key government officials, including Chris Wright, the U. S. energy secretary, participated via video link, as did the energy security minister of Italy.

It is still unclear whether prominent C. E. O. s and others will feel safe enough to attend this year’s investment summit, set for Oct. 26-29.

The WPC Energy Congress was initially scheduled for April, but it was postponed after the United States and Israel launched military strikes against Iran on Feb. 28, igniting what later became a wider conflict in the Middle East.

The event, which started in the 1930s and originally called the World Petroleum Council, is held every three years. This is the first time Saudi Arabia has hosted. The event is taking place in Riyadh’s exhibition and conference center, about 10 miles from the international airport.

Analysts said keeping major events on schedule despite the attacks was both an economic and a security calculation for the kingdom.

“Despite all the mess happening in the region, they continued with the agenda because that is ultimately what keeps confidence,” said Yousef M. Alshammari, president of the London College of Energy Economics, a think tank.

“If there is no confidence, it would be difficult to attract foreign investments,” he said.

Beyond the economic implications, analysts note there is a strategic imperative at play. In addition to weakening investor confidence, canceling flagship events in Riyadh could also hand the Houthi militant groups a “psychological” victory, said Neil Quilliam, a Middle East energy policy expert at Chatham House, a London-based research institute.

“It would suggest that attacks on the kingdom are succeeding in disrupting the economic transformation and damaging Saudi Arabia’s international standing,” he said.

Still, Mr. Quilliam cautioned that continued assaults would make it harder for the government to maintain that message.

“Hosting major events demonstrates resilience, but there are limits to what symbolism can achieve,” he said.

The WPC Energy Congress was expected to draw more than 25,000 attendees. The number who turned out was not yet clear. Many of the conference attendees appeared to take the threats of fresh attacks in stride, and some ministers and executives from the Persian Gulf said they made a point of attending in person.

“Especially when the kingdom suffers heinous attacks against its infrastructure, we stand up and be counted with the Saudis,” Sheikh Nawaf S. Al-Sabah, the deputy chairman and chief executive of the Kuwait Petroleum Corporation, said in an interview in Riyadh.

For Saudi Arabia, projecting stability is also critical to preserving the kingdom’s reputation as the world’s central banker of oil.

Inside the hall, security was the theme of the day. Prince Abdulaziz sought to reassure jittery markets, declaring Riyadh “the capital of energy security” and casting Saudi Arabia as a reliable energy supplier despite deepening conflict in the Middle East.

He highlighted the rapid restoration of the Saudi East-West pipeline, a critical system that was temporarily shut down in September after a drone attack launched from Iraqi territory.

The pipeline, which delivers crude from Saudi Arabia’s eastern oil fields to a port along the Red Sea coast, has been described as the country’s lifeline in recent months because it bypassed the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran effectively blocked shortly after the war began.

Prince Abdulaziz said the kingdom planned to expand the pipeline’s capacity to approximately 10 million barrels per day from its current maximum of seven million barrels.

“Energy security can’t be taken for granted,” Prince Abdulaziz said, adding, “For Saudi Arabia, these circumstances have tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people and our resilience. They have also tested decisions made long before the present crises, because resilience is built before crises begin.”

Jenny Gross contributed reporting from London.

Lisa Friedman is a business correspondent covering energy for The New York Times.

Top G. O. P. Groups Pull Support From First House Incumbents

Two major Republican super PACs are said to be withdrawing cash from the races of the incumbent Representatives Thomas H. Kean Jr. of New Jersey and Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa in an effort to triage the midterm map.

By Shane Goldmacher

Shane Goldmacher is a national political correspondent covering the midterm elections.

Top Republican super PACs aligned with President Trump and congressional Republican leadership are cutting off financial support for two Republican House members seeking re-election, according to three people with direct knowledge of the plans.

The decision represents the first instance this cycle of national Republican groups abandoning incumbents as the party scrambles to prevent more widespread losses in the midterm elections.

Officials with the two super PACs decided to cancel all remaining advertising booked for Representative Thomas H. Kean Jr. of New Jersey and Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa over the weekend after internal G. O. P. polling had showed their re-election chances dimming.

National Republicans, after withdrawing funds last week from the open Nebraska seat of Representative Don Bacon, who is retiring, have now essentially ceded three House districts the party currently holds.

In 2024, Republicans emerged from the election holding only a three-seat majority in the House. Since then, the party has tried to pad that slim margin through an aggressive redistricting push that reshaped the 2026 map.

The Republican triage efforts also include withdrawing all of the remaining funds that had been reserved for targeting two Democrats running for re-election, Representatives Greg Landsman of Ohio and Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan, according to the three people with direct knowledge. One of the people said other seats were under active consideration to be abandoned as soon as this week.

All told, the super PAC aligned with Speaker Mike Johnson, the Congressional Leadership Fund, is redirecting $10 million from the seats it is effectively ceding in Iowa, Michigan, New Jersey and Ohio and spreading it across 16 new districts, two of the people said.

“For two years, we’ve built the resources and infrastructure that allow us to maneuver in a difficult environment,” Chris Winkelman, the president of the Congressional Leadership Fund, said in a statement. “These moves keep the pressure on the most vulnerable Democrats and preserve a path to 218 seats.”

It was unclear how much money was being redirected from the constellation of super PACs aligned with Mr. Trump. Those groups have reserved more than $6 million in the districts in Iowa, New Jersey and Ohio, according to AdImpact, the ad-tracking service.

The new money from C. L. F. is being redirected to shore up a number of incumbent Republicans, including some whom the group has not previously spent money on this year.

Two of those notable Republicans include Representative Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, who represents a swing district in the Philadelphia suburbs that President Trump lost in 2024, and Representative Monica De La Cruz of Texas, who holds a seat that Mr. Trump carried by 18 points in 2024.

Other Republicans set to receive new support from C. L. F. include Representative Bryan Steil of Wisconsin, Representative Rob Wittman of Virginia and Representative Bill Huizenga of Michigan.

C. L. F. officials declined to disclose how much would be spent in the new seats in which it was investing.

Mr. Kean, whose father was once governor of New Jersey, had vanished from Congress for months earlier this year with almost no explanation, only later revealing he had been hospitalized to treat depression. He is facing a top Democratic recruit, Rebecca Bennett, a former Navy helicopter pilot.

The leadership fund has spent more than $2 million against Ms. Bennett in October alone, federal records show.

Ms. Miller-Meeks of Iowa has won two of the closest House races in the country in recent years, including a remarkable six-vote margin in 2020. Both parties have already spent more than $36 million on the race, according to AdImpact, with $5 million coming from the Congressional Leadership Fund, according to federal records. An affiliated nonprofit group spent $4 million on more ads.

Iowa is home to three competitive House races. At least some of the funds cut are expected to go to other races in the state.

The decision to give up on challenging Ms. McDonald Rivet, a Michigan Democrat, was not a huge surprise. The district had been among just a few nationwide that voted for both a Democratic representative and Mr. Trump in 2024, and though Republicans had been targeting it this cycle, they did not field a candidate likely to challenge her: Tom Smith, who won the primary, defeated Mr. Trump’s preferred candidate despite suspending his campaign.

The fund still spent $2 million on the race across September and October before giving up on Mr. Smith.

Officials with C. L. F. said they were also adding money to races in California’s 22nd District, Colorado’s Eighth, Maine’s Second, Michigan’s Seventh and 10th, New Mexico’s Second, North Carolina’s First, Virginia’s Second, Florida’s 22nd and South Carolina’s First.

Shane Goldmacher is a Times national political correspondent.

OpenAI and Anthropic Tell British Lawmakers: Regulate Us

Wired October 13, 2026

Representatives for OpenAI and Anthropic told a British parliamentary hearing that voluntary pledges were no longer enough to ensure safety and that new laws should be introduced, deepening a public schism with Google DeepMind and Meta, both of which declined to back new legislation.

The Business, Innovation, Science, and Trade Committee, comprising a cross-party panel of MPs, held an evidence session on Tuesday with appearances from four frontier AI firms, four former staff of the firms turned whistleblowers and senior British civil servants.

“The rules should be binding,” Anthropic’s head of Europe Liam Booth-Smith told the committee, when asked if the company’s view was that AI safety now needs a statutory framework. The company, he said, has “consistently believed that there should be binding rules on companies and that voluntary commitments are not enough.”

OpenAI vice president Tom Duff Gordon was more cautious but still supportive, backing a statutory framework and an international convention. Duff Gordon said “there should be some elements that should be mandatory,” starting with incident reporting. “We don’t think basing everything on voluntary commitments for frontier risk is a good long-term plan,” he said.

However, their rivals would not follow. Asked directly whether he supported a statutory framework, Google DeepMind’s Owen Larter said: “Focus on the standards is what we would be doing.” Meta’s Rob Sherman pointed to Britain’s existing regulators, telling MPs they were “not writing on a blank page.”

The hearing exposed an existing divide on the subject of regulation, putting the conflicting approaches of AI leaders on the British parliamentary record. Exposing this divide in a second jurisdiction was the point, according to select committee chair Liam Byrne. The committee set out “to light up the wide differences in opinions between some of the wealthiest firms on Earth,” he told WIRED after the hearing, and to show “that you couldn’t rely on voluntary self-regulation.”

While the four executives gave evidence to the committee on AI safety, only a few hundred meters away, Britain’s security service director issued a warning about the dangers of AI.

MI5 director Ken McCallum used his annual threat update to warn of bioweapon misuse as a significant threat from AI. “Not yet realized, but the misuse case to which I’d attach greatest weight, is AI’s potential to change the stakes on existing or even new bioweapons,” McCallum said.

Responding to this comment, Byrne told WIRED: “The fact that the head of MI5 is warning about incredibly dangerous capability uplifts for bioterrorists in one part of Whitehall, and then in another part of Whitehall the permanent secretary of the Cabinet Office is basically admitting that our regulatory regime for AI is voluntary, tells you everything you need to know.”

In the final part of the evidence session, civil servants conceded to the committee how little the current system compels. Britain’s AI Security Institute (AISI) tests frontier models before release, but only when companies choose to hand them over.

Henry de Zoete, director of AISI, acknowledged that the institute was entirely reliant on the cooperation of the companies and foreign governments in order to gain access. Cat Little, the top civil servant at the Cabinet Office, which houses AISI, was pressed on whether the whole regime was voluntary. “At the moment, yes, it is,” she said.

When asked what would happen if AISI judged a model to be too dangerous, but it was released by a company anyway, de Zoete acknowledged AISI had no ability to prevent them from doing so.

“What we’re not doing is kite marking,” de Zoete said, using the British term for a safety certification. “We’re not saying yes or no to any sort of model.” He added: “These companies are either American or Chinese who are building at the frontier … There’s only so much we, as the UK, can do in that kind of context.”

The frontier executives also made plain that British access runs through Washington. “We provide our models predeployment to CAISI,” OpenAI’s Duff Gordon said, referring to AISI’s US counterpart. “We will continue to provide our models pre-deployment to AISI in the UK … and as long as we’re able to do that under the US government, we will continue to do it.”

The tension of the existing arrangement was made clear to British officials by Anthropic’s Booth-Smith. “We unfortunately were not able to provide full unrestricted access to [Mythos 5.1] to UK AISI at that time ... That’s a question for the US government,” he said before adding that AISI now had access.

The session also heard from four former lab researchers, among them ex-OpenAI staffer Daniel Kokotajlo. “I don’t think the companies can be trusted to self-regulate,” he told MPs. Steven Adler, who left OpenAI in late 2024, said he was “not confident in the safety culture across the industry.” Geoffrey Irving said the labs believe they are locked in a race that governments will not interrupt and that they cannot leave. “Both of those are false,” he said. “They could just stop.”

Following the hearing Byrne told WIRED that his committee would now dedicate a lot of time examining the UK’s path forward as a middle power on AI. He wants ministers to use Britain’s coming G20 presidency, alongside South Korea, which follows it in the chair, to broker an international convention that does not depend on the current White House. “The G20 presidency will outlive the US presidency of Trump,” he said.

“The risks,” he added, “are multiplying faster than our safety regime can control.”

The 9 Best Movies to Stream This Month

Wired October 13, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

October has rolled around, and that means only one thing: Spooky season is here! And what better way to celebrate Halloween than with some of the finest fright fests of the last 50 years?

We’re bringing you a more retro-tinged selection of the best films on streaming this month, but the mix of crowd-pleasers and cult classics offers something for horror fans of all tastes. For instance, David Cronenberg’s grotesque revamp of The Fly, buzzing onto Hulu, and Ken Russell’s Altered States materializing on The Criterion Channel, both bring uniquely visceral takes on body horror to your screens, while sleeper hit Under the Skin on Netflix offers slow-burn sci-fi scares, and Midsommar on Prime Video takes to the hills for a sun-drenched approach to folk horror.

If you fancy something a bit newer, fear not. Well, fear lots actually—Zach Cregger’s shockingly original horror debut Barbarian smashes its way onto Hulu, while Netflix brings the final chapter in the sumptuously scary Mononoke trilogy, an anime extravaganza that looks like nothing else. Plus, there’s even one post-credits stinger of an entry that’s too scary to mention here …

Here are WIRED’s picks of the best movies to watch right now.

When Tess (Georgina Campbell) finds her Airbnb in a sketchy neighborhood double booked with Keith (Bill Skarsgård), you’ll probably think you know where Barbarian is headed. You don't—and you should brace yourself for everything that follows. Written and directed by Zach Cregger (in a seismic departure from his early comedy background), Barbarian constantly flips the script, regularly subverting viewer expectations of horror movie clichés at every turn.

Smartly written, brilliantly shot, and psychologically disturbing on multiple levels, Barbarian is a genuinely terrifying entry in the modern horror canon. If you’ve discovered Cregger’s work from the Academy Award–winning Weapons or his recent horror-comedy reboot of Resident Evil, this is where he first made his mark on the silver screen.

Under the Skin almost defies explanation. Scarlett Johansson plays an alien in human form, roaming Glasgow and the Scottish Highlands, luring isolated and lonely men to their doom, drowning them in an inexplicable oily abyss that seems to exist in a null space. All the while, she’s observed by a motorcyclist, trailing her from victim to victim.

No names are given, no purpose explained (not even to the cast; director Jonathan Glazer shot many of the alien’s initial encounters with humans using hidden cameras, only explaining and asking for their involvement afterward), but it’s far better to watch this blind and make your own mind up. Be warned, though—Johansson’s performance is truly unearthly, and in conjunction with Glazer’s bizarre imagery and a soundscape that maddeningly claws at your nerves, this is a deeply unsettling slice of sci-fi.

This acclaimed indie horror movie stars Florence Pugh as Dani, an American student struggling to deal with a family tragedy, who joins her boyfriend Christian (Jack Reynor) and his friends on a trip to Sweden. The vacation sounds like the perfect escape—nine days of communing with nature at a festival held only once every 90 years; a true once-in-a-lifetime experience. The problem? The festival is a front for a pagan cult, and things get rapidly, wildly out of hand.

Midsommar is a deeply effective and distressing folk horror film, with none other than Jordan Peele, director of the smash hit Get Out, declaring it has "the most atrociously disturbing imagery I've ever seen on film." Perfect date night material for Halloween season, then.

South Korean cinema seems to love combining the end of the world and trains. Bong Joon Ho’s Snowpiercer got things on track in 2013, but director Yeon Sang-ho really left the station with this 2016 zombie horror masterpiece.

Seok-woo (Gong Yoo) starts his journey on the express train from Seoul to Busan just wanting to drop daughter Su-an off with her mother. Unfortunately, the last passenger to board might be a teensy bit infected with the zombie plague that’s kicking off outside, turning the ride into the express train to hell. The tight confines allow for some incredibly inventive action choreography, while genre fans are treated to a revolting twist on the undead themselves, a misshapen, juddering, ravenous horde that moves like a liquid mass of corpses.

Like all the best zombie films, though, it’s the social commentary that really elevates Train to Busan, with its exploration of class and status standing alongside Romero’s work at his peak. A decade on from release, this is still one of the freshest takes on zombies you’re likely to find—look up animated prequel Seoul Station and stand-alone sequel Peninsula if it leaves you wanting another bite.

A bit of a deep cut, but director Ken Russell’s 1980 outing will really mess with your head. No, really—this tale of psychological horror and transformational terror is loosely based on real-world tests of the effects of psychoactive drugs and sensory deprivation on the human brain. The film sees researcher Eddie Jessup (William Hurt) subjecting himself to highly questionable experiments with hallucinogenics and isolation in an effort to tap into other states of being. Unfortunately, he’s wildly successful, not only opening his mind to genetic memories and shared consciousnesses, but seeing his physical body horrifyingly warp and devolve beyond recognition with each trip.

And what a trip—Russell masterfully creates a sense of psychedelic overload with a pioneering use of bizarre imagery and sound, the film shifting with each of Jessup’s transformations until you feel you’ve taken mind-altering substances yourself. An uncomfortably weird experience, Altered States will stay on your mind long after the credits roll.

Anne Hathaway is literally a monster—at least she is in this darkly comedic crossover between kaiju flick and character study. After her life in New York falls apart, Gloria (Hathaway) moves back home to New Hampshire. At the same time, a giant monster starts rampaging across Seoul, destroying buildings and causing mass panic. Yet these two incompatible events aren't unrelated, as Gloria starts to realize that she can somehow control the beast from half a world away—but her heavy drinking and constant bad decisions may get in the way of saving the world. Director Nacho Vigalondo lovingly pastiches the likes of Godzilla, Gamera, and King Kong in this quirky film festival favorite.

A nameless Medicine Seller (Hiroshi Kamiya in Japanese, Crispin Freeman in English) traveling Edo period Japan may seem a humble figure, but his strange tinctures and concoctions make him one of the few capable of tackling mononoke—powerful spirits corrupting places and people alike. This trilogy-capping third movie takes the enigmatic traveler back to the cursed Imperial Palace visited in predecessors Phantom in the Rain and Ashes of Rage, seeking to uncover once and for all why it seems to attract so many dangerous monsters.

A master class in tension and otherworldly horror, Mononoke maintains its stunning visual approach of kaleidoscopic watercolors swirling on parchment, making for one of the most sumptuous and visually striking pieces of animation you’ll ever see. It’s worth noting that there is some real-world controversy over a returning voice actor embroiled in a scandal in Japan, so this might be a rare case where the English dub is the better option.

Despite being a remake, David Cronenberg’s quintessential slice of 1980s body horror has almost completely supplanted the 1958 original in the public consciousness (although the original stars Vincent Price and is definitely still worth checking out on Prime Video).

This wholesale reimagining twists expectations away from mad science clichés—it almost feels like a superhero origin movie to start, with scientist Seth Brundle (Jeff Goldblum) accidentally splicing his genes with a fly during a teleportation experiment, and emerging with enhanced physical prowess in every respect. But with great power comes great personality shifts, wiry black hairs growing along his back, and the need to vomit acid onto his food before eating. And, as animal instincts take over, the self-proclaimed “Brundlefly” starts looking at science reporter Ronnie Quaife (Geena Davis) very differently.

The groundbreaking effects work that marked Brundle’s slow metamorphosis into a repulsive hybrid monster won the film the Oscar for Best Makeup, but its ability to pack in some genuine emotion alongside the scares make it easy to see why this is the de facto iteration of The Fly.

Oh, you think this isn’t horror? Ask yourself: What could possibly be scarier than the deleterious impact social media has had on the human condition? Director David Fincher and writer Aaron Sorkin’s biopic telling of the rise, and rise, and rise of Facebook, is the kind of film you watch through your fingers, too.

There’s an almost predatory hunger in Jesse Eisenberg’s Mark Zuckerberg, as he goes from a Harvard student whose hotness-ranking website was popular enough to crash the college’s whole network to a Silicon Valley darling attracting unheard-of sums of investment and power. Like most “based on a true story” horror films, it’s not entirely historically accurate and, true to genre norms, there’s a not-as-good sequel, with Sorkin returning to write and direct the newly released The Social Reckoning, but if you’ve been paying attention to reality the past few decades, this will definitely chill you to the bone.

Godzilla Minus Zero’s Filmmakers Terrified Bystanders With Their Monster Sounds

Wired October 13, 2026

Actor Seth Green—yes, that one—has seen Godzilla Minus Zero and says it’s awesome.

While introducing the New York Comic Con panel for the 39th film in the Godzilla franchise, Green stressed that the filmmakers behind the movie “have created kaiju that feel physically real and, trust me, emotionally terrifying.”

While a lot of that terror came from the work of Oscar-winning visual effects artist Tatsuji Nojima, some it came from the shrieking of Godzilla and his three-headed nemesis, King Ghidorah. Those roars were the work of sound designer Natsuko Inoue and her team, who created the monsters’ outsize vocalizations by rolling speakers to the top of an outdoor dam—much to the horror of people nearby.

“There were people having a picnic, maybe people just taking a stroll,” Hisafumi Takeuchi, who also worked on sound for the film, said during the panel. “The person walking their dog, though—they had the worst time, because the dog was freaking out and barking back at us.”

Since the creatures are imaginary, getting their screams to sound realistic is essential to making them seem believable—and genuinely scary—onscreen. At first, Inoue wasn’t sure if the idea of recording at the dam would work. Those fears were quickly put to rest.

“The first time we sent that roar out on the speakers, I could see the relief and confidence in everyone's eyes,” Inoue said. “By using speakers and projecting it into the real world, capturing the reverb, the echo, the reflection of the sound back with the mic, it manifests it in our world.”

For other kaiju sound effects, Inoue’s team took an analog foley approach. To simulate Ghidorah’s dragon-like wings, for example, they flapped a rubber fisherman’s suit and mixed that noise with the sounds of an accordion-like air duct.

Getting two of Toho’s most famous monsters right was a huge undertaking, especially after the success of Zero’s predecessor, Godzilla Minus One, which brought home $114 million worldwide at the box office. Following that 2023 film’s harrowing mix of post–World War II malaise and bracing kaiju destruction will be tough, but a new trailer shown during the film’s panel at NYCC promised a sequel full of aerial dogfights and a punch-’em-up for the ages between Godzilla and Ghidorah.

Like the previous film, Godzilla Minus Zero is directed by Takashi Yamazaki and features visual effects from Tatsuji Nojima, whom Green called “the first Gen Z Oscar-winner” for his work on One.

Nojima began doing visual effects as a hobby while he was still a teenager before joining animation house Shirogumi as a compositor. After Yamazaki noticed a crude animation of waves that Nojima was working on, the director tasked the budding animator with developing the idea. Nojima turned around a fully rendered shot of ocean water over rocks that looked indistinguishable from reality. After that, Nojima recalled, Yamazaki said, “OK, I think you’re ready to animate and do VFX for Godzilla now.”

During the panel, Nojima broke down how he created a shot from the trailer showing Godzilla bursting out of the ocean while chasing a seaplane. “I simulated 200 million particles to get the whitewater effect correct in Godzilla Minus One,” he said. “With this shot in Godzilla Minus Zero, the scale is absolutely different with the new Imax aspect ratio, plus there was no live-action plate, so we're dealing with a lot of CG on screen. We required 2 billion particles.”

Godzilla Minus Zero is set to hit US theaters on November 6 and Japanese theaters on November 3, which has become known as Godzilla’s birthday since it marks the date in 1954 that Ishirō Honda’s original film was released in Japan.
